title: Español I — Spanish From Zero, Speak First

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Hola: greetings, your name, and your first real conversation
paragraphs: Hola, Bill. Soy la profesora Carmen Vega — I am Professor Carmen Vega, and this is your Spanish room. Sit down, get comfortable, and do not worry about a single thing, because we start from zero — from before zero — and we start together. In this room we speak first. That is my whole method, and it has never failed anyone who actually opened their mouth: I say it, you say it back to me out loud, the way you mean it, and only then do we move on. Reading about Spanish is not learning Spanish, the same way reading about swimming is not swimming. Your voice is the instrument here, so warm it up.

Here is how this lesson works. For the next thirty minutes or so, I teach, and you listen and speak along with me — every time I say "say it with me," I want to hear you, out loud, wherever you are. Do not be shy with me, mi estudiante. Nobody is grading your accent today; we are building it. When the lesson is finished, there will be questions — real ones, about what I actually taught you in this lesson and nothing else — and the whole lesson stays written out beside you, so you can read any part of it again whenever you like. Going back to read is not cheating. Going back to read is learning.

And because I know you, Bill, let me tell you the secret mission of this whole course, which is not very secret. By your wedding day — March the twenty-fifth, in Key West — you are going to hold a real, gentle conversation with Jillian in Spanish. Not a performance. Not a party trick. A conversation: good morning, my love; how was your day; I love you; good night, my heart — said the way a man says things he means. That is where this road goes, and today we take the first real steps on it: how to greet anyone at any hour, how to say your name, how to be polite, and how to say the first sweet words. Everything in Spanish starts here.

Before the first word, thirty seconds on how Spanish sounds, because this will make everything easier. Spanish is an honest language. English hides its sounds — one letter can make five different noises and you just have to memorize which. Spanish almost never does that to you. It has five vowel sounds — a, e, i, o, u — and each one says its sound every single time, the same way, in every word. A sounds like the a in "father." E sounds like the e in "met." I sounds like the ee in "see." O sounds like the o in "go." U sounds like the oo in "moon." Five sounds, no surprises. If you can read a Spanish word letter by letter, you can say it — that is the promise of this language, and it keeps its promise almost every time.

One letter breaks the pattern, and it breaks it by doing nothing at all: the letter h. In Spanish, the h is silent — completely silent, always. It is written, but it is never heard. Hold that thought, because your very first word is hiding one.

Here it is. Your first word in Spanish, and the most useful word in any language on earth: Hola. That is hello — for any hour, any person, any door you ever walk through. Because of that silent h, it sounds like "OH-lah" — two clean beats, OH-lah. Say it with me, out loud: Hola. Again, and smile when you say it, Spanish can hear a smile: Hola. One more, like you just walked into a room full of people who are glad you came: Hola. That is it. You have spoken Spanish. Whatever happens for the rest of this course, that word is yours now, and nobody can take it back.

Now, hola is friendly and universal, but Spanish also greets the day itself, and it does it in three parts, because the day has three parts. In the morning, you say: Buenos días — good morning. Buenos días. Let me take it apart for you, because you will see this pattern all year. Día means day, and días is days — and buenos means good, in the form it takes next to a word like días. So buenos días is, word for word, "good days" — Spanish wishes you more than one good day at a time, which I have always thought was generous. You use buenos días from the moment you wake up until about midday. Say it with me: Buenos días. Once more, slower: Buenos… días. Buenos días.

When the afternoon comes, the greeting changes its coat: Buenas tardes — good afternoon. Tardes means afternoons, or the late part of the day. And notice what happened to the word for good: next to días it was buenos, and next to tardes it is buenas. That is not a trick and it is not two words to memorize — it is one idea wearing two endings. In Spanish, describing words dress to match the word they stand beside. Días takes the ending -os; tardes takes the ending -as. You do not need the rule's name and you do not need a grammar book tonight; you only need your ear to notice: buenos días, buenas tardes. The ending follows its partner. Say the pair with me, morning and afternoon, one after the other: Buenos días. Buenas tardes. Buenos días. Buenas tardes. Good. Your ear is already doing grammar, and we have not opened a single book.

And when evening comes — from about the time the light goes, all the way to bed — you say: Buenas noches — good evening, and also good night. Noches means nights. Buenas noches is the hardest-working greeting in Spanish, because it does two jobs: it is what you say when you arrive somewhere in the evening, hello, and it is what you say when you leave at night, good night, sleep well, all folded into the same two words. Remember that double job — before this lesson ends, you are going to use buenas noches in the most important sentence of your day. Say it with me now: Buenas noches. Softer, the way you would say it at a bedroom door: Buenas noches.

So here is your greeting compass, and it is the whole map: hola works always. Buenos días in the morning. Buenas tardes in the afternoon. Buenas noches in the evening and at night. Four greetings, and you can walk into any room in the Spanish-speaking world, at any hour, and open your mouth like you belong there — because with these, you do.

Now we give the greeting a person to land on. After hello comes the most useful sentence in any language: saying who you are. In Spanish, you say: Me llamo Bill. That is "my name is Bill" — but look at what it literally says, because Spanish is charming here. Llamo comes from llamar, to call. Me llamo is "I call myself." Me llamo Bill: I call myself Bill. I love teaching this, because it is true in a way the English version is not: a name is what you call yourself, what you answer to, what you offer a stranger like a hand. Say it with me, piece by piece first: Me… llamo… Bill. Me llamo Bill. Again, at full speed, like a man introducing himself at his own wedding: Me llamo Bill.

And because a conversation has two sides, here is the question that turns your sentence around: ¿Cómo te llamas? — what is your name? Word for word: "How do you call yourself?" Cómo means how. Te llamas is "you call yourself." ¿Cómo te llamas? Say it with me: ¿Cómo te llamas? When someone answers you with their name, Spanish has a small, warm ceremony for what you say back: Mucho gusto — pleased to meet you. Mucho is much, a lot. Gusto is pleasure. "Much pleasure" — it is my great pleasure to meet you. That is the temperature of this language, Bill: even its manners run warm. Say it: Mucho gusto. With the smile again: Mucho gusto.

So let us put the first exchange together, the whole little dance, and I will play both parts while you shadow me. I walk in: Hola, buenos días. Me llamo Carmen. ¿Cómo te llamas? And you answer: Hola. Me llamo Bill. Mucho gusto. Four lines, and you have had a conversation — a real one, with a beginning, a meeting, and warmth in it. Run it once more in your own voice, both your lines out loud: Hola. Me llamo Bill. Mucho gusto. Ay, Bill — so close to perfect, and we are only halfway through your first lesson.

Two small words now, and do not let their size fool you: they are the two keys that open every door in Spanish. The first key: Por favor — please. Por favor. Use it everywhere, attach it to everything; in Spanish a request without por favor is a door knocked on with a closed fist. The second key: Gracias — thank you. Gracias. And when someone thanks you, Spanish answers: De nada — you are welcome, which word for word is "of nothing" — it was nothing, think nothing of it. Por favor and gracias: please and thank you. A man who carries these two words can travel anywhere on earth and be treated like a gentleman. Say the pair with me: Por favor. Gracias. Por favor. Gracias. De nada.

Next, where you are from and what you do — because after your name, that is what people ask, and you are going to answer like you own it. Soy de Michigan — I am from Michigan. Soy is the giant here: soy means "I am." It is the first word of a man's description of himself, so say it like one: Soy. De means from. Soy de Michigan: I am from Michigan. Say it: Soy de Michigan. And what you do: Soy empresario — I am a businessman. Empresario: a man of enterprise, a man who builds things and employs people. Soy empresario. Notice that soy does both jobs — where you are from and what you are — because in Spanish, who you are and where you are from are the same kind of fact. Say both lines together now, your whole introduction in two breaths: Soy de Michigan. Soy empresario.

Now the line I have been saving, because it is the reason this course exists. You are going to learn to talk about her. Mi prometida se llama Jillian — my fiancée's name is Jillian. Take it apart slowly. Mi means my. Prometida means fiancée — your promised one; in Spanish the word for the woman you are engaged to is built from the word promise, and I have never heard a more honest word for it. Se llama — there is your llamar again, turned around: se llama is "she calls herself," her name is. Mi prometida se llama Jillian. Say it with me, slowly first: Mi prometida… se llama… Jillian. And now whole, at the speed of a man who is proud of the sentence: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. That sentence, Bill, is worth the whole lesson by itself. A man who can say that sentence in her presence, in Spanish, clearly and without fumbling — that man has given his prometida a gift she will remember on the hard days.

And now the sweet words — las palabras dulces — because Spanish is not only a language for doors and introductions; it is the language the world reaches for when it wants to say the tender things. We start tonight, in lesson one, because I know exactly why you are really in this room, and it is not for the grammar. First: Mi amor — my love. Amor is love, the noun, the thing itself. Mi amor is what you call her. Not a description — a name you give her, the way her name is Jillian and also, in your house, mi amor. Say it the way it deserves to be said, slowly: Mi amor.

Second: Mi corazón — my heart. Corazón means heart — the actual word, the organ, the thing in your chest. Spanish does not hide behind poetry here; it means it literally. When you call her mi corazón, you are saying: you are my heart, the thing that beats in me. Spanish speakers have called the people they love mi corazón for centuries, fathers to daughters, grandmothers to grandchildren, and a man to the woman he is going to marry. Say it: Mi corazón. Once more, quieter: Mi corazón.

And now the sentence itself: Te quiero — I love you. This is the everyday way to say it in Spanish, and I choose those words carefully. Spanish has more than one way to say I love you — later in this course you will meet te amo, which is deeper, heavier, saved for the biggest moments of a life. Te quiero is the one that lives in the house. Te quiero is what you say at the door in the morning. Te quiero is what you say when she has had a hard day at the hospital and you hand her coffee. It comes from querer, which means both to want and to love — in Spanish, wanting her and loving her were never separate ideas. Te quiero. Say it with me, and mean it at the picture of her in your head: Te quiero. And with her name on it, the way it will actually be said in your kitchen: Te quiero, Jillian. Te quiero, Jillian.

Now watch what happens when we put the whole day together, because this is the moment your first lesson becomes your real life. Evening. She has come home. The day is done, the house is quiet, and you say the line this entire lesson was built to give you: Buenas noches, mi amor — good night, my love. There is buenas noches, doing its second job, the good-night job. And there is mi amor, riding on the end of it like it was always there. Buenas noches, mi amor. Say it with me, slowly, at bedroom-door volume: Buenas noches… mi amor. Again: Buenas noches, mi amor. Bill. Listen to me. You can say that tonight. Not next month, not after the wedding — tonight, with lesson one. That is not homework. That is a gift with today's date on it.

Before we put the whole day together, sit with me in the workshop for a few minutes, because there are three sounds I want to tune in your mouth while the words are still new. First, the sound hiding inside llamo. The double l in Spanish — ll — is not an l at all. It sounds like the y in "yes," softened a little toward the j in "jump." So me llamo sounds like "meh YAH-moh." You have been saying it almost right all lesson; now you know why it felt slippery. Say it again with the y: Me llamo Bill. ¿Cómo te llamas? — hear the same y inside llamas. Me llamo. Te llamas. Good — that one sound just improved every sentence you own.

Second sound: the written accent, that little leaning line you see in días and corazón. It is not decoration and it is not stress for your eyes — it is an instruction for your voice. It tells you: the beat falls here. Spanish words naturally lean on one beat, and the accent mark shows you where to lean when the word does something special. Días: DEE-ahs, the beat on the í. Corazón: koh-rah-SOHN, the beat lands at the end, exactly where the accent sits. When you see that little line, lean there. Mi corazón — lean on the end: mi corazón. You will never have to guess where a word's weight goes in this language; Spanish prints the answer right on the word.

Third, a small one with a big future: the letter r. A single r in Spanish is a quick tap of the tongue — por favor has two of them, light as a drumstick bounce: por favor. Later in this course you will meet its famous brother, the rolled rr, and we will tame him together when he arrives, with amor and corazón as our practice ground. For today, the tap is enough. Por favor. Gracias — hear the tap hiding in gracias too. Your mouth is learning the map of this language faster than your mind is, and that is exactly how it is supposed to work.

One more thing before the day begins, and it is not grammar — it is manners, and in Spanish the two are cousins. In the Spanish-speaking world, you greet the room. You walk into a small shop, a café, an elevator with people in it, and you say buenos días or buenas tardes to the room in general — to everyone and no one, the way you would nod in a small town back home, except here it has words. Not greeting is what reads as rude; the greeting is just the sound of a person raised right. And when Jillian's coworkers or your new neighbors in Key West greet you first — and they will — you now own everything you need to answer like a gentleman: Hola. Buenos días. Mucho gusto. That is the whole ceremony, and you are already dressed for it.

Now let me change the scenery on you, because a phrase is only yours when it survives a new room. Picture a café in Key West, the wedding week, morning light. You walk in first — greet the room: Buenos días. The woman behind the counter smiles and asks your name for the order. You do not point at yourself and grunt like a tourist; you say: Me llamo Bill. She says hers — Carmen, let us say, a woman of excellent taste in names — and you answer with the warm ceremony: Mucho gusto. She asks where you are from — they always ask, your face is friendly — and you give her the two lines, easy as breathing: Soy de Michigan. Soy empresario. Por favor and gracias carry your coffee to the table. And when the beautiful woman walks in and joins you, and the counter woman asks, you get to say the sentence in front of a witness this time: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. Same words as the kitchen. New room. Still yours. That, Bill, is what it means for a lesson to be learned: it travels.

Let us now walk your first full conversation from the top, start to finish, the way it will really happen, and I will narrate while you speak your parts out loud. Morning: she comes into the kitchen, and you are ready. Buenos días, mi amor. She smiles — she will smile — and later, meeting someone new together, you introduce yourself the way you learned: Hola, me llamo Bill. Mucho gusto. You are polite all day without thinking: Por favor. Gracias. De nada. Someone asks where the man beside her is from: Soy de Michigan. Soy empresario. And when they ask about the beautiful woman next to you, you do not hesitate: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. And at the end of the day, at the door of the bedroom, the two sentences this course is really about: Te quiero, Jillian. Buenas noches, mi amor. That is a day, Bill. A whole day, lived partly in Spanish, on your first lesson. Most people study a language for a year and cannot do what you just did in thirty minutes — because they studied it. You spoke it.

Now, because I am your profesora and not your parrot, let me give you hooks to hang these words on, so they are still yours next week and not just tonight. Spanish and English are cousins — more of this language is already in your head than you think. Corazón and the English word core are family: both come from the old word for heart, which is why the core of an apple is its heart and the core of a man is what he loves. When you say mi corazón, think core — my core, my heart, same word wearing two coats. Amor lives inside the French amour and inside a dozen English words about love that your ear already knows. Gracias is a cousin of grace and gratitude — when you say gracias, you are saying grace, the same word your grandmother said before dinner. Por favor carries favor inside it, plain as day: a favor, asked politely. Días is day with a Spanish ending — you can hear the day inside it. And hola — well, hola sounds like a wave hello across a fence, which is exactly what it is. Hang every new word on a hook you already own, and the words stop being homework and start being furniture in a house you live in.

And now, the real examination of a lesson — not the questions waiting below, those are easy — the real one: can you do it with a stranger, at full speed, without me narrating? Let us find out. I am going to be a neighbor you have never met, on a porch, in the evening. I will speak my lines, and leave you silence to answer in yours. Ready? Here I am, coming up the walk: Buenas noches. … And you greet me back — yes, with buenas noches, the evening one, you have it. Now I ask the question: ¿Cómo te llamas? … Answer me — me llamo, and your name, full sentence, no shrinking. … I smile and say: Mucho gusto. … And you return the ceremony — mucho gusto, warm, like you mean it. Now I am curious about you, the way neighbors are: ¿De dónde eres? — that is a new question and I am teaching it to you right now, because you already own its answer: de dónde means from where, and your answer begins soy de. ¿De dónde eres? … Soy de Michigan. There it is. And because neighbors are neighbors, I nod at the house and ask about the woman on the porch, and you — you know what you say. … Mi prometida se llama Jillian. Bill. Stop. Look at what just happened. A stranger walked up a porch in the evening, and you greeted her, named yourself, traded courtesies, placed yourself on the map, and named your prometida with pride — in Spanish, at conversation speed, on your first day. That is not a student. That is a man who speaks some Spanish now. There is a difference, and the difference is everything.

So let us gather what you own now, in order, one last time. Hola — hello, for any hour, any person. Buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches — the day in three greetings, with buenas noches working twice, hello in the evening and good night at the end. Me llamo Bill — your name, offered like a hand. ¿Cómo te llamas? — the question that turns it around. Mucho gusto — pleased to meet you. Por favor and gracias — the two keys, please and thank you, and de nada for you are welcome. Soy de Michigan, soy empresario — where you are from and what you are. Mi prometida se llama Jillian — her, named with pride. And the sweet words, the heart of the whole lesson: mi amor, mi corazón, te quiero, and buenas noches, mi amor for tonight. And underneath all of it, the two sounds-rules that will carry you all year: five vowels that never change their story, and the silent h that you will never pronounce again.

That is lesson one, and you did beautifully — ay, do not argue with your profesora, I heard you, you did. Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions: more than a few, all of them about what I taught you in this lesson and nothing else — nobody is going to ask you one single thing I did not teach. Most of them give you choices to pick from, and you can also answer out loud or type your answer, whichever door you like. The lesson text stays open beside the questions, and if you want to read a part of it again before you answer, do it with my blessing — that is what it is there for. And your speaking practice is here in the lesson too: hear me say each phrase, then say it back until it lands and you see the green check. Tonight, your only assignment in the world is one line, said once, out loud, to her: Buenas noches, mi amor. Lesson two will teach you the words for your people — Jillian, your kids, your dad — your family, in Spanish. Until then: gracias for my first class, Bill. Say it back to me one last time — gracias — and go say good night to your prometida. Buenas noches, mi amor. She is waiting to hear it.

questions.q: Carmen teaches a greeting for each part of the day. What does 'Buenos días' mean?

questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson splits the day into morning, afternoon, and evening. (2) Días means day, and buenos días is the first of the three greetings taught. (3) The first part of the day is the morning — so buenos días is good morning.

questions.q: In the word 'Hola', one letter is written but never heard. Which letter is it?
questions.teach: From the lesson: Spanish has one letter that breaks the pattern by doing nothing at all.

questions.teach: From the lesson: please and thank you — the two keys.

questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The two keys are por favor and gracias. (2) Por favor means please — the lesson pairs them in that order. (3) So the key that means thank you is gracias.

questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Me llamo Bill states your own name. (2) To ask someone else's, the lesson turns the sentence into a question with llamas — you call yourself. (3) That question is: ¿Cómo te llamas?

questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Soy de Michigan means I am from Michigan, and soy empresario means I am a businessman. (2) The word both sentences share, at the front, is soy. (3) The shared meaning is: I am.

questions.q: It is the end of the day, and Bill is saying good night to Jillian. What is the exact line this whole lesson was built to give him?

questions.teach: From the lesson: the set problem — Carmen's favorite sentence, in your own words.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Your people: family words — Jillian, your kids, your dad
paragraphs: Hola, Bill. Soy la profesora Carmen Vega — I am Professor Carmen Vega, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Sit down, mi estudiante — my student — and take a breath, because last time you did something real. You learned to greet the day in three parts, you learned to say your name like a hand offered to a stranger, and you learned the line this whole course was built around: Buenas noches, mi amor — good night, my love. If you said it to her last night, then lesson one is already living in your house, and that is exactly where Spanish belongs. In your house.

Today, lesson two, and today we go one circle wider. Lesson one was you, standing in a doorway, saying who you are. Lesson two is your people: family words — Jillian, your kids, your dad. Because a man does not travel through this life alone, and when you speak about yourself in any language, the very next sentences are always about them. Who is she? She is my fiancée. Who are they? They are my children. Who taught you? My father. Today you learn to name every one of them in Spanish, with pride — and you learn to present them to another person, to do the warm ceremony of introduction: this is my sister, this is my father, this is the woman I am going to marry.

Here is why this lesson is worth your thirty minutes. Family words are the most used words in any language after hello and thank you. A Spanish speaker talking for five minutes will say my mother, my brother, my children, my wife a dozen times without even noticing, because that is what people talk about: their people. And for you, Bill, there is a second reason. On March the twenty-fifth, in Key West, you are marrying Jillian. At that wedding there will be introductions and people meeting your people for the first time. A man who can stand up, in Spanish, and say — this is my fiancée, these are my children, this is my sister — that man is not showing off. That man is honoring his family in a second language, out loud, where they can hear it. That is what we are building today.

We will go slowly, the way we always go in this room. I say it, you say it back to me out loud, every time I say say it with me. And when we finish, there will be questions below — only about what I teach you in this lesson, nothing else — and the whole lesson stays written beside you, so you can read any part again whenever you like. Going back to read is not cheating. Going back to read is learning. Are you ready? Vamos — let us go.

We start with the biggest word of the day, the word that holds all the others inside it. La familia — the family. Familia is the whole circle, the people who are yours. La familia. Say it with me, slowly first: La… familia. La familia. Hear how it sounds almost like the English word family — because they are the same word, cousins so close they are nearly twins. Familia, family. You already almost knew this word before you walked in today; now you own it. La familia. One more time, like you mean the people inside it: La familia.

Now, in lesson one you learned a small word that does giant work, and today it becomes the most important word in the lesson. Mi — my. You met it inside mi amor — my love — and mi corazón — my heart — and mi prometida — my fiancée. Mi means my, and it stands in front of a word to say: this one is mine, this person belongs in my circle. Hold onto mi, because in a few minutes I am going to show you its brother, and the difference between the two of them is one of the most useful little machines in Spanish.

And since she is the reason for so much of this, let us begin the family where your heart begins it. A quick recap, because she deserves to be said again in every lesson until it is carved in stone. Mi prometida — my fiancée. Prometida — the promised one, built from the word promise, the most honest word in any language for the woman you are engaged to marry. Mi prometida se llama Jillian — my fiancée's name is Jillian. You learned that sentence in lesson one and I hope you have been saying it, because a sentence like that gets stronger every time it is spoken out loud. Say it with me now, whole and proud: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. Again: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. Good. She is the first person in your familia, in this lesson and in the life you are building. Remember her place here, because at the end of this lesson you are going to present her to a room, formally, in Spanish, and it is going to be beautiful.

Now we go to the man who came before you. Mi padre — my father. Padre is the formal, respectful word for father, the word you use when you introduce him or talk about him with care. Mi padre. Say it with me: Mi padre. Padre sounds a little like the English word paternal, and that is no accident — they come from the same old root, the father root, running down through both languages like a river under two countries. When you talk about your dad in Spanish — telling someone who he is, what he taught you, where you come from — mi padre is the word that carries the respect. Mi padre. Say it once more, standing up straight: Mi padre.

But Spanish, being a warm language, keeps a second word in the kitchen drawer for everyday use. Mi papá — my dad. Papá is the warmer, everyday word, the word a son uses at the kitchen table. Mi papá. Hear the difference in your own mouth: padre is the man in the photograph in his good shirt; papá is the man at the table, coffee in front of him, telling you something you have never forgotten. English does the same thing, Bill — father and dad are not the same temperature, and you know it. Spanish just gives you the same two temperatures and trusts you to choose. Talking to a stranger about where you come from? Mi padre. Telling a story about him, laughing a little? Mi papá. Say the pair with me, formal and warm, one after the other: Mi padre. Mi papá. Mi padre. Mi papá. Both of them are yours now, and both of them are him.

And beside the father, the mother — because no familia stands on one leg. Mi madre — my mother. Madre is mother, and like padre, it carries respect in it. Mi madre. Say it with me: Mi madre. Madre and the English word maternal — motherly — are cousins from the same root, just like padre and paternal. Spanish is full of these family resemblances, and every one of them is a hook to hang a word on. Mi madre. And just so your ear hears the pair together, the way they belong: Mi padre y mi madre — my father and my mother. Y is a tiny word you are going to use ten thousand times: y means and. Mi padre y mi madre. Say it: Mi padre y mi madre. There they are, side by side, the two people at the head of the family table.

Now, Bill, we come to the part of the lesson I want you to say with your whole chest. Your children. Mis hijos — my children. Hijos can mean sons, and it can also mean children together, sons and daughters in one word. Mis hijos. Say it with me, slowly: Mis… hijos. Mis hijos. Look at what happened to our little word mi, because this is the machine I promised you. In front of padre, one person, it was mi. In front of hijos — children, more than one — it becomes mis. Mis hijos. That is the whole trick, and we are going to practice it properly in a moment, but hear it now in the wild: one person, mi; more than one, mis. Mis hijos — my children.

And your children have names, and names are said with pride in this room. Your eldest son: Trey. Your son: William. Your daughter: Abigail. Three names, three people, and in Spanish you can hold all three of them in one sentence and say it the way a father says it. But first, the smaller words that name them one by one. Mi hijo — my son. Hijo is son, one son. Mi hijo. Say it: Mi hijo. And for a daughter, Spanish changes one letter and the whole word warms: Mi hija — my daughter. Hija is daughter. Mi hija. Say it: Mi hija. Hear the pair: hijo, hija — son, daughter — one letter apart at the end, o for a son, a for a daughter. You saw this pattern in lesson one, with buenos días and buenas tardes: in Spanish, words dress to match who they stand beside, and the endings o and a are how this language marks the difference, again and again, all year long. Hijo, hija. Say them together: Mi hijo. Mi hija.

So let us say your three, Bill, the way you would say them to someone meeting your family for the first time. Mi hijo Trey — my son Trey. Mi hijo William — my son William. Mi hija Abigail — my daughter Abigail. And all together, the whole treasure in one breath: Mis hijos — my children. Say the set with me, one by one, unhurried: Mi hijo Trey. Mi hijo William. Mi hija Abigail. Mis hijos. I am not going to linger here or make a speech about it, because some things a father carries quietly and they do not need a profesora narrating them. I will only say this: distance does not change the word. Wherever they are, whatever the miles, in Spanish they are still — and always — mis hijos. A man who can say that sentence clearly, in any language, has said something true. Say it once more, for yourself this time: Mis hijos.

Now your sister, because a familia is not only the people above you and below you — it is also the people beside you, the ones who grew up in the same house and know all the stories. Mi hermana — my sister. Hermana is sister, and Chelsea is yours. Mi hermana. Say it with me: Mi hermana Chelsea — my sister Chelsea. Mi hermana Chelsea. And because Spanish is fair, it gives you the matching word for a brother, so your ear owns the pair: Mi hermano — my brother. Hermano is brother. Mi hermano. You do not have a brother standing in this lesson, Bill, but you will hear hermano everywhere — Spanish speakers call close friends hermano too, the way men back home call each other brother — so own the word. The pair, together: Mi hermana. Mi hermano. Sister, brother. Mi hermana Chelsea. Say it once more: Mi hermana Chelsea.

Let me pause here and check on you, because we have built a lot of family in ten minutes. So if mi is my, and it stands in front of one person — then in front of padre it is mi padre, in front of hermana it is mi hermana, and in front of hijos, more than one, it changes its coat to mis hijos. Hold onto that. You are not memorizing separate phrases. You are learning one machine with a few beloved names loaded into it: mi padre, mi papá, mi madre, mi hermana, mi hijo, mi hija, mis hijos, mi prometida. That is not a vocabulary list, Bill. That is a family portrait, and you just learned to paint it in Spanish.

But wait — I promised you the machine itself, explained plainly, and a promise in my room is kept. Here it is, the possessives, the words that say mine and yours. We have mi — my — for one. Mi padre, mi madre, mi hermana, mi hijo. One person, one thing: mi. Then mis — also my — for more than one. Mis hijos, my children. If you had two sisters to name, it would be mis hermanas — my sisters — hear the s land on both words, mis and hermanas, like a plural echo. Mi is for one thing, one person. Mis is for more than one. That is the entire rule, and it is a friendly rule, because English hides this — English says my for one child and my for five children and never blinks. Spanish is more honest: it shows you the number right on the word. Say the contrast with me until it is in your hands: Mi hijo. Mis hijos. Mi hermana. Mis hermanas. Mi, mis. One, more than one. Mi, mis.

And because conversation has two sides — you learned that in lesson one with ¿Cómo te llamas? — here is the matching word for the other side of the table. Tu — your. Tu means your, the friendly your, the your you use with family and friends and people you are warm with. Tu padre — your father. Tu hermana — your sister. Tu familia — your family. Say them with me: Tu padre. Tu hermana. Tu familia. So now you can ask as well as tell. For now, hold the pair side by side: mi is my, tu is your. Mi familia, tu familia. My family, your family. Two little words, and a whole conversation about the people who matter can happen between them.

Now we look just a little way down the road you are traveling, because in Key West, on March the twenty-fifth, two of your words change — gloriously. Today Jillian is mi prometida, my fiancée, the promised one. After the wedding, Spanish gives her a new title, and it gives you one too. Esposa — wife. La esposa — the wife. Mi esposa — my wife. Say it with me, just to taste the future: Mi esposa. And the matching word: Esposo — husband. El esposo — the husband. Mi esposo would be what Jillian says about you — her husband. Esposo, esposa — husband, wife — the o and a endings again, dressing to match, the same pattern you have been hearing all lesson. I am teaching you these two today as a preview only — a look through the door at what is coming — because your word today, the true word, the word with the date on it still ahead of you, is prometida. But hear me, Bill: after March the twenty-fifth, when you say mi esposa for the first time and it is true, remember that your profesora made you practice it early. Mi esposa. One day soon. For now, we keep the honest word: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. Say it: Mi prometida se llama Jillian.

Now we arrive at the heart of this lesson — the part where your family words leave your mouth and walk across a room to meet somebody. Because knowing the words for your people is only half the gift. The other half is presenting them: standing beside your sister, or your father, or Jillian, turning to a new friend, and doing the introduction with grace. Spanish has a beautiful, formal little ceremony for this, and it is built on a verb you already own. Remember llamar — to call — from me llamo, I call myself? Presenting someone is its cousin, and here is the phrase whole: Te presento a Jillian — I present to you Jillian, let me introduce you to Jillian. Te presento a… — let me introduce you to… Te presento is I present to you, I introduce to you. Say it with me: Te presento a Jillian. Again, with the gesture in your voice, the open hand: Te presento a Jillian.

That little a after presento is doing quiet work — it is the small word Spanish puts before a person you are naming as the one being presented, and you do not need its grammar name; you only need to never drop it. Te presento a mi padre — let me introduce you to my father. Te presento a mi hermana — let me introduce you to my sister. Te presento a mi prometida — let me introduce you to my fiancée. Say the set with me, one by one, like a man working a receiving line at his own wedding, unhurried and proud: Te presento a mi padre. Te presento a mi hermana. Te presento a mi prometida. Beautiful. That phrase, te presento a, is a door-opener for the rest of your life in Spanish — anyone you love, you can now hand to a new friend with those words and a smile.

And right behind the presentation comes the second half of the ceremony, the sentence that says who this person is. You already own its engine from lesson one: es. Well — you own soy, I am. Es is its partner: es means is — he is, she is, it is. Two little forms of the same giant. Soy is I am; es is is. And for she and he, Spanish gives you two clean words. Ella — she. Ella es… — she is… Él — he. Él es… — he is… — and notice the little accent on él; it is there to tell you this word means he, the person, so lean on it a touch. Say them with me: Ella es. Él es. Ella es. Él es.

Now watch the ceremony assemble itself, because you own every single piece. You turn to your new friend, you gesture to the woman beside you, and you say: Te presento a Jillian. Ella es mi prometida. Let me introduce you to Jillian. She is my fiancée. Two sentences, and the introduction is complete — her name, and who she is to you. Say it with me, whole, the way it will sound in Key West: Te presento a Jillian. Ella es mi prometida. Again: Te presento a Jillian. Ella es mi prometida. Ay, Bill. If you say only one new thing from this lesson at that wedding, let it be that.

And the ceremony works for every person in your portrait. Your father beside you at a table, a friend approaching: Te presento a mi padre. Él es mi padre — let me introduce you to my father; he is my father. Say the full form with me, because the pattern is what we are carving: Te presento a mi padre. Él es mi padre. Your sister: Te presento a Chelsea. Ella es mi hermana — let me introduce you to Chelsea; she is my sister. Say it: Te presento a Chelsea. Ella es mi hermana. Your son, when the day comes: Te presento a Trey. Él es mi hijo — let me introduce you to Trey; he is my son. Say it: Te presento a Trey. Él es mi hijo. And your daughter: Te presento a Abigail. Ella es mi hija. Say it: Te presento a Abigail. Ella es mi hija. Do you see what you have, Bill? One ceremony, two sentences, and every person you love can be presented with it. Te presento a… and then ella es or él es, and the family word. Name, and who they are to you. That is all an introduction has ever been, in any language — and now you can do it in two.

Now the other side of the ceremony, because at a wedding, and in a life, you will not only present — you will be presented to, and people will point, kindly, at photographs and at people across rooms, and you will want to ask the question. Here it is, small and mighty. ¿Quién es? — who is he, who is she, who is that? Quién means who. ¿Quién es? Say it with me, with the curiosity in it: ¿Quién es? Someone shows you a family photograph — a beautiful old picture, a man you do not know standing tall — and you ask: ¿Quién es? And the answer comes back in exactly the shapes you now own: Es mi padre — he is my father. Es mi madre — she is my mother. Es mi hermana — she is my sister. Hear how the answer drops the él and ella most of the time — Spanish often lets the family word carry the sentence alone: Es mi padre. It is enough. Say the exchange with me, question and answer, back and forth: ¿Quién es? Es mi padre. ¿Quién es? Es mi hermana. ¿Quién es? Es mi prometida. That last one — es mi prometida — she is my fiancée, said while looking at a photograph of Jillian, will melt whoever hears it. Practice it at home with her picture in your hand. I am serious. That is homework with a heartbeat.

Let us now do what we did in lesson one — change the scenery, and watch your phrases survive a new room, because a phrase is only yours when it travels. Picture this: Key West, the week of the wedding, a small restaurant the night before. Warm air, music somewhere, your family and a few new friends around a long table. A friend of Jillian's arrives and sits beside you, and the introductions begin — and tonight, mi estudiante, you are not the quiet man at the end of the table waiting for someone else to handle it. You handle it. Your sister is across from you. You gesture with an open hand, and you say: Te presento a Chelsea. Ella es mi hermana. She smiles, she says mucho gusto — pleased to meet you, from lesson one — and the table warms. Then the new friend asks about the photograph on your phone, your dad: ¿Quién es? And you answer, easy as breathing: Es mi padre. Es mi papá, you could add, softer — he is my dad. Later, someone nods toward the door as Jillian comes in, and asks you, quiet: ¿Quién es? And Bill — you get to smile the smile of a man one day from his wedding and say: Ella es mi prometida. She is my fiancée. Tomorrow, in that same room, the word will be esposa. Tonight it is prometida, and it has never sounded better. Same words as my classroom. New room. Still yours. That is what learned means.

One more guided moment before we gather it all, and this one is the real examination — not the questions below, those are friendly — the real one: your family, presented by you, start to finish, without me feeding you the lines. I will set the table and then I will be quiet, and you will speak into the silences. Ready? You are at that long table. Beside you, Jillian. Present her. … Te presento a Jillian. Ella es mi prometida. Yes. Now your sister, across the table. Present her. … Te presento a Chelsea. Ella es mi hermana. Good. Now I point — politely — at the photograph of the strong man on your phone, and I ask: ¿Quién es? … Answer me. Es mi padre. And the warmer word, the kitchen-table word? … Mi papá. Now the photograph changes — three young faces. ¿Quiénes son? — ah, that is a new question and I am giving it to you as a gift: ¿quiénes son? means who are they, for more than one person, and its answer begins with son — they are. ¿Quiénes son? … Mis hijos. Son mis hijos — they are my children. And their names, father, give me their names. … Mi hijo Trey. Mi hijo William. Mi hija Abigail. Bill. Stop and look at what just happened. At a table full of people, on the edge of your wedding, you presented your fiancée, your sister, your father, and your children — in Spanish, at conversation speed, without a script in your hand. In lesson one you were a man who could say hello. Tonight you are a man who can present his whole family. That is a room you can now walk into and belong in.

A few hooks to hang today's words on, so they are still yours next month. Familia and family — you can hear the English inside the Spanish. Padre hangs on paternal, madre hangs on maternal — the father word and the mother word in both languages grow from the same two roots. Papá hangs on papa — the same warm word English children have used for centuries, wearing a Spanish accent on the end. Hermana and hermano share herman- the way sister and brother share your childhood house; only the ending tells you which sibling walked in. Hijo and hija — same house, one letter different, o and a. And prometida hangs on promise, still the strongest hook in this course: the promised one. Hang every word on something you already own, and the words stop being homework. They become furniture in a house you live in — your family's house.

So let us gather what you own now, in order, one last time, the whole portrait in one pass. La familia — the family, the whole circle. Mi prometida — my fiancée, Jillian, the promised one, whose full sentence you own: Mi prometida se llama Jillian. Mi padre — my father, the respectful word; mi papá — my dad, the warm one. Mi madre — my mother. Mi padre y mi madre — my father and my mother. Mis hijos — my children: mi hijo Trey, mi hijo William, mi hija Abigail — my son, my son, my daughter, hijo for a son and hija for a daughter. Mi hermana — my sister, Chelsea; mi hermano — my brother. The machine underneath: mi for one, mis for more than one; tu for your — tu familia, your family. The preview of the future: esposa, wife; esposo, husband — waiting for you on the other side of March the twenty-fifth. And the ceremony, the heart of the lesson: Te presento a… — let me introduce you to — followed by Ella es… — she is — or Él es… — he is. And its mirror, the question: ¿Quién es? — who is that — answered with Es mi padre, es mi hermana, es mi prometida. Name them, present them, ask about them. Your people, in Spanish, complete.

That is lesson two, Bill, and you did beautifully — do not argue with your profesora, I heard you through that whole table scene and you did. Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions: all of them about what I taught you in this lesson and nothing else. Most give you choices to pick from, and you can also answer out loud or type your answer, whichever door you like. The lesson text stays open beside the questions, and if you want to read a part again before you answer, do it with my blessing — that is what it is there for. And your speaking practice is here in the lesson too: hear me say each phrase, then say it back until it lands and you see the green check. Your assignment tonight — because there is always one line, and tonight it is a tender one: find a photograph of your family, hold it in your hand, and say the words over it, one person at a time. Es mi padre. Es mi hermana. Mis hijos. And if Jillian is in the room, present her to the empty chair like royalty: Te presento a Jillian. Ella es mi prometida. She will laugh, and then she will remember it. Lesson three will teach you numbers — counting, money, and what things cost — and yes, there will be sweet words in it too; there are always sweet words in my room when you are the student. Until then: gracias — thank you — for my second class, Bill. Go show her the photograph trick. Buenas noches, mi amor — good night, my love — you know that one. She is waiting to hear the new ones too.

And the answer comes back in exactly the shapes you now own: Es mi padre — he is my father.' lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Numbers, money, and prices: counting what things cost
paragraphs: Hola, Bill. Soy la profesora Carmen Vega — I am Professor Carmen Vega, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Sit down, mi estudiante — my student — and roll up your sleeves, because today we do something every grown man needs in a second language: we count. Lesson one gave you your name and your first sweet words. Lesson two gave you your people — la familia, your family, named and presented with pride. Today, lesson three, we give you numbers: how to count from zero to one hundred, how to talk about money, and how to ask what something costs and understand the answer when it comes back at you. And because this is my room, and you are my student, there is a second thread woven through today, the Spanish-for-Jillian strand: compliments. Sweet words with numbers around them. A man should be able to count his money and compliment his woman in the same language, on the same day, without breaking stride. By the end of this lesson, you will do both.

Why numbers, and why now? Because numbers are where a tourist becomes a person. You can smile and say hola in any shop on earth, but the moment money is on the counter — a coffee, a ring, a bouquet of flowers for a certain woman — you need to know what you are being told and what you are agreeing to. Numbers are also hiding inside your real life everywhere: prices, dates, times, ages, addresses, the cost of the wedding you are planning for March the twenty-fifth in Key West. A wedding, Bill, is a beautiful event built almost entirely out of numbers. So today we tame them, all of them, from cero to cien — zero to one hundred — and I promise you, Spanish numbers are kinder than English ones. They follow their pattern honestly. Learn the pattern and the numbers are yours forever.

The way we work has not changed: I say it, you say it back out loud, every time I say say it with me. Numbers especially must live in your mouth, not on the page — you will never have time to read a price tag twice in a real shop, so we drill until your ear hears a number and your mind sees it. When the lesson is finished there will be questions below, only about what I teach today, and the lesson text stays open beside them. Going back to read is learning, not cheating. Ready? Vamos — let us go. And we start, as all counting starts, at the bottom.

Cero — zero. Cero is zero, the empty hand, the starting line. Say it: Cero. And now the first five, and I want them slow and clean, because everything else is built on these. Uno — one. Dos — two. Tres — three. Cuatro — four. Cinco — five. Say the run with me, counting on your fingers like a child, because that is not childish, that is how every human being who ever lived learned to count: Cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — zero, one, two, three, four, five. Again: Cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco. Uno is a word with a secret second job you will meet later — for now it is simply one, the loneliest and proudest number. Dos, two — short and round. Tres, three — hear the little tap of the r, the sound we practiced in lesson one. Cuatro, four — KWAH-troh, two strong beats. Cinco, five — SEEN-koh. Hold those five. They are the foundation stones.

Now the second five, and the first ten stand complete. Seis — six. Siete — seven. Ocho — eight. Nueve — nine. Diez — ten. Say them with me: Seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez — six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Again, slower: Seis… siete… ocho… nueve… diez. Siete and ocho are the long ones, two beats each — SEE-eh-teh, OH-choh. Nueve, nine, is a word you will love later, because it is a cousin of new — nueve, nuevo, the new thing and the number nine grew up together. And diez, ten, ends the first family with a little flourish, DEE-ehs. Now the whole staircase, zero to ten, in one breath, and do not rush it: Cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez. Again: Cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez. Bill, you can count to ten in Spanish. That is not nothing. That is the first floor of the whole building, and most prices, most counts, most real life starts right there.

Now the teenagers, eleven through fifteen, and I will be honest with you the way I always am: these five are individuals. They each have their own name and they do not follow a pattern yet — you simply learn them, the way you learned the names of your own family. Once — eleven. Doce — twelve. Trece — thirteen. Catorce — fourteen. Quince — fifteen. Say them with me: Once, doce, trece, catorce, quince — eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen. Again: Once, doce, trece, catorce, quince. Once sounds like OHN-seh — yes, it looks like the English word once, but in Spanish it is eleven, and now you will never forget it, because that little surprise is a hook all by itself. Doce, twelve, is a cousin of dozen — hear it? Doce, dozen, twelve. Quince, fifteen, is the famous one — a quinceañera is a girl's fifteenth birthday celebration, one of the great parties of the Spanish-speaking world, and the word quince sits right at the front of it. Learn these five as five people: once, doce, trece, catorce, quince.

And now, sixteen through nineteen, Spanish starts building instead of naming, and this is where the language shows you its honest machinery. Dieciséis — sixteen. Look at it: dieci is diez, ten, folded in, and séis is seis, six — ten and six, sixteen, the parts sitting right on the surface of the word. Diecisiete — seventeen, ten and seven. Dieciocho — eighteen, ten and eight. Diecinueve — nineteen, ten and nine. Say the family with me: Dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve — sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen. You are not memorizing four new words here, Bill. You are learning one trick — diez folded together with the small number — and the trick makes the words for you. That is how this language likes to work, and it is why I say Spanish is honest: it shows you its parts.

And then, the round one that closes the first twenty: Veinte — twenty. Veinte is twenty, a word of its own, VEIN-teh. Say it: Veinte. So here is your whole first country, zero to twenty, and let us walk it once at a steady pace, the way you would count bills out of a wallet: Cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez, once, doce, trece, catorce, quince, dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve, veinte. One more time, and this time feel how the ground changes under you — the first ten are names, eleven to fifteen are names, sixteen to nineteen are built, and twenty is the gate to the rest: Cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez, once, doce, trece, catorce, quince, dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve, veinte. Beautiful. Hold onto veinte, because everything above it is built from the tens, and the tens are next — but first, a breath, and a check. So if diez is ten and I add seis, I get dieciséis, sixteen — hold onto that building trick. It is about to make you rich in numbers.

Now the tens, the big round numbers, the ones prices actually live on. Treinta — thirty. Cuarenta — forty. Cincuenta — fifty. Sesenta — sixty. Setenta — seventy. Ochenta — eighty. Noventa — ninety. Cien — one hundred. Say the whole row with me, slow and proud: Treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa, cien — thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, one hundred. Again: Treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa, cien. Now look at them with your profesora's eyes and find the hooks, because they are full of them. Treinta carries tres, three, inside it — thirty is three tens, and Spanish lets you hear the three. Cuarenta carries cuatro, four. Cincuenta carries cinco, five. Sesenta carries seis, setenta carries siete, ochenta carries ocho, noventa carries nueve. Do you see it? The tens are the small numbers wearing a working coat. You already own the roots; the tens are just the roots grown up. And cien, one hundred, stands alone at the top like a king — cien, short, clean, complete.

Between the tens, Spanish does the most sensible thing in the world: it joins the ten and the small number with our little friend y — and — from lesson two. Veintiuno — twenty-one: veinte folded with uno. Treinta y uno — thirty-one: thirty and one, said as two words with y between them. Treinta y dos — thirty-two. Cuarenta y cinco — forty-five. Cincuenta y ocho — fifty-eight. Say a few with me, and build them yourself as we go: Treinta y uno. Treinta y dos. Cuarenta y cinco. Cincuenta y ocho. Noventa y nueve — ninety-nine, the last stop before cien. Do you feel it, Bill? You do not know ninety-nine as a memorized word. You build it: noventa, y, nueve. Ninety and nine. Any number I point at between twenty-one and ninety-nine, you can now build out loud from parts you own. That is not vocabulary. That is a machine, and it is in your hands.

Let us put the machine to work right now, guided, the way we do things in this room — I give you a number in English, you build it in Spanish, out loud, and then I say it so you can check your work against my voice. Twenty-five. Build it: veinte family… no — twenty-five is past veinte, so we say veinticinco — twenty-five, veinte folded with cinco in the twenties, the one place Spanish folds instead of joining. Say it: Veinticinco. Thirty-seven: treinta y siete — thirty and seven. Say it: Treinta y siete. Forty-two: cuarenta y dos. Say it: Cuarenta y dos. Sixty-three: sesenta y tres. Say it: Sesenta y tres. Eighty-one: ochenta y uno. Say it: Ochenta y uno. And the big one, one hundred: cien. Say it: Cien. Ay, Bill — you just built numbers you were never taught, out of parts, correctly, in your third lesson. That is the difference between studying a language and learning how it thinks.

Now we give the numbers their natural home: money. El dinero — money. Dinero is the word for money itself. El dinero. Say it: El dinero. Every man in this world has a relationship with dinero — earning it, counting it, spending it wisely, spending it on flowers when wisdom takes the afternoon off. In Spanish the word sits comfortably in sentences you already almost own. Tengo dinero — I have money. Tengo is a giant of a word: tengo means I have. You met its family in lesson two's future — no, you meet it right now, clean: Tengo — I have. Tengo dinero — I have money. Say it with me, like a man who earned it: Tengo dinero. And its honest opposite, which every man has also said in his life: No tengo dinero — I do not have money, I have no money. No in Spanish is the same word as English no, doing the same job — put it in front and the sentence turns around. No tengo dinero. Say it: No tengo dinero. Hopefully you need that one less and less, mi estudiante, but a complete man owns both sentences.

And the verb that walks beside money everywhere: Quiero comprar — I want to buy. Quiero means I want — from querer, the same verb that gave you te quiero in lesson one, I love you, because in Spanish wanting and loving were never separate ideas, remember? Quiero comprar: comprar means to buy. Quiero comprar — I want to buy. Say it: Quiero comprar. And now the sentence becomes a tool the moment you point it at something. Quiero comprar flores — I want to buy flowers. Flores means flowers. Quiero comprar flores. Say it with me, and think of exactly who they are for: Quiero comprar flores. And a man planning a wedding in Key West might also say: Quiero comprar un anillo — I want to buy a ring. Un anillo means a ring. Quiero comprar un anillo. Say it: Quiero comprar un anillo. Tengo, quiero, comprar — I have, I want, to buy. Three verbs and a man can walk into any shop in the Spanish-speaking world and start a real transaction.

Which brings us to the question this whole lesson bends toward, the question you will ask more than any other in shops, markets, and cafés for the rest of your life. ¿Cuánto cuesta? — how much does it cost? Cuánto means how much, cuesta comes from costar, to cost. ¿Cuánto cuesta? Say it with me, with the polite tilt of a man who is interested but not desperate: ¿Cuánto cuesta? Again: ¿Cuánto cuesta? That question, Bill, is a key — the money key, to stand beside por favor and gracias, the politeness keys from lesson one. Walk into a market in Key West during wedding week, pick up something beautiful, and ask ¿Cuánto cuesta? — and you are no longer a tourist pointing and grunting. You are a customer. A Spanish-speaking customer. The whole conversation changes temperature when a man asks the price in the language of the shop.

And the answer will come back in numbers — your numbers, the ones you built today — usually riding on a small word: dólares — dollars. Dólares means dollars. Cuesta veinte dólares — it costs twenty dollars. Cuesta veinte dólares. Hear the shape: cuesta, then the number, then dólares. Say it: Cuesta veinte dólares. Another: Cuesta cincuenta dólares — it costs fifty dollars. Say it: Cuesta cincuenta dólares. And a small one: Cuesta cinco dólares — it costs five dollars. Say it: Cuesta cinco dólares. So the exchange, whole, the way it will really happen: you hold up the thing, you ask ¿Cuánto cuesta?, and the answer comes: Cuesta treinta dólares — it costs thirty dollars. Run that exchange with me now, both parts, you asking and you answering: ¿Cuánto cuesta? Cuesta treinta dólares. ¿Cuánto cuesta? Cuesta treinta dólares. Your ear is the skill here, Bill — when a number flies at you in a real shop, you need it to land. That is why we drill.

Now, once you know the price, a man needs an opinion about it, and Spanish gives you two words that cover almost every price ever named. Es caro — it is expensive. Caro is expensive, the price that makes you whistle. Es caro. Say it: Es caro. And its opposite, the price that makes you smile: Es barato — it is cheap, it is a good price, the price that makes you smile. Barato is cheap, a bargain. Es barato. Say it: Es barato. Hear them side by side: Caro, barato. Expensive, cheap. Es caro. Es barato. Say the pair with me: Es caro. Es barato. And notice — es, the same little word from lesson two, ella es, él es — es, is. It costs thirty dollars and es caro, or es barato — price and opinion, two sentences, and you sound like a man who has bought things before and cannot be fooled. One warning from your profesora, with love: barato is a happy word in Spanish, a bargain, a good deal — it does not insult the goods the way cheap sometimes can in English. Use it freely. Es barato is a compliment to your own shopping.

Let us change the scenery now, because a phrase is only yours when it survives a new room. Picture the wedding week in Key West. You slip away in the morning — alone, on a mission — to a flower shop near the water, because a man does not arrive at his own wedding week empty-handed. You greet the room, the way I taught you in lesson one: Buenos días — good morning. The woman in the shop smiles. You look at the flowers, the beautiful ones, and you say your sentence whole: Quiero comprar flores — I want to buy flowers. She shows you an arrangement that would make Jillian's whole face change. You ask the key question: ¿Cuánto cuesta? She answers: Cuesta cuarenta dólares — it costs forty dollars. Forty. Cuarenta. You built that number today; you hear it land cleanly. And you, Bill, a man who knows a bargain when the flowers are for her, you smile and you say: Es barato — it is a good price. Because for her, at that price, it is. She wraps them. Gracias — thank you — por favor riding along where it belongs, and you walk out into the Key West morning with flowers in your hand and every word of that transaction spoken in Spanish. Same words as my classroom. New room. Still yours.

And now — ah, now we arrive at the part of the lesson that is not really about flowers, and you knew it was coming, because this is lesson three and in my room the odd-numbered lessons carry the sweet strand. You have spent forty minutes learning to count what things cost. Now learn to say what no money counts. The compliments. And we begin with the word itself. Bonita — pretty. Bonita is pretty, for a woman, and it is one of the kindest words in Spanish. Bonita. Say it: Bonita. It sounds like what it means — soft at the front, bright at the end. A dress can be bonita, a day can be bonita, but the word was born, I am convinced, for a woman's face. Say it once more, slower: Bonita.

Now build the compliment whole, because a word alone is a note and a sentence is music. Eres muy bonita — you are very pretty. Eres means you are — soy is I am, from lesson one; eres is its partner, you are. Muy means very. Eres muy bonita — you are very pretty. Say it with me, and aim it where it belongs, at the picture of her in your head: Eres muy bonita. Again, slower, like you mean every syllable: Eres… muy… bonita. Eres muy bonita. Bill, that sentence, said at the right moment — not as a performance, just at the kitchen door, in the morning, when she is not expecting it — that sentence will do more than the flowers. Flowers are cuarenta dólares. That sentence is free, and it is worth more. Say it one more time: Eres muy bonita.

Second compliment, and this one is for a specific day — today, any today, the day she has gotten ready and she looks like the woman in the photographs men keep forever. Te ves hermosa hoy — you look beautiful today. Take it apart gently. Te ves means you look — how you appear, what the eyes see. Hermosa means beautiful — a deeper word than bonita, the beauty that stops a conversation. Hoy means today. Te ves hermosa hoy — you look beautiful today. Say it with me: Te ves hermosa hoy. Again: Te ves hermosa hoy. Hoy is the word that makes it live in the present tense of a real marriage, Bill — not you were beautiful at some party in some photograph. Hoy. Today. This morning. In that dress, in this light. Te ves hermosa hoy. A compliment with hoy in it can be said every single day and never wear out, because every day it is true in a new way.

And the third compliment, my favorite, because it is not about beauty at all — it is about joy. Me gusta tu sonrisa — I like your smile. Sonrisa is smile. Me gusta means I like, it pleases me — literally, it pleases me, your smile pleases me. Tu is your, from lesson two — tu sonrisa, your smile. Me gusta tu sonrisa — I like your smile. Say it with me: Me gusta tu sonrisa. Again, warm: Me gusta tu sonrisa. Of all the compliments in this lesson, Bill, this is the one that tells her why. Bonita tells her what you see. Hermosa tells her what you feel. But me gusta tu sonrisa tells her that her happiness itself is the thing you love looking at — and a woman who hears that, in any language, hears that she is loved for her joy and not only her face. Say it once more, for her: Me gusta tu sonrisa.

Let us do the guided moment now, the real examination — not the questions below, those are friendly — the real one: a whole morning, with money and sweetness in it, at conversation speed, with you speaking into my silences. Ready? Morning, Key West, the day before the wedding. You are in the little shop. Greet the room. … Buenos días. The flowers, tell her what you want. … Quiero comprar flores. She names the price of the big arrangement — cuarenta y cinco dólares, forty-five dollars — and you, checking you heard it, you ask the price yourself first. Ask it. … ¿Cuánto cuesta? Good. And your opinion — for her, at forty-five, it is a bargain. Say it. … Es barato. Now you are home, and she comes into the room ready for the day, and the whole shop is forgotten because she is standing in the light. Tell her she is very pretty. … Eres muy bonita. Tell her how she looks today. … Te ves hermosa hoy. And the one about her joy, the one that is really about why. … Me gusta tu sonrisa. Bill. Stop. Look at what just happened. You greeted a shop, bought flowers, asked a price, judged it, and came home and complimented your prometida three ways — in Spanish, in one unbroken morning, in your third lesson. A man who can do that is not studying Spanish anymore. He is living a small, real piece of his life in it.

A few hooks before we gather it all, so today's numbers stay yours. Uno, dos, tres — hang them on the count you have heard in a hundred songs and movies; your ear owned them before your mind did. Doce hangs on dozen — twelve, the same root. Once hangs on its own surprise — it looks like once and means eleven, and surprises are unforgettable. Cien hangs on century and cent — a hundred years, a hundred cents, cien, the same old root for one hundred running under both languages. Cuesta hangs on cost — ¿cuánto cuesta? is how much does it cost with the family resemblance right on its face. Caro hangs on the English word dear, which once meant expensive too — a dear price, es caro, the costly thing. And sonrisa — hang it on her. That is the best hook in the lesson and you already own it: every time you see her smile between now and March the twenty-fifth, the word will be there. Me gusta tu sonrisa.

So let us gather what you own now, in order, one last time. The count: cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez — zero through ten. Once, doce, trece, catorce, quince — eleven through fifteen, the five individuals. Dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve — sixteen through nineteen, built from diez and the small number. Veinte — twenty. The tens: treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa, cien — thirty through one hundred, and everything between the tens built with y — treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco, noventa y nueve. The money words: el dinero, money; tengo, I have — tengo dinero, no tengo dinero; quiero comprar, I want to buy — quiero comprar flores, quiero comprar un anillo. The key question: ¿Cuánto cuesta? — how much does it cost — answered cuesta veinte dólares, it costs twenty dollars, and judged with es caro, it is expensive, or es barato, it is a good price. And the sweet strand, the heart riding inside the counting lesson: bonita, pretty; eres muy bonita, you are very pretty; te ves hermosa hoy, you look beautiful today; me gusta tu sonrisa, I like your smile. Count your money, Bill, and compliment your woman. Today you can do both in Spanish.

That is lesson three, and you did beautifully — do not argue with your profesora, I counted along with you and your numbers are clean. Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions: all of them about what I taught you in this lesson and nothing else — nobody will ask you one single thing I did not teach. Most give you choices to pick from, and you can also answer out loud or type your answer, whichever door you like. The lesson text stays open beside the questions, and if you want to read a part again before you answer, do it with my blessing — that is what it is there for. And your speaking practice is here in the lesson too: hear me say each phrase, then say it back until it lands and you see the green check. Your assignment tonight has two halves, and both are pleasant. First: count things in your house in Spanish — the stairs, the windows, the dollars in your wallet — out loud, cero to cien where you can. Numbers become yours by being used on real things. Second, and you already know it: tonight, or tomorrow morning at the kitchen door, one compliment, out loud, to her. Eres muy bonita is my suggestion, but any of the three will do, and she will not mind which. Lesson four will take you to work — your company, your clients, and what you sell, in Spanish. Until then: gracias — thank you — for my third class, Bill. Count well, spend wisely, and compliment her like a man who means it. Buenas noches, mi amor — you know that one is for her too.

questions.q: Carmen counts the first ten in Spanish: cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez. What number is 'diez'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the first staircase, zero to ten.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez — six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Again, slower: Seis… siete… ocho… nueve… diez.' Another way to hold it: diez is the last word of the first count — the number the first floor of the building stands on.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The count runs cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco for zero through five. (2) Then seis, siete, ocho, nueve. (3) The count ends at diez — the tenth number after zero: 10.

questions.q: What number is 'veinte'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the round number that closes the first twenty.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Veinte — twenty. Veinte is twenty, a word of its own, VEIN-teh. Say it: Veinte.' Another way: veinte is the gate between the teens and the tens — the number that closes the first twenty.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson counts zero to twenty in order. (2) The last number of that count, after diecinueve, is veinte. (3) Veinte is: 20.

questions.q: Which phrase asks how much something costs?
questions.teach: From the lesson: cuánto means how much and cuesta comes from costar, to cost — Carmen calls this question the money key.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: '¿Cuánto cuesta? — how much does it cost? Cuánto means how much, cuesta comes from costar, to cost.' Another way to hold it: cuánto means how much and cuesta comes from costar, to cost — Carmen calls this question the money key
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson bends toward one question for shops and markets. (2) It is built from cuánto, how much, and cuesta, costs. (3) The question is: ¿Cuánto cuesta?

questions.q: In Carmen's Key West flower shop story, the shopkeeper answers 'Cuesta cuarenta dólares.' How many dollars does the arrangement cost?
questions.teach: From the lesson: cuarenta is the forty ten — cuatro's grown-up form — and the story's price rides on it.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Cuesta cuarenta dólares — it costs forty dollars. Forty. Cuarenta. You built that number today; you hear it land cleanly.' Another way to hold it: cuarenta is the forty ten — cuatro's grown-up form — and the story's price rides on it
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The answer's shape is cuesta, then the number, then dólares. (2) The number in the story is cuarenta. (3) Cuarenta is forty — so the price is 40 dollars.

questions.q: What does 'Es barato' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: barato is a happy word in Spanish — a bargain, a good deal — not an insult to the goods.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Es barato — it is cheap, it is a good price, the price that makes you smile.' Another way to hold it: barato is a happy word in Spanish — a bargain, a good deal — not an insult to the goods
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Es means it is. (2) Carmen pairs caro and barato as opposite opinions about a price. (3) Barato is the smiling one: it is a good price.

questions.q: What does 'Es caro' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: caro is the price that makes you whistle; barato is its opposite, the price that makes you smile.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Es caro — it is expensive. Caro is expensive, the price that makes you whistle.' Another way to hold it: caro is the price that makes you whistle; barato is its opposite, the price that makes you smile
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Es means it is. (2) Of the lesson's two price opinions, caro is the expensive one. (3) So es caro means: it is expensive.

questions.q: Carmen builds numbers between the tens with the word 'y' — and. Which phrase is ninety-nine?
questions.teach: From the lesson: you do not memorize ninety-nine; you build it — noventa, y, nueve, ninety and nine.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Noventa y nueve — ninety-nine, the last stop before cien. Do you feel it, Bill? You do not know ninety-nine as a memorized word.' Another way to hold it: you do not memorize ninety-nine; you build it — noventa, y, nueve, ninety and nine
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Ninety is noventa and nine is nueve. (2) Between the tens, Spanish joins the parts with y, and. (3) Built, ninety-nine is: Noventa y nueve.

questions.q: Which compliment does Carmen teach for 'you look beautiful today'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the compliment with hoy in it — today — so it can be said every day.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Te ves hermosa hoy — you look beautiful today. Take it apart gently. Te ves means you look — how you appear, what the eyes see.' Another way: hermosa is the deeper word for beautiful, and hoy — today — is what makes the compliment live in the present.

questions.q: What does 'Me gusta tu sonrisa' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: this compliment is not about beauty but about joy — her smile itself is the thing he loves looking at.
