Me gusta means I like, it pleases me — literally, it pleases me, your smile pleases me.' Another way to hold it: this compliment is not about beauty but about joy — her smile itself is the thing he loves looking at
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Tu, from lesson two, means your. (2) Sonrisa is the word Carmen defines as smile. (3) Me gusta says I like — so the sentence means: I like your smile.

questions.q: In your own words: how does Carmen build a number like thirty-seven in Spanish?
questions.teach: From the lesson: between the tens, Spanish joins the ten and the small number with y — and — instead of making you memorize a new word.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'treinta y siete — thirty and seven. Say it: Treinta y siete. Forty-two: cuarenta y dos.' Another way to hold it: between the tens, Spanish joins the ten and the small number with y — and — instead of making you memorize a new word
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Thirty is treinta and seven is siete. (2) Carmen joins a ten and a small number with y, and. (3) So thirty-seven is built as treinta y siete.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Your business: the company, clients, and what you sell
paragraphs: Hola, Bill. Soy la profesora Carmen Vega — I am Professor Carmen Vega, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Sit down, mi estudiante — my student — and today, bring your working self with you, because today we go to work. Lesson one gave you your name and your first sweet words. Lesson two gave you your people, your familia, named and presented. Lesson three gave you numbers, money, and prices — and a few compliments I hope Jillian has already heard. Today, lesson four, we build the third great room of your life in Spanish: your business. The company, the clients, and what you sell. You are a man who built a company with his own hands — soy empresario, I am a businessman, you learned to say that in lesson one and you said it like you meant it. Today we go inside that sentence and furnish it: the office, the phone, the work itself, the clients who trust you, and the verbs that make a business run — work, speak, call, sell — taught by feel, the way this room teaches everything, in your mouth and not in a grammar book.

Why business words, and why now? Because you, Bill, are not a man learning Spanish for a vacation. You are a man building a life and a company at the same time, and half your waking hours are spent inside your work: talking to clients, answering calls, writing messages, sitting in meetings, selling what you sell. If your Spanish only lives at the kitchen table, it lives in half your life. Today it moves into the other half. And there is a practical reason too, the kind you respect: a client who hears a businessman greet him, introduce his company, and talk about the work in Spanish — even simple Spanish, honestly spoken — hears a man who took the trouble. Trouble taken is trust earned, in every language on earth. That is what we are building today: your working voice in Spanish.

The way we work has not changed, and it will never change in my room: I say it, you say it back out loud, every time I say say it with me. Business phrases especially must be said out loud, because at work you will say them on the phone, in a doorway, across a desk — never silently to a page. When the lesson is finished there will be questions below, only about what I teach today, nothing else, and the lesson text stays open beside them so you can read any part again. Going back to read is learning, not cheating. Are you ready to go to work? Vamos — let us go — a trabajar, to work. And yes, that last phrase is your first piece of business Spanish, given free: a trabajar — let us work, to work.

We start with the biggest word of the day, the house everything else lives in. La empresa — the company, the business as a whole, the thing you built. La empresa. Say it with me, slowly first: La… empresa. La empresa. Empresa is a beautiful word when you take it apart: it comes from an old word for undertaking, for a thing a man takes on with both hands. An empresa is not just a company on paper. It is the undertaking. The thing you undertook. When you say la empresa, Spanish hears the weight of that — the risk, the building, the years. Say it once more, like a man who built his: La empresa.

And right beside it, its everyday brother. El negocio — the business, the deal, the work of making a living. El negocio. Say it: El negocio. Negocio is the business in motion — the deals, the trade, the daily turning of the wheel. If empresa is the house, negocio is the work that happens inside the house. You will hear negocio everywhere in the Spanish-speaking world: men talk about el negocio the way men back home talk about the business, the shop, the trade — with respect, because it feeds the family. And hear the hook hiding in it: negocio is a cousin of negotiate — the dealing word. El negocio, the business. Say the pair with me, the house and the work inside it: La empresa. El negocio. La empresa. El negocio.

Now, your company has a name, and Spanish asks for it with a sentence you already own in your bones — because it is built on llamar, the very first verb of this course, the me llamo verb, I call myself. Mi empresa se llama… — my company is called, my company's name is. Mi empresa se llama. Say it with me: Mi empresa se llama. Hear it? Se llama — it calls itself, its name is — the exact same music as me llamo Bill and mi prometida se llama Jillian. You learned this shape in lesson one for a man, you used it in lesson two for the woman you love, and now it names your company. One shape, three treasures: yourself, your prometida, your empresa. A man could build a whole introduction out of that one shape, and before this lesson ends, you will. Say it once more, and put your company's weight behind it: Mi empresa se llama. We will leave the name itself for you to say in the practice — the sentence frame is what I am carving today, and the frame is yours.

A company is not a building, though — a company is people, and the people who make a business a business are the ones on the other side of the desk. Los clientes — the clients, the customers, the people who trust you with their money and their name. Los clientes. Say it with me: Los clientes. Clientes and clients — you can hear the English cousin inside it immediately, KLEE-en-tehs, the same word wearing Spanish clothes. And notice los — the, for more than one, masculine — standing in front of clientes the way la stands in front of empresa and el stands in front of negocio. Spanish gives every noun a little flag like that — el, la, los, las — and for now your ear only needs to hear that the flag changes with the word it flies over. Los clientes. These are your people at work, Bill — the business owners who believed you could help them, who signed, who paid, who trust the company with their livelihoods. Say the word with the respect it deserves: Los clientes.

And what do you and your clientes do together? You work. So here is the word for the work itself. El trabajo — the work, the job. El trabajo. Say it: El trabajo. Trabajo is a word with sweat in it — in the old language underneath Spanish, its root carried the idea of effort, of something that costs you something. Spanish never forgot that. El trabajo is not a task on a list; it is the labor, the job, the whole working life in two beats: tra-BA-ho. Hear the j in the middle — in Spanish the letter j sounds like a strong h, a breath pushed out: trabajo, with that breath at the end. Say it again, with the breath: El trabajo. And the verb, the action itself: Trabajar — to work. Trabajar is to work. Say it: Trabajar. Tra-ba-HAR, the beat and the breath at the end. Trabajar. Hold that verb in your hand, Bill, because in a few minutes it is going to become the key that opens every working verb in this lesson — and I am going to show you the trick by feel, without a single grammar chart.

But first, the room where the work happens, and the tools on the desk, because a businessman should be able to name his own workplace. La oficina — the office. La oficina. Say it: La oficina. Oficina and office — cousins again, so close your ear gets this one free. El teléfono — the telephone, the phone. El teléfono. Say it: El teléfono. Teléfono carries its Greek roots on its face — tele, far, and fono, sound — the far-sound, the voice carried far. Every businessman alive lives on el teléfono. El correo — the mail, the email. El correo. Say it: El correo. Correo is mail — the letter kind and, in modern life, the email kind; el correo electrónico is the full name for email, but in daily talk, el correo does the work, and context tells everyone which mail you mean. La computadora — the computer. La computadora. Say it: La computadora. Computadora, the machine that computes — longer than the English word, more honest too; it names the machine by what it does. Say the desk set with me, one by one, like a man walking into his own office in the morning and touching each thing as he passes: La oficina. El teléfono. El correo. La computadora. Office, phone, mail, computer. Your workplace, in Spanish, named.

And the event that fills a businessman's calendar like weather: Una reunión — a meeting. Una reunión means a meeting — a gathering, a coming-together; reunión is built from unir, to unite, to bring together, with re- in front of it: a bringing-together-again. Una reunión. Say it: Una reunión. Every man who runs a company knows this word in his bones even before Spanish gives it to him: the meeting with the client, the meeting about the numbers, the meeting that should have been a phone call. And speaking of the phone — here is the sentence you will say at work more than almost any other, so I want it carved deep. Tengo una llamada — I have a call, I have a phone call. Tengo una llamada. Tengo you own from lesson three — tengo, I have, tengo dinero, I have money. Una llamada is a call — and look, Bill, look at that word: llamada. It is llamar, to call, wearing a noun's clothes. The call is the calling, turned into a thing. You have owned this root since your very first lesson — me llamo, I call myself — and it has been following you ever since: se llama, llamada. One root, a whole family of words. Tengo una llamada. Say it with me, like a man whose phone just lit up with a client's name: Tengo una llamada. Again: Tengo una llamada.

Let me walk you through one ordinary working morning with these words, so they stop being vocabulary and start being your day. You arrive at la oficina — the office — and the first thing waiting for you is el correo — the mail, the email — clients writing in the night, the way clients do. You read it on la computadora — the computer — coffee going cold the way coffee does. Then una reunión — a meeting — with a client who wants to talk about his negocio, his business, because that is what your empresa does: it helps other men's negocios grow. In the middle of the reunión, el teléfono — the phone — lights up: tengo una llamada, you say, I have a call, and you step out for two minutes like a gentleman. Every word in that morning, Bill, you now own in Spanish: la oficina, el correo, la computadora, una reunión, el teléfono, tengo una llamada. That is not a vocabulary list. That is Tuesday. And a man who can narrate his own Tuesday in a second language is a man whose Spanish has left the classroom and reported for work. Say the morning back to me, touching each thing as you pass it: La oficina. El correo. La computadora. Una reunión. El teléfono. Tengo una llamada. Good. That is your workplace, named and claimed.

Now we come to the engine room of this lesson — the part I have been promising you — the verbs of work, taught by feel. Here is the secret, and I am going to give it to you the way a good mechanic gives you a tool: by putting it in your hand, not by describing it. A great family of Spanish verbs ends in -ar in their full form: trabajar, hablar, llamar, comprar — to work, to speak, to call, to buy. And when you, the man himself, do the action — when I do it — Spanish changes the ending to -o. Watch it happen, and do not study it, feel it. Trabajar, to work, becomes: Trabajo — I work. Trabajo. Say it with me, and stand up a little straighter when you say it, because it is a working man's sentence in one word: Trabajo. It ends in o. I work. Trabajo.

Now the second one, and you already own its root without knowing it. Hablar — to speak, to talk. Hablar is to speak. And with the -o ending, the I form: Hablo — I speak, I talk. Hablo. Say it: Hablo. Hablo español — I speak Spanish. Hablo español. Say that whole sentence with me, Bill, because it is true now, a little more every week, and a man should be able to say what is true: Hablo español. Again: Hablo español. Ends in o again. Trabajo, hablo. I work, I speak. Feel the pattern in your mouth — the o at the end is your signature on the verb. It says: I am the one doing this.

And the third one is an old friend coming home. Llamar — to call. You have known llamar since lesson one, hiding inside me llamo. Its I form: Llamo — I call. Llamo. Say it: Llamo. And comprar, from lesson three, to buy — quiero comprar, I want to buy — its I form: Compro — I buy. Compro. Say it: Compro. Now line the four brothers up and look at them, Bill, because this is the whole trick and it is beautiful: Trabajo, hablo, llamo, compro — I work, I speak, I call, I buy. Four verbs, four different jobs, one ending. The -o ending. In Spanish, when a verb's full form ends in -ar, the I form ends in -o — and you do not need to recite that rule to anyone, ever. You need to feel it: the verb puts on the o, and the o means I. Say the four with me, slow, like a man counting his tools: Trabajo. Hablo. Llamo. Compro. Again, faster, at working speed: Trabajo, hablo, llamo, compro. That, mi estudiante, is the first real engine of Spanish grammar inside you — not memorized, felt. Every new -ar verb you ever meet, and there are hundreds, you can now pick up and use in the I form the day you meet it. That is not a lesson. That is a machine for making lessons unnecessary.

Let me check your feel for it, the way we check things in this room — gently, out loud, together. So if trabajar is to work, then I work is… trabajo. If hablar is to speak, then I speak is… hablo. If llamar is to call, I call is… llamo. Hold onto that o. It is yours. And now watch the engine pull a real train. Trabajo en mi empresa — I work in my company, I work at my company. En means in, at. Trabajo en mi empresa. Say it: Trabajo en mi empresa. Hablo con los clientes — I speak with the clients. Con means with. Hablo con los clientes. Say it: Hablo con los clientes. Two sentences, Bill, and you have just described your working day in Spanish: I work in my company. I speak with the clients. A man who can say those two sentences is not playing at business Spanish. He is doing it.

And now the verb that pays for everything — because a company that does not sell does not stay a company, and you, I happen to know, are a man who sells. Vender — to sell. Vender is to sell. Say it: Vender. Vender ends in -er, not -ar, so it belongs to the second family of verbs, and I am only introducing it today — its full pattern is a lesson for another day. But you need its I form now, because a businessman needs to say what he sells. Vendo — I sell. Vendo. Say it: Vendo. Hear the difference in the ending: the -ar family signs with -o after dropping -ar — trabajo — and vender signs vendo, I sell. Do not wrestle it today; just own the word. Vendo. And the question that follows a seller everywhere: ¿Qué vendes? — no. That one is for another lesson too, and your profesora does not teach ahead of the road. Today you own the statement: Vendo. I sell. One word, and a client on the other side of a desk knows exactly what kind of man he is talking to. Say it once more, with a seller's calm: Vendo.

One more turn of the engine before we assemble everything, because I want the -o feel deep in your hands, not just in your head. Run the four brothers through your real day, out loud with me, as full little sentences. In the morning, at the desk: Trabajo — I work — trabajo en mi empresa. A client walks in and the conversation starts: Hablo — I speak — hablo con los clientes. The phone rings and it is on you to make the call out: Llamo — I call. A purchase for the empresa, supplies, something the oficina needs: Compro — I buy. Trabajo, hablo, llamo, compro. Four verbs, four corners of a working day, one ending doing all the signing. And notice what you did not do, Bill: you did not open a book, you did not recite a chart, you did not conjugate anything. You felt the verb put on its o and step forward as you. That is how this room teaches grammar — by feel, in the mouth, on real sentences from your real life — and it is why the pattern will still be in your hands next month when a brand-new -ar verb walks into your life and you pick it up, turn it over, and use its I form without asking anyone's permission. That is fluency being born, mi estudiante, quietly, in an office, on a workday.

Now, before we assemble your whole working introduction, one small line about your own house — your company's house — because no lesson about your business would be honest without him, and I will keep it light, one line, the way you like it. Mi ayudante se llama Dave — my assistant is called Dave, my helper's name is Dave. Ayudante means assistant, helper — the one who helps. Mi ayudante se llama Dave. Say it with me: Mi ayudante se llama Dave. There it is — se llama again, the shape that names you, names Jillian, names your empresa, now naming the help. Dave is part of how your empresa runs, Bill, and now you can say so in Spanish, in one line, and move on like a man with work to do. Which you are. So let us move on.

Let us change the scenery now, because a phrase is only yours when it survives a new room — and today the new room is a room you know better than any classroom: a client's office, or better, the doorway of a small business in Michigan, a good business, the kind you help. A new client, a Spanish speaker, a man who built his own empresa the way you built yours, and today he is meeting you properly for the first time. You greet him — you own this: Buenos días — good morning. Mucho gusto — pleased to meet you. He asks, in Spanish, about your work, and Bill, you do not shrink and you do not wave for an interpreter. You stand in his doorway and you give him your working introduction, whole. Mi empresa se llama… — and your company's name rolls out. Trabajo en mi empresa — I work in my company. Hablo con los clientes — I speak with the clients. Vendo — I sell — and what you sell, you name with pride. His eyebrows go up, the way eyebrows do when a man hears his own language spoken back to him with respect by a stranger who took the trouble. The meeting — una reunión — has not even started, and already the trust in the room is different, because trust is built out of exactly this: trouble taken, in the other man's language, before any contract is mentioned. Same verbs as my classroom. New room. Still yours. That is what learned means, at work as much as at the wedding table.

Now the guided moment, the real examination — not the questions below, those are friendly — the real one: your whole working introduction, start to finish, at conversation speed, with you speaking into my silences. Ready, empresario? I am the new client, I have just walked into your oficina, and I am listening. Greet me and tell me your company's name-frame. … Mi empresa se llama. Good. Tell me where you work. … Trabajo en mi empresa. Tell me who you talk to all day. … Hablo con los clientes. Tell me the verb of your living. … Vendo. Now your phone lights up — a client, of course — tell me what you have. … Tengo una llamada. And the machine on your desk where the correo lives — name it. … La computadora. And your right hand, your helper — one line. … Mi ayudante se llama Dave. Bill. Stop. Look at what just happened. A client walked into your office and you named your company, stated your work, named your clients, claimed your selling, took your call, and introduced your help — in Spanish, unbroken, in your fourth lesson. In lesson one you were a man who could say hello. This morning you are a man who can open a business meeting. That is not a small step for an empresario. That is a new door in a building you already own.

A few hooks before we gather it all, so today's words stay yours. Empresa hangs on enterprise — say them side by side, empresa, enterprise, and hear the family resemblance; both words carry the undertaking, the thing taken on. Negocio hangs on negotiate — the dealing, the business in motion. Clientes hangs on clients — nearly free, that one. Oficina hangs on office — free again; Spanish has been generous to you today, Bill, and a wise man accepts generosity without suspicion. Teléfono hangs on telephone — the same Greek roots in both languages, the far-sound. Correo hangs on courier — the one who carries the mail; correo, courier, the carrier running under both words. Reunión hangs on reunion — a bringing together again; every reunión is a little reunion of people with work to do. And trabajo — hang that one on your own life. You do not need a word-hook for work. You have a life-hook. Every morning you have ever gotten up and built something is the hook. El trabajo. It was yours before Spanish named it.

So let us gather what you own now, in order, one last time. The house and the work inside it: la empresa — the company; el negocio — the business. Its name-frame: mi empresa se llama — my company is called. The people: los clientes — the clients. The work itself: el trabajo — the work; trabajar — to work. The workplace, named piece by piece: la oficina — the office; el teléfono — the phone; el correo — the mail, the email; la computadora — the computer; una reunión — a meeting. The working sentence: tengo una llamada — I have a call, built on llamada, from llamar, the root you have owned since lesson one. The engine, felt and not memorized: the -ar verbs sign their I form with -o — trabajo, I work; hablo, I speak; llamo, I call; compro, I buy — and hablo español, I speak Spanish, which is truer every week. The seller's word: vender, to sell; vendo, I sell. The full working sentences: trabajo en mi empresa, I work in my company; hablo con los clientes, I speak with the clients. And the one light line about your help: mi ayudante se llama Dave — my assistant is called Dave. Your name, your people, your numbers, and now your business, Bill. Four rooms of your life, standing in Spanish.

That is lesson four, and you did beautifully — do not argue with your profesora, I heard that introduction and it sounded like a man who signs his own checks. Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions: all of them about what I taught you in this lesson and nothing else — nobody will ask you one single thing I did not teach. Most give you choices to pick from, and you can also answer out loud or type your answer, whichever door you like. The lesson text stays open beside the questions, and if you want to read a part again before you answer, do it with my blessing — that is what it is there for. And your speaking practice is here in the lesson too: hear me say each phrase, then say it back until it lands and you see the green check. Your assignment today is a working one, and it is simple: once today, at real work — at your desk, on a call, anywhere — say your introduction out loud to the empty room before the work starts. Mi empresa se llama. Trabajo en mi empresa. Hablo con los clientes. Vendo. Say it to the oficina like you are opening the doors for the day. A business that gets greeted in Spanish by its own owner is a business that is going somewhere new. Lesson five will build on this — more of your day, more of your life, in Spanish. Until then: gracias — thank you — for my fourth class, Bill. Now go run your empresa. Y esta noche — and tonight — you know the line for her: Buenas noches, mi amor — good night, my love. Work all day, mi estudiante. Love her all night. That is the whole curriculum.

questions.q: What does 'La empresa' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: empresa comes from an old word for an undertaking — the thing a man takes on with both hands.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'La empresa — the company, the business as a whole, the thing you built.' Another way to hold it: empresa comes from an old word for an undertaking — the thing a man takes on with both hands
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Carmen opens with the biggest word of the day, the house everything else lives in. (2) That word is la empresa. (3) It means: the company.

questions.q: What does 'El negocio' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: if empresa is the house, negocio is the work that happens inside the house — the business in motion.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'El negocio — the business, the deal, the work of making a living. El negocio.' Another way to hold it: if empresa is the house, negocio is the work that happens inside the house — the business in motion
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson gives two big words: empresa for the company as a whole. (2) Its everyday brother is el negocio. (3) Negocio means: the business.

questions.q: What does 'Los clientes' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: clientes and clients are cousins — the same word wearing Spanish clothes — and they are Bill's people at work.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Los clientes — the clients, the customers, the people who trust you with their money and their name.' Another way to hold it: clientes and clients are cousins — the same word wearing Spanish clothes — and they are Bill's people at work
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) A company is people, and the lesson names the people on the other side of the desk. (2) Their word sounds almost like its English cousin. (3) Los clientes means: the clients.

questions.q: What does 'El trabajo' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: trabajo is a word with sweat in it — the labor, the job, the whole working life.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'El trabajo — the work, the job. El trabajo. Say it: El trabajo. Trabajo is a word with sweat in it — in the old language underneath Spanish, its root carried the idea of effort, of something that costs you something.' Another way to hold it: trabajo is a word with sweat in it — the labor, the job, the whole working life
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Clientes and the company do something together: they work. (2) The word for that work itself is el trabajo. (3) It means: the work.

questions.q: Which phrase means 'I have a call'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: tengo is I have, from lesson three, and llamada is a call — llamar, to call, wearing a noun's clothes.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Tengo una llamada — I have a call, I have a phone call. Tengo una llamada.' Another way to hold it: tengo is I have, from lesson three, and llamada is a call — llamar, to call, wearing a noun's clothes
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Tengo means I have — tengo dinero, I have money. (2) A call is una llamada. (3) Joined, I have a call is: Tengo una llamada.

questions.q: What does 'Una reunión' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: reunión is built from unir, to unite — a bringing-together-again of people with work to do.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Una reunión means a meeting — a gathering, a coming-together; reunión is built from unir, to unite, to bring together, with re- in front of it: a bringing-together-again.' Another way to hold it: reunión is built from unir, to unite — a bringing-together-again of people with work to do
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson names the event that fills a businessman's calendar. (2) It is built on the idea of people coming together. (3) Una reunión means: a meeting.

questions.q: Which Spanish word means 'the computer'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: computadora names the machine by what it does — the machine that computes — and it is where el correo lives.
questions.teach2: From the lesson: 'La computadora — the computer. La computadora. Say it: La computadora. Computadora, the machine that computes — longer than the English word, more honest too; it names the machine by what it does.' From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'La computadora — the computer. La computadora. Say it: La computadora.' Another way to hold it: computadora names the machine by what it does — the machine that computes — and it is where el correo lives
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson names the desk piece by piece: oficina, teléfono, correo. (2) The machine among them is la computadora. (3) It means: the computer.

questions.q: Carmen teaches the -ar verbs by feel: trabajar is 'to work.' What is 'I work'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the -ar ending steps aside and the verb signs with -o — and the o means I.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Trabajar, to work, becomes: Trabajo — I work. Trabajo. Say it with me, and stand up a little straighter when you say it, because it is a working man's sentence in one word: Trabajo.' Another way to hold it: the -ar ending steps aside and the verb signs with -o — and the o means I
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Trabajar is the full form, to work. (2) When Bill himself does the action, Carmen changes the ending to -o. (3) So I work is: Trabajo.

questions.q: What does 'Hablo con los clientes' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: hablo is I speak — hablar wearing the -o — and con means with.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Hablo con los clientes — I speak with the clients. Con means with. Hablo con los clientes.' Another way to hold it: hablo is I speak — hablar wearing the -o — and con means with
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Hablo is the I form of hablar, to speak. (2) Con means with, and los clientes are the clients. (3) Whole: I speak with the clients.

questions.q: What does 'Vendo' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: vender is to sell, from the second verb family, and vendo is the I form a businessman needs at a desk.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Vendo — I sell. Vendo. Say it: Vendo. Hear the difference in the ending: the -ar family signs with -o after dropping -ar — trabajo — and vender signs vendo, I sell.' Another way to hold it: vender is to sell, from the second verb family, and vendo is the I form a businessman needs at a desk
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson introduces vender, to sell. (2) Its I form is the seller's statement. (3) Vendo means: I sell.

questions.q: Which sentence does Carmen teach for naming Bill's assistant, Dave?
questions.teach: From the lesson: ayudante is the assistant, the helper — and se llama is the same naming shape that names Bill, Jillian, and the empresa.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mi ayudante se llama Dave — my assistant is called Dave, my helper's name is Dave.' Another way to hold it: ayudante is the assistant, the helper — and se llama is the same naming shape that names Bill, Jillian, and the empresa
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Ayudante means assistant or helper. (2) Se llama is the naming shape from lesson one. (3) The sentence is: Mi ayudante se llama Dave.

questions.q: In your own words: what happens to a verb like 'trabajar' when Bill is the one doing the action, and what does the new ending say?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the verb puts on the o, and the o is Bill's signature on the verb — it says: I am the one doing this.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'In Spanish, when a verb's full form ends in -ar, the I form ends in -o — and you do not need to recite that rule to anyone, ever.' Another way to hold it: the verb puts on the o, and the o is Bill's signature on the verb — it says: I am the one doing this
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Trabajar, hablar, llamar, comprar all end in -ar. (2) Carmen changes the ending for the I form. (3) The new ending is -o, and it means I: trabajo, hablo, llamo, compro.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Food and drink: ordering like you live there
paragraphs: Hola, Bill — hello, Bill. Soy la profesora Carmen Vega — I am Professor Carmen Vega, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Sit down, get comfortable, and bring your appetite, because today we eat. This is lesson five: food and drink, and ordering like you live there. Not ordering like a tourist who points at a picture and hopes. Ordering like a man who belongs at that table, who knows what he wants, who asks for it clearly, who enjoys it out loud, and who asks for the check like he has done it a hundred times — because after today, in your head, you will have.

Here is why this lesson matters, and it matters more than it looks. A man can greet people beautifully and still go hungry in a foreign language. Food is where a language stops being a classroom and starts being a life. You will sit in cafés in Key West during your wedding week. You will sit across from Jillian at breakfast the morning after you arrive, tired from traveling, happy, starving. You will want coffee. She will want coffee. And you, Bill, are going to be the man who orders it for both of you, in Spanish, calmly, without reaching for your phone. That is what today buys you. Every phrase in this lesson will be used by you, out loud, in a real place, within the year. I do not teach museum Spanish. I teach table Spanish.

Our method is the same as always, because it works. I say it, you say it back to me out loud, the way you mean it, and only then do we move on. When I say say it with me, I want to hear you — in the kitchen, in the truck, wherever you are sitting. Your mouth learns this language before your mind does, and today your mouth has delicious work to do. And remember how this room works: when the lesson ends, the questions wait below, all of them about what I teach you right here and nothing else, and the full text of this lesson stays open beside you. Reading it again is not cheating. Reading it again is learning.

We begin before the restaurant. We begin in your body, because that is where every meal begins. In English, you say I am hungry — as if hunger were something you are. Spanish is more honest and more practical: Spanish says you have hunger, the way you have a coat or a key, something you carry and can set down when the food arrives. So: Tengo hambre — I am hungry. Word for word, I have hunger. Tengo means I have. Hambre means hunger. Tengo hambre. Say it with me, and put a hand on your stomach like you mean it: Tengo hambre. Again, like a man who skipped lunch: Tengo hambre.

Hambre has a small sound lesson hiding in it, and you already own the key. Remember lesson one: the letter h in Spanish is silent — written, never heard. Hambre starts with that silent h, so hambre sounds like AHM-breh, no h sound at all. And tengo — listen to the ending, that warm -go sound. You will hear tengo again before this lesson is over, in another costume, so keep it in your pocket. Say the whole sentence once more, clean: Tengo hambre. Good. That sentence, said at the right moment, has started more good evenings than almost any sentence I know.

Now its brother. If hunger is what you have for food, thirst is what you have for drink, and Spanish builds it the exact same way — that is the kindness of this language, it reuses its own bricks. Tengo sed — I am thirsty. I have thirst. Sed means thirst. Tengo sed. Notice sed is a short word, one clean beat: sed. Say it with me: Tengo sed. And now put the brothers side by side, because in real life they travel together: Tengo hambre. Tengo sed. I am hungry. I am thirsty. One more time, both, like a man arriving at a table after a long hot drive: Tengo hambre. Tengo sed.

Hold onto the pattern, because this is a moment where Spanish shows you its machinery, and the machinery is friendly. Tengo plus a thing you feel in your body equals how you say you feel it. Tengo hambre, tengo sed. Later in your Spanish life this same frame will carry other feelings, but today two is plenty — hunger and thirst are the two that get you fed. So if tengo means I have, then hambre and sed are simply the names of what you have. You are not describing your soul. You are reporting your cargo. I have hunger. I have thirst. Honest, plain, and every waiter on earth understands it instantly.

Now, you are hungry, you are thirsty — what does a man do next? He wants. And wanting, in a restaurant, is not rude; wanting clearly is a courtesy, because it lets the other person help you fast. Here is the verb that runs every restaurant on earth: Quiero — I want. Quiero. It comes from querer — to want, and also to love; yes, Bill, it is the same family as te quiero — I love you — from lesson one. In Spanish, wanting and loving live in the same house, and at a table, quiero is simply the wanting branch of the family, doing honest work. Say it with me, firm and friendly: Quiero. Quiero.

Watch how quiero works, because it is a handle you can attach almost anything to. Quiero plus the thing. That is the whole machine. Quiero café — I want coffee — and we will get to café properly in a moment. The point right now is the shape: quiero, and then the thing you want, riding behind it like a cart behind a horse. You do not need a new sentence for every dish. You need one strong handle and the names of the things. Today I am going to give you the names of the things a man actually needs first: water, coffee, breakfast, chicken, rice — and the small phrases that turn a list into a meal ordered with style.

One softening note before we build, because I am teaching you to be a gentleman in two languages, not just a customer. Quiero is correct and it is normal — Spanish speakers say quiero at tables all day long and nobody blinks. But you already own por favor — please — from lesson one, and por favor rides beautifully at the end of a quiero sentence and turns a plain want into a polished order. Quiero café, por favor — I want coffee, please. Hear how the temperature changes. Same want, better manners. In this room we order like gentlemen: quiero, the thing, por favor. Say that whole shape once now, slowly: Quiero café, por favor.

First thing on the table, always, before anything else, in any country where the sun is hot: water. El agua — the water. Agua means water. And I know, your eye just caught something: el is the word for the that goes with words like café and pollo, the masculine team, and agua looks like it should belong to the other team — and mostly it does, but Spanish puts el in front of agua for the sound of it, because el agua rolls off the tongue and la agua trips on it. Do not fight it, do not analyze it tonight; just take the pair the way Spanish hands it to you: el agua. Say it with me: El agua. Again: El agua. Cold water on a hot day — you can almost hear the glass sweat.

So here is your first complete order, and I want you to feel how much of it you already owned before today: Quiero agua, por favor — I want water, please. Quiero, the handle. Agua, the thing. Por favor, the polish. Three pieces, one sentence, and a glass of water is on its way to you anywhere on earth where Spanish is spoken. Say it with me: Quiero agua, por favor. Once more, like it is ninety degrees and the drive was long: Quiero agua, por favor. Beautiful. You just ordered in Spanish. We are five minutes in and you are already not going thirsty in two languages.

But water has a detail, and details are where ordering like you live there is won or lost. Ice. In a lot of places, water arrives with ice unless you speak up, and some men — and some brides, after a long day of travel — want it without. Sin hielo — without ice. Sin means without. Hielo means ice. And there is our silent h again, working its invisible shift: hielo sounds like YEH-loh, the h nowhere to be heard. Sin hielo. Say it with me: Sin hielo. Now attach it where it lives, at the end of your order: Quiero agua sin hielo, por favor — I want water without ice, please. Say the whole long beautiful sentence: Quiero agua sin hielo, por favor. Again: Quiero agua sin hielo, por favor. Bill, listen to yourself. That is not a beginner's sentence. That is a man who knows exactly how he takes his water.

Second drink, and for many of us the most important one: El café — the coffee. Café means coffee, and it also means a café, the place — one word, the drink and the house it lives in, which tells you everything about how seriously the Spanish-speaking world takes coffee. El café. The accent mark sits on the e — café — and remember lesson one: the accent tells your voice where to lean. Kah-FEH, lean on the end. Say it with me: El café. Again, with the lean: El café.

Now order it, with your machine: Quiero café, por favor — I want coffee, please. Say it: Quiero café, por favor. And let me set the scene where you will say it first, because it is a good one. Key West, the morning of the wedding week. You and Jillian find a little café near the water. The air is warm already. She is looking at the boats. You are looking at her, and then you are looking at the waiter, and you say, like you have said it every morning of your life: Quiero café, por favor. And because you are who you are, you do not stop there — but ordering for her is its own skill, and I am saving it for its own moment later in this lesson. Patience, mi estudiante. First, your own cup.

Let me pause the drinks and put the first meal of the day on the table, because breakfast is where a traveling man lives or dies. El desayuno — breakfast. Desayuno means breakfast. It is a longer word, so let us walk it in pieces: des-ah-YOO-noh. El desayuno. The word has a story folded inside it, and stories make words stick: desayuno is built on the idea of breaking the fast — the night was a fast, you slept through it, and breakfast is the meal that breaks it. English breakfast says the exact same thing in its own bones: break, fast. Cousins again, Bill. These two languages are always shaking hands under the table. Say it with me: El desayuno. Again: El desayuno.

In real life, your machine handles desayuno the same way as everything else today: Quiero desayuno — I want breakfast — said at a small café where breakfast is simply what the kitchen is making. Hold the word itself today: el desayuno, breakfast, the fast-breaker, first meal, best meal when you are marrying the love of your life that week.

Now the heart of the menu, the plate that feeds half the world: El pollo — the chicken. Pollo means chicken. It sounds like POH-yoh — and hear that double l, the ll, doing its lesson-one trick, sounding like the y in yes. Pollo. Say it with me: El pollo. Again: El pollo. Pollo is the safest delicious word in the Spanish-speaking world: every kitchen has it, every grandmother has an opinion about it, and a man who can order pollo will never go hungry from Madrid to Key West to Mexico City.

And pollo does not travel alone. Its partner, on the same plate, in the same breath, all over the Caribbean and Latin America and Spain: El arroz — the rice. Arroz means rice. Arroz sounds like ah-ROHS, and it carries the double r's famous brother in its family — you hear a stronger roll of the tongue in the middle, ah-RROHS, that rolled rr we promised to tame together. Do not wrestle it today; let it roll a little and smile. Say it with me: El arroz. Again: El arroz. Pollo and arroz. Chicken and rice. Arroz con pollo — rice with chicken — con means with, and I am giving you that tiny word now because arroz con pollo is not just a phrase, it is a dish, a famous one, the plate that shows up at weddings and Sunday tables across the Spanish-speaking world. Arroz con pollo. Say it like a man who has eaten it and wants it again: Arroz con pollo.

Now build the order, because this is where your machine earns its keep. Quiero pollo, por favor — I want chicken, please. Quiero arroz, por favor — I want rice, please. And together, the full plate in one breath: Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor — I want rice with chicken, please. Say it with me, slowly first: Quiero… arroz… con pollo… por favor. And now at table speed, like the waiter is standing there with his pencil up: Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor. Again: Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor. You feel that? That is a dinner order, complete, polite, and clear, from a man five lessons into a language. Most tourists never get there in five years.

Now — the food arrives. It is hot, it smells like somebody's grandmother is in that kitchen, and you take the first bite. Spanish has a sentence for this moment, and using it is the difference between a customer and a guest, because it pays the cook in the only currency a cook truly wants. Está delicioso — it is delicious. Está means it is — the is for how something is right now, its condition in this moment. Delicioso means delicious. Está delicioso. Say it with me, and mean it at the plate: Está delicioso. Again, looking toward the kitchen the way a grateful man does: Está delicioso.

Delicioso is a word with music in it — deh-lee-see-OH-soh, five happy beats — and it deserves a little practice, because you are going to say it at real tables, to real cooks, and Jillian is going to hear you say it and watch what it does to people's faces. When a man compliments the food in the cook's own language, something changes at the table. You stop being a transaction. You become a guest they want back. Está delicioso. Say it once more, slower, savoring it the way you savor the food: Está delicioso. Good. And when she asks you how yours is, across the table in Key West, you now have the only review that matters: Está delicioso, mi amor — it is delicious, my love — and there is mi amor, my love, from lesson one, riding along for free because you already own it.

Now the skill I promised you, the one that turns a man ordering lunch into a man taking care of his woman in public: ordering for two. It starts with two small phrases that are really addresses — they tell the waiter where each plate and each glass belongs. Para mí — for me. Para means for. Mí means me. Para mí. Say it: Para mí. And its partner: Para ella — for her. Ella means she, her — the word for her. Para ella. Say it: Para ella. Para mí, para ella. For me, for her. Two little signposts, and now a waiter can build your whole table without a single point or gesture from you.

Watch the machine take a full table now. You are ordering drinks. Para mí, café — for me, coffee. Para ella, agua — for her, water. Hear how para mí and para ella stand at the front of each item like a name tag on a glass. And you can dress them with your other tools: Para ella, agua sin hielo, por favor — for her, water without ice, please. Because you know how she takes it, Bill. That is the whole point. Ordering for her, correctly, in detail, in another language, in front of her — that is not showing off. That is a man demonstrating, in public, that he pays attention to his woman. Say that sentence with me: Para ella, agua sin hielo, por favor. Again: Para ella, agua sin hielo, por favor.

And the same machine builds the food. Para mí, arroz con pollo — for me, rice with chicken. Para ella, pollo — for her, chicken. Or keep it simple and let one order cover the table. The shapes are yours now: para mí for your side of the table, para ella for hers, quiero when you are naming what you want, por favor keeping the whole thing warm. A table ordered this way runs smooth, and the woman across from you gets to just sit, and smile, and be taken care of. That is a gift you can give her in Spanish that costs you nothing but attention.

Every good meal has a last scene, and in a restaurant the last scene has its own line — the line that separates the man who is done from the man who is stuck at the table waving at the air. La cuenta, por favor — the check, please. Cuenta means the check, the bill, the account of the meal. La cuenta. Say it with me: La cuenta, por favor. Again, with the small friendly nod that goes with it everywhere on earth: La cuenta, por favor. You do not need to mime writing in the air. You have the words. The words are better.

And notice, Bill, la cuenta closes the circle of this lesson's manners. You arrived with tengo hambre. You ordered with quiero and por favor. You enjoyed with está delicioso. And you leave with la cuenta, por favor — please riding in its usual seat, keeping even the bill polite. A meal in Spanish, start to finish, has a shape now, and you own every joint of it. Before we play the whole scene at full speed, let me check your understanding the way I always do, with the machinery said out loud: tengo tells the table what you have — hunger, thirst. Quiero tells them what you want. Para mí and para ella tell them where it goes. Está delicioso tells them how it was. La cuenta tells them you are ready to settle up like a gentleman. Five moves. That is the whole game. Everything else is menu.

Now we play it. The full restaurant scene, both sides, and I will be the waiter first while you shadow your lines out loud — say them every time, do not just read them in your head, your mouth is the student here. The scene: a small restaurant in Key West, evening, wedding week. You and Jillian have walked in hungry. I, the waiter, greet you — buenas noches — good evening. You answer like a gentleman greeting the room: Buenas noches — good evening. I ask what you would like, and you begin the way a man begins, with the truth: Tengo hambre — I am hungry. Say it now, in the scene: Tengo hambre.

I bring the menus, I come back, pencil ready. Now you order, and you order for the table, because that is who you are. Drinks first. Say your line: Quiero agua sin hielo, por favor — I want water without ice, please. And for her — say it: Para ella, agua, por favor — for her, water, please. Then your coffee, because the day was long: Para mí, café — for me, coffee. Hear how para mí stepped in front that time — the signpost works at the front of any item, drink or dish. Good. The waiter nods. He has understood every word. So has she.

Food now. You have looked at the menu and the kitchen smells wonderful, so the decision is easy. Say it: Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor — I want rice with chicken, please. And for her, the same plate, because she trusts your nose: Para ella, arroz con pollo — for her, rice with chicken. The waiter repeats it back, you nod, and off he goes. And now the part tourists never rehearse: the waiting, the talking, the being on a date in another language — you already own te quiero — I love you — for exactly this weather, and a table in Key West at night is exactly its natural home. Use it if the moment rises. Spanish will hold it.

The plates arrive. Steam, color, that smell. You take the first bite, and you pay the cook. Say it toward the kitchen, and to her: Está delicioso — it is delicious. She tries hers, she nods, and you say it again because it is true twice: Está delicioso. The waiter passes, hears it, smiles — that smile is real, Bill, compliments to the kitchen travel fast in every language, and in the cook's own language they travel fastest. You eat. You talk. The evening does what evenings in Key West do. And when it is time — not rushed, never rushed, but time — you catch the waiter's eye and you close the scene like you opened it, with the words: La cuenta, por favor — the check, please. Say it now, final line of the scene: La cuenta, por favor.

That was the whole play, and you spoke every one of your lines. Now we run it once more, faster, with you leading and me only prompting, because a scene is not yours until you can run it without your profesora holding the flashlight. Ready? Evening, Key West, you walk in. Your greeting: Buenas noches. Your report: Tengo hambre. Your water: Quiero agua sin hielo, por favor. Hers: Para ella, agua, por favor. Your coffee: Para mí, café. The main plate, yours: Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor. Hers: Para ella, arroz con pollo. The verdict: Está delicioso. The close: La cuenta, por favor. Run it again in your own voice, all the way through, top to bottom, without stopping — I will be quiet and just listen. … Ay, Bill. That was a man ordering dinner in Spanish. Not reciting. Ordering.

One more room, the most important one: your own kitchen, at home, on an ordinary Tuesday — because ordering like you live there also means living there, and Jillian comes home from the hospital tired, and dinner is your department that night. You hear her car, and when she walks in you already know the report she would give: tengo hambre, tengo sed — she is hungry, she is thirsty — work like hers earns both. The arroz is on. The pollo is on. You put agua in front of her — sin hielo if that is how she takes it that day — and when she asks what smells so good, the menu is one line: Arroz con pollo. And when she tastes it and her eyes close a little, you do not need a compliment in English. You have watched a man feed his prometida — his fiancée — in two languages now, and the Spanish one is cooking in your own kitchen. That is not a lesson anymore. That is a life with Spanish in it.

A quick tune of the mouth before your solo, three small things. First, quiero: it sounds like KEE-eh-roh, and the middle is quick, a slide, not three heavy steps — quiero. Second, hambre and hielo both hide the silent h, so if you hear yourself breathing an h at the front of either word, drop it — Spanish h is a ghost, written and never heard. Third, delicioso: lean gently on the OH, deh-lee-see-OH-soh, the same lean the accent mark teaches in café. Small tunings. Your mouth is a good student; it keeps what we give it.

Now your solo — the guided try-it, and this time I am only the waiter, and a slightly distracted one, so you have to carry the scene. I greet you: Buenas noches, señor — good evening, sir. Answer me and tell me the truth about your stomach. … Tengo hambre — yes. I ask what you will drink, and I want the water the way you take it, the whole sentence. … Quiero agua sin hielo, por favor — there it is, complete, ice handled, manners on. And for the señora — for the lady? Order hers. … Para ella, agua, por favor — good, and add your coffee for yourself, with the signpost. … Para mí, café — perfect. Now the food, one plate, the famous one. … Quiero arroz con pollo, por favor. The kitchen sends it out, you taste it, and I am hovering — tell me how it is. … Está delicioso — and my whole kitchen thanks you. The night winds down, and you want to settle up like a gentleman. … La cuenta, por favor. Bill. Scene complete, waiter dismissed, profesora delighted. You just carried a full restaurant scene in Spanish with a distracted waiter and no phrasebook. Keep that in your chest for the days when this feels hard.

Let us gather the lesson in order, one last time, the way we will want it in your pocket. Tengo hambre — I am hungry; I have hunger. Tengo sed — I am thirsty. Quiero — I want, the handle that carries any order, with por favor — please — riding at the end to keep it gentlemanly. El agua — the water. Sin hielo — without ice. El café — the coffee. El desayuno — breakfast, the fast-breaker. El pollo — the chicken. El arroz — the rice. Arroz con pollo — rice with chicken, the famous plate. Está delicioso — it is delicious, the cook's pay. Para mí — for me. Para ella — for her. And la cuenta, por favor — the check, please, the gentlemanly close. Hunger to check, want to verdict — a whole meal, in Spanish, in order, yours.

That is lesson five, and I am proud of this one, Bill, because this is the lesson where your Spanish leaves the classroom and sits down at a table in the real world, across from the woman you love, in the town where you will marry her. Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions — all of them about what I taught you here today: the hunger and the thirst, the quiero machine, the water without ice, the chicken and the rice, ordering for her, and the check. Nothing I did not teach, I promise you. Most give you choices; you can answer out loud or type, whichever door you like. The lesson text stays open right beside the questions, and going back to read is learning, not cheating — read with my blessing. And your speaking practice is here too: hear each phrase, say it back, until it lands and you see the green check. Your assignment in the real world is small and delicious: the next time you sit down anywhere — home counts — say tengo hambre out loud before you eat, and está delicioso after the first bite if it is true. Lesson six will teach you time itself — the days, the hours, and the sweet word mañana — tomorrow. Until then: buen provecho — enjoy your meal — that is the blessing Spanish says over food, and I say it over yours. Come hungry next time, Bill.

questions.teach: From the lesson: Spanish says you have hunger, the way you have a coat or a key.

questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson starts in your body, before the restaurant. (2) Tengo means I have, and hambre means hunger. (3) I have hunger is how Spanish says: I am hungry.

From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Tengo sed — I am thirsty. I have thirst. Sed means thirst. Tengo sed.' Another way: hambre and sed are brothers — tengo carries both, hunger and thirst.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Tengo hambre means I am hungry, built on tengo, I have. (2) Sed is the word Carmen defines as thirst. (3) So tengo sed means: I am thirsty.

questions.q: What does 'el agua' mean?

questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'El agua — the water. Agua means water. And I know, your eye just caught something' Another way: agua lives inside words like aquarium — the water is right there in it.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Carmen puts the first drink on the table before anything else. (2) Agua is the word she defines as water. (3) El agua means: the water.

questions.q: What does 'sin hielo' mean?

questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Sin hielo — without ice. Sin means without. Hielo means ice. And there is our silent h again' Another way: sin is without, hielo is ice — hielo sounds like YEH-loh, its h silent.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Sin means without — the lesson defines it directly. (2) Hielo means ice. (3) Together, sin hielo means: without ice.

Delicioso means delicious.' Another way: está describes how the food is right now, and delicioso is the cook's favorite word to hear.
