lessons.title: Lesson 6 — Time and days: schedules, appointments, and mañana
paragraphs: Hola, Bill — hello, Bill. Soy la profesora Carmen Vega — I am Professor Carmen Vega, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Sit down, mi estudiante — my student — and look at the clock with me, because today we learn time itself. This is lesson six: time and days — schedules, appointments, and the sweetest word in the Spanish language, mañana — tomorrow. By the end of this half hour you will be able to say what day it is, ask what time it is, say when your appointment is, tell whether you are early or late, and — because this course always has a second mission running under the first — you will own the sweet everyday words for the door of your own house: the good morning, the good day wish, and the I love you that Jillian hears before the day takes her.

Here is why time comes now, at lesson six, and not later. A language without time in it can only talk about this exact second. You can greet, you can eat — lesson five fed you well — but you cannot plan, and your life, Bill, is a plan with a date on it. March the twenty-fifth, twenty twenty-seven, Key West: la boda — the wedding — and I am using that word early today on purpose, because next lesson is built on it. Between now and that date there are appointments, arrivals, dinners, a schedule with her name and yours all over it. A man who can handle days and hours in Spanish can handle a wedding week in Spanish. That is what we are building today: your calendar, in her favorite language.

Same method as always, because it has carried you five lessons without failing: I say it, you say it back to me out loud, the way you mean it, and only then do we move on. When I say say it with me, I want to hear you. And when the lesson ends, the questions wait below — all about what I teach here, nothing else — and the full text stays open beside you while you answer. Reading again is learning, not cheating. You know this. Now, we start where every schedule starts: with the three days you actually live in.

First day, the one you are standing in: Hoy — today. Hoy means today. It is a small word with that silent h doing its invisible work again — hoy sounds like oy, the h written and never heard, exactly as lesson one promised you. Hoy. Say it with me: Hoy. Everything you do before midnight tonight happens hoy. This lesson is happening hoy. Say it once more, and point at the floor under your feet, because that is where today lives: Hoy.

Second day, the famous one, the word this lesson is named for: Mañana — tomorrow. Mañana means tomorrow. And mañana has a secret I want you to hold gently: the same word, mañana, also means morning — la mañana — the morning. Spanish uses one word for tomorrow and for morning, and once you hear why, you will never forget it: tomorrow is just the next morning, arriving. When a Spanish speaker says mañana, they are picturing the sun coming up on the next day. It is the most hopeful word in the language — nothing is ever finished, there is always a mañana. Say it with me, slowly, it is a beautiful word: Mañana. Again: Mañana. And hear the ñ in it — that n with the little wave on top, which sounds like the ny in canyon. Mah-NYAH-nah. Mañana.

Third day, and I will teach this one lightly, the way I promised — just enough to recognize it and use it simply: Ayer — yesterday. Ayer means yesterday. Ayer sounds like ah-YEHR. Say it with me: Ayer. Three days, three words, and your whole life fits inside them: Ayer, hoy, mañana. Yesterday, today, tomorrow. What happened ayer is done. What you do hoy is yours. What you promise for mañana is hope with a date on it. Say the three in order, like a man walking across his own week: Ayer. Hoy. Mañana. Again: Ayer, hoy, mañana.

Now watch how these three words plug into sentences you already own, because Spanish rewards a man who combines. Hoy tengo hambre — today I am hungry — and there is your lesson-five tengo hambre — I am hungry — wearing a day on its front. Days ride at the front of Spanish sentences like a name tag on the day itself: hoy, this; mañana, that. Mañana tengo una cita — tomorrow I have an appointment — and I just spent a phrase we have not built yet, una cita — an appointment — so hold it in your hand for a few minutes; we are coming to it properly, and it is one of today's headline words. First, the week itself, because appointments live in weeks.

La semana — the week. Semana means week. La semana. Say it with me: La semana. A week is seven days standing in a row, and Spanish lines them up starting on Monday — the Spanish week begins with work, and rests at the end, which any working man will tell you is the honest order. Here come los días de la semana — the days of the week — and días you already own from buenos días — good morning — back in lesson one: días means days. Los días de la semana: the days of the week. We will take them one at a time, in order, and I will give each one a small hook, because seven new words in a row is a parade and I want you to remember every soldier in it.

Lunes — Monday. Lunes is the day of la luna — the moon — and luna is right there inside the English word lunar; Monday in Spanish is moonday, plain as the sky. Lunes. Say it: Lunes. Martes — Tuesday. Martes carries Mars, the old war god, inside it — Tuesday was his day; you can hear Mars clearing his throat inside martes. Martes. Say it: Martes. Miércoles — Wednesday. Miércoles is the long one, so walk it in pieces: mee-EHR-koh-les. Miércoles carries Mercury, the fast one, the messenger — a busy middle-of-the-week day with a busy name. Say it in pieces with me: Miér… coles. Miércoles. Again, whole: Miércoles.

Jueves — Thursday. Jueves carries Jupiter, the king — the biggest planet for the day that is almost, almost the weekend. Jueves sounds like HWEH-ves, and yes, that j at the front is a strong breathy h sound in Spanish, nothing like the English j — one more honest sound for your collection. Say it: Jueves. Viernes — Friday. Viernes carries Venus, the goddess of love — and Bill, I have always loved that Spanish puts love's day at the end of the work week, as if the week itself is walking toward her. Viernes. Say it with a smile: Viernes.

And the weekend, the two days the whole week leans toward. Sábado — Saturday. Sábado is the sabbath day, the rest day — you can hear sabbath inside sábado if you listen with your heart. Sábado. Say it: Sábado. And domingo — Sunday. Domingo is the Lord's day, from the old word for the Lord — the quiet day, the family day, the day a man in Michigan might drive to see his dad or sit on a porch doing absolutely nothing, on purpose. Domingo. Say it: Domingo.

Now the whole parade, in order, and I want you to say them with me twice — once slow, once at the speed of a man reading his own calendar. Slow first: Lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Again, at calendar speed: Lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo. Good. And notice what your ear just learned: five of the seven end in that same -es drumbeat — lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes — and the weekend sings a different tune, sábado, domingo. That rhythm is a memory hook all by itself. The week marches, then the week rests.

How do you use a day once you own it? The first use is simply naming today, and Spanish keeps it simple: Hoy es lunes — today is Monday — hoy, today; es, is. Hoy es lunes. Change the day and the sentence follows like a dog: Hoy es viernes — today is Friday. Say both with me: Hoy es lunes. Hoy es viernes. And the second use is planning, where mañana does the heavy lifting: Mañana es sábado — tomorrow is Saturday. Say it: Mañana es sábado. A man who can say what today is and what tomorrow is can hold a whole conversation about a schedule standing on those two sentences alone, and I have heard men do exactly that at hotel desks all over the Spanish-speaking world.

Now, inside each day live the hours, and here is the question that unlocks them — the question you will ask in train stations, hotel lobbies, and your own kitchen: ¿Qué hora es? — what time is it? Word for word: what hour is it. Qué means what. Hora means hour — and hora is a cousin of the English word hour itself, same old root, and it hides another silent h: hora sounds like OH-rah. ¿Qué hora es? Say it with me: ¿Qué hora es? Again, like a man checking whether he is late for the best appointment of his life: ¿Qué hora es?

The answer has a shape, and the shape changes exactly once, at one o'clock, and Spanish is very proud of the tidiness of it. For one o'clock, you say: Es la una — it is one o'clock. Es, it is. La una, the one. Una is one, in the form it takes beside hora — because hora belongs to the la team, the feminine team, and una dresses to match it, the same matching you saw in lesson one with buenos and buenas. Es la una. Say it with me: Es la una. Only one o'clock gets es la — because there is only one of it. One hour, singular, es la una. Hold that: the one is special.

Every other hour stands in a crowd, so the verb grows to match: Son las dos — it is two o'clock. Son means they are, it is, for the plural hours. Las dos — the two. Dos means two. Son las dos. Say it: Son las dos. And the machine just keeps building: Son las tres — it is three o'clock — tres means three. Son las cuatro — it is four o'clock — cuatro means four. Son las cinco — it is five o'clock — cinco means five. Hear the frame holding steady: son las, and then the number rides in the last seat. Son las dos, son las tres, son las cuatro, son las cinco. Say the run with me, up the clock: Son las dos. Son las tres. Son las cuatro. Son las cinco. And step back down to the special one, so your ear owns the difference: Es la una. Son las dos. One is es la; everything after is son las. That is the whole law of the Spanish clock, and you just learned it in one breath.

Let me check your understanding the way I always do, by making you drive. I ask: ¿Qué hora es? — what time is it? — and the clock on the wall says two. You answer: Son las dos. The clock says one — careful now, the special one: Es la una. The clock says five: Son las cinco. Good. Your mouth hesitated at la una and then got it — that hesitation is the sound of a new rule settling in, and it settles faster every time you use it. One more round, quick: three o'clock — Son las tres. Four o'clock — Son las cuatro. One o'clock — Es la una. Perfecto — perfect — and that word you may have just because you earned it.

Now, what are hours for? In a grown man's life, hours are for appointments — the moments where a day and an hour shake hands. Tengo una cita — I have an appointment. Una cita means an appointment — una, an; cita, appointment. And listen to tengo doing its second job of your course: in lesson five, tengo hambre meant I have hunger; here, tengo una cita means I have an appointment. Same tengo — I have — carrying a new load. That is the compound interest of this language, Bill: every strong word you learn keeps paying you in new sentences. Say it with me: Tengo una cita. Again, like a man whose calendar matters: Tengo una cita.

And una cita has a sweet second meaning I will give you honestly, because you will smile when you hear it: cita is also the word for a date — the romantic kind. Una cita can be the dentist, and una cita can be dinner with Jillian. Spanish uses one word for both, and context — and your face — tells everyone which kind you mean. When you say tengo una cita about an evening in Key West, nobody in that restaurant is picturing a dentist. Context is king. Say it once with the appointment meaning, businesslike: Tengo una cita. And once with the other meaning, the Key West meaning, slower: Tengo una cita. Hear that? Same words. Different evening entirely.

Now build a real schedule sentence, the kind a wedding week runs on, stacking today's bricks in order: day, then the cita, then the hour. Mañana tengo una cita — tomorrow I have an appointment. Add the hour with a — at — the little word a means at when it stands before a time: a las tres — at three o'clock. Mañana tengo una cita a las tres — tomorrow I have an appointment at three o'clock. Say it with me in pieces: Mañana… tengo una cita… a las tres. Whole now: Mañana tengo una cita a las tres. Again: Mañana tengo una cita a las tres. Bill, that is a sentence a man's whole week can hang on. And it is wedding-week true, by the way — there will be a rehearsal, a license errand, a dinner reservation, a hundred citas, and you can now name every one of them in Spanish.

Two words remain in the time toolkit, and they are the two that decide whether a man is calm or running: Temprano — early. Temprano means early. Tem-PRAH-no. Say it: Temprano. And its opposite: Tarde — late. Tarde means late — and tarde is a double agent you have actually met before: buenas tardes — good afternoon — from lesson one, because tarde also means afternoon, the late part of the day. Same word, two jobs, and the connection is honest: the afternoon is the day's late part, and arriving tarde is arriving in the day's late part of where you were supposed to be. You will never confuse them in real life; the sentence around the word tells you which job it is doing. Say the pair: Temprano. Tarde. Early. Late. Temprano, tarde.

Use them where they live. A man checks his watch outside an office and says, with relief: Es temprano — it is early — es, it is; temprano, early. Or the other truth, said at a run: Es tarde — it is late. And for the wedding week, here is the sentence I actually want in your pocket, because grooms earn it: the morning of la boda, somebody will ask if there is time, and you, calm as a lake, will answer with the clock and the calm together. But that scene belongs to next lesson. Today, just own the pair cold: temprano, early; tarde, late. Say them once more, and put the feeling in each: Temprano — relaxed. Tarde — hurrying. There. Your body knows them now too.

Time to change rooms — from the calendar to the front door of your own house — because here is where the Spanish-for-Jillian strand of this lesson lives, and it is the part of today you will use first, tomorrow morning, before any appointment on any calendar. The scene: early morning, your kitchen, Jillian heading out to the hospital or just starting her day, and you are the man at the door. Spanish has a whole little ceremony for this, and you already own its first line from lesson one. Buenos días, mi amor — good morning, my love — buenos días, good morning; mi amor, my love. Say it with me, at kitchen-in-the-morning volume: Buenos días, mi amor. Again, like you have been waiting to say it: Buenos días, mi amor.

Second line of the ceremony, a wish you send out the door with her: Que tengas un buen día — have a good day. Word for word, it is a wish: may you have a good day. Que tengas — may you have. Un buen día — a good day — and there is día, day, from lesson one, and buen, good, the short strong form of the word you met as buenos. Que tengas un buen día. It is the longest sentence in today's strand, so take it in pieces: Que tengas… un buen día. Whole: Que tengas un buen día. Say it again, to the picture of her with her bag on her shoulder: Que tengas un buen día. That sentence, Bill, is a man blessing his woman's day before she walks into a hard one — and nurses' days are hard ones. She will carry it into that hospital like a note in her pocket.

Third line, the one you already own and love, now placed exactly where it lives in a real day — at the door, as she leaves: Te quiero — I love you — the everyday I love you, the one from lesson one, the one that lives in the house. Te quiero at the door is not a small thing. Te quiero at the door, said every morning, is a marriage being built one ordinary day at a time, and the wedding in March is just the day everybody else finds out. Say it the way it will actually be said, quick and warm and certain, because she is already halfway to the car: Te quiero. Again: Te quiero. And if she is mi amor in the morning greeting, she can be the full sentence too: Te quiero, mi amor — I love you, my love. Say it: Te quiero, mi amor.

And when she comes home, or when you are the one leaving and the goodbye is only for a few hours, Spanish keeps the door gentle: Hasta luego — see you later. Hasta means until. Luego means later, soon. Hasta luego: until later. It is the softest goodbye in the language — not an ending, a pause. Nobody says goodbye forever at a kitchen door at seven in the morning; you say hasta luego, because you will see her at dinner and you both know it. Say it with me: Hasta luego. Again, with a hand raised at the door: Hasta luego.

And the last sweet word of the strand, for the end of the day or the quiet moment in it: Mi corazón — my heart — from lesson one, the word that means it literally, the organ in your chest. Buenos días, mi corazón — good morning, my heart — works in the morning. Te quiero, mi corazón — I love you, my heart — works at the door. The strand gives you two names for her, mi amor and mi corazón, my love and my heart, and a man rotates them the way the day rotates: amor for the morning, corazón for the night, or the other way around — she will not be grading the rotation, Bill. She will be hearing that her name, in your mouth, in Spanish, is love and heart and nothing else. Say both names now, one after the other: Mi amor. Mi corazón.

Now let us run the whole door ceremony, start to finish, the way tomorrow morning can actually go, and I will narrate while you speak your lines out loud. She comes into the kitchen, bag in hand, keys in hand, the day already pulling at her. You are ready. Line one: Buenos días, mi amor — good morning, my love. She smiles — she will smile. Line two, the blessing for her day: Que tengas un buen día — have a good day. Line three, at the door itself, the one that lives in the house: Te quiero — I love you. And as the door opens and the morning takes her, the soft goodbye: Hasta luego — see you later. Four lines. Buenos días, mi amor. Que tengas un buen día. Te quiero. Hasta luego. Run it once more, all four, in your own voice, no narration from me. … That, Bill, is a morning. Not a lesson exercise — a morning, in your house, starting mañana, if you want it. Mañana. Tomorrow. See how the word keeps its promise?

Now your guided try-it, the schedule round, because I am your profesora and the calendar must be driven, not just admired. I am the front desk of a hotel in Key West, wedding week, and you are the groom with arrangements to make. I ask you: ¿Qué día es hoy? — what day is it today? — qué, what; día, day; hoy, today — a new question, and you already own its answer's shape. The calendar says Wednesday. Answer me: Hoy es miércoles — today is Wednesday. Say it: Hoy es miércoles. Good. Now you have an errand — the marriage license office, let us say, because grooms have errands — and you tell me when: Mañana tengo una cita — tomorrow I have an appointment. Say it: Mañana tengo una cita. At what hour? The office said three. Add it: A las tres — at three o'clock. Whole sentence now, groom, all of it: Mañana tengo una cita a las tres. And I, the desk, check the clock and ask: ¿Qué hora es? It says one. Careful — the special one. Answer: Es la una. And because it is one and your cita is tomorrow, you are not late, you are the other word: Temprano — early. Say the verdict with the relief it deserves: Temprano. Scene complete. You just ran a hotel desk in Spanish, and every arrangement survived.

One more drive around the block, faster, mixing the calendar and the door, because real days mix them. It is Friday morning — hoy es viernes — today is Friday. She is leaving for the hospital. The door ceremony, quick and warm: Buenos días, mi amor. Que tengas un buen día. Te quiero. Hasta luego. The day turns. Your phone buzzes: a cita, hoy, a las cinco — today, at five o'clock — hoy, today; a las cinco, at five. You check the time: ¿Qué hora es? — son las dos — it is two o'clock — so you have hours, you are temprano, early, a man ahead of his own day. Evening comes, she is home, and the day closes the way lesson one taught you it could. That is a whole day run in Spanish, Bill — calendar, clock, appointment, and heart — and you drove every mile of it.

Hooks, so today sticks. Mañana and morning are one word because tomorrow is the next morning — you will never lose that one. Hora is hour with its h asleep — the same root, the same word, wearing Spanish clothes. Cita — appointment — sounds a little like city, and a man's citas do tend to happen where the buildings are; better hook: a cita is a citation to appear — the court cites you, the calendar cites you, and the romantic cita is the one appointment you are happy to be summoned to. Temprano — early — I remember it as the temper of a calm man: the temprano man is never in a temper, because he is never late. And tarde you already own twice — afternoon and late — the day's late part, both times. Hang the words on what you already know, and they stay furniture, not homework.

Let us gather the lesson in order, one last time. Hoy — today. Mañana — tomorrow, and also morning, the next morning arriving. Ayer — yesterday, lightly held. La semana — the week, and los días de la semana — the days of the week: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo — Monday through Sunday. Hoy es lunes — today is Monday — the shape for naming any day. ¿Qué hora es? — what time is it? Es la una — it is one o'clock, the special one. Son las dos, son las tres, son las cuatro, son las cinco — it is two, three, four, five o'clock, the crowd pattern. Tengo una cita — I have an appointment, and maybe, in Key West, a date. Temprano — early. Tarde — late. And the door strand, the heart of the day: Buenos días, mi amor — good morning, my love. Que tengas un buen día — have a good day. Te quiero — I love you, at the door. Hasta luego — see you later. Mi corazón — my heart.

That is lesson six, and you did it the way you do everything that matters, Bill — all the way through. Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions, all of them about what I taught you here: the three days, the week, the clock and its special one o'clock, the cita, early and late, and the words for the door. Nothing I did not teach. Most give you choices; answer out loud or type, whichever door you like. The lesson text stays open beside the questions, and reading any of it again is learning, not cheating — that is what it is there for. Your speaking practice is here too: hear each phrase, say it back, until the green check lands. And your real-world assignment is the door ceremony, tomorrow morning, all four lines, to her, at the actual door. Mañana, Bill. The word is a promise, and so is the assignment. Lesson seven is the big one — la boda, the wedding itself, in Key West, and the deepest words I will ever teach you. Sleep well tonight. Hasta luego, mi estudiante. Mañana we marry off your Spanish.

phrases.meaning: it is one o'clock — the special one

questions.q: What does 'hoy' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the first of the three days you actually live in.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Hoy means today. It is a small word with that silent h doing its invisible work again' Another way: hoy is the day you are standing in — everything before midnight tonight happens hoy.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson teaches three days: ayer, hoy, mañana. (2) Hoy is the middle one, the day under your feet. (3) Hoy means: today.

questions.q: What does 'mañana' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the sweetest word in Spanish — tomorrow is just the next morning arriving.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mañana — tomorrow. Mañana means tomorrow. And mañana has a secret I want you to hold gently: the same word, mañana, also means morning' Another way: mañana does two jobs — tomorrow, and morning — because tomorrow is the next morning.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Ayer is yesterday and hoy is today. (2) The third day, the hopeful one, is mañana. (3) Mañana means: tomorrow.

questions.q: What does '¿Qué hora es?' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the question that unlocks the hours, in stations, lobbies, and your own kitchen.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: '¿Qué hora es? — what time is it? Word for word: what hour is it. Qué means what.' Another way: qué is what, and hora is hour — the question asks what hour it is.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Hora means hour, a cousin of the English word hour. (2) ¿Qué hora es? asks about the hour. (3) It means: what time is it?

questions.q: The clock says one o'clock. What is the correct answer to '¿Qué hora es?'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: one o'clock is the special one — the only hour that gets es la.
questions.teach2: From the lesson: 'For one o'clock, you say: Es la una — it is one o'clock. Es, it is. La una, the one.' From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Es la una — it is one o'clock. Es, it is. La una, the one. Una is one' Another way: one hour is singular, so it stands alone with es la; the plural hours use son las.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Every hour after one uses son las. (2) One o'clock is the exception, because there is only one of it. (3) One o'clock is: Es la una.

questions.q: The clock says two o'clock. What is the correct answer to '¿Qué hora es?'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: every hour after one stands in a crowd, so the verb grows to match.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Son las dos — it is two o'clock. Son means they are, it is, for the plural hours.' Another way: the frame is son las plus the number — dos is two, so son las dos is two o'clock.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Es la una belongs to one o'clock only. (2) Two is a plural hour, so it takes son las. (3) With dos, two, the answer is: Son las dos.

questions.q: Which day of the week is 'miércoles'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the long one in the middle of the parade of days.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Miércoles — Wednesday. Miércoles is the long one, so walk it in pieces: mee-EHR-koh-les.' Another way: the week runs lunes, martes, miércoles — Wednesday is the third soldier in the parade.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Los días de la semana run lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo. (2) The third day is miércoles. (3) Counting from Monday, the third day is: Wednesday.

questions.q: What does 'Tengo una cita' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: tengo doing its second job — I have, carrying an appointment this time.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Tengo una cita — I have an appointment. Una cita means an appointment' Another way: una cita can also be a date, the romantic kind — context, and your face, tell everyone which.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Tengo means I have — the same tengo as tengo hambre. (2) Una cita is an appointment. (3) Together they mean: I have an appointment.

questions.q: What does 'temprano' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: one of the two words that decide whether a man is calm or running.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Temprano — early. Temprano means early. Tem-PRAH-no. Say it: Temprano. And its opposite: Tarde — late.' Another way: temprano is the calm word; its opposite, tarde, is late.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Carmen teaches the pair together: temprano and tarde. (2) Tarde is the late one. (3) So temprano means: early.

questions.q: Jillian is heading out the door, and Bill wants to bless her day the way Carmen taught him. What does 'Que tengas un buen día' mean?
accept: may you have a good day
questions.teach: From the lesson: the second line of the door ceremony — a wish you send out the door with her.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Que tengas un buen día — have a good day. Word for word, it is a wish: may you have a good day.' Another way: un buen día is a good day, and the sentence wishes it to her as she leaves.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Día means day, and buen means good. (2) The sentence is a wish for her day, said at the door. (3) Que tengas un buen día means: have a good day.

questions.q: Bill has a wedding-week errand at the license office. Which sentence tells the hotel desk it is tomorrow at three o'clock?
questions.answer: Mañana tengo una cita a las tres
accept: tomorrow I have an appointment at three o'clock
choices: Mañana tengo una cita a las tres
questions.mcAnswer: Mañana tengo una cita a las tres
questions.teach: From the lesson: a full schedule sentence — day, cita, and hour stacked in order.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Mañana tengo una cita a las tres — tomorrow I have an appointment at three o'clock.' Another way: mañana sets the day, tengo una cita sets the appointment, and a las tres sets the hour.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The errand is mañana, tomorrow — not hoy. (2) It is una cita, an appointment, at a las tres, at three o'clock. (3) Stacked in order: Mañana tengo una cita a las tres.

questions.q: Jillian is leaving for the hospital, and Bill wants the soft goodbye — the one that is a pause, not an ending. What does he say?
questions.teach: From the lesson: hasta luego — until later — nobody says goodbye forever at a kitchen door.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Hasta luego — see you later. Hasta means until. Luego means later, soon. Hasta luego: until later.' Another way: hasta is until and luego is later — until later, because he will see her at dinner.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Buenos días greets the morning; it does not say goodbye. (2) The lesson's soft goodbye is built from hasta, until, and luego, later. (3) That goodbye is: Hasta luego.

questions.q: In your own words: why does one o'clock get 'es la una' while two o'clock gets 'son las dos'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the whole law of the Spanish clock, in one breath.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Only one o'clock gets es la — because there is only one of it. One hour, singular, es la una.'
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) One o'clock is a single hour, singular, so it uses es la una. (2) Two and every hour after stand plural, in a crowd. (3) Plural hours use son las — son las dos.

lessons.title: Lesson 7 — The wedding: Key West — love words, vows, and the day itself
paragraphs: Hola, Bill — hello, Bill. Soy la profesora Carmen Vega — I am Professor Carmen Vega, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Sit down, and take a breath with me, because today is not an ordinary lesson. This is lesson seven: the wedding. La boda — the wedding — in Key West, with the love words, the vows, and the day itself. Everything in this course has been walking toward a date — March the twenty-fifth, twenty twenty-seven — and today we walk straight into that date and learn to speak inside it. By the end of this half hour, you will own the words for the day: the wedding, the ring, the beach, the dress, the vows — and you will own the deepest sentence in the Spanish language, placed exactly where it belongs, and a short vow, in Spanish, that you can actually say, standing up, in front of everybody, with your whole heart in it.

Let me tell you plainly why this lesson sits here, at seven, and not at the end of the course. Because you are not learning Spanish for a test, Bill. You are learning it for a woman and a day. A man preparing to marry learns the words of the marriage the way he learns everything that matters: early, carefully, and with time to practice until they feel like his own skin. You have months between hoy — today — and the day itself, and that is exactly right. These words deserve months. A vow is not a phrase you cram the night before. A vow is a sentence you live inside until saying it is as natural as breathing. So we learn it today, and then you carry it, and practice it, and by the time you stand on that beach it will not be Spanish you memorized. It will be Spanish you mean.

Our method holds, as always: I say it, you say it back to me out loud, the way you mean it — and in this lesson, mi estudiante — my student — I ask you to mean it a little more than usual, because these are not restaurant words. When I say say it with me today, say it the way you will say it there. Quiet counts. Standing in your kitchen saying these words at practice volume is not silly; it is rehearsal, and every groom who ever lived has rehearsed in a kitchen. And when the lesson ends, the questions wait below, all about what I teach here, and the text stays open beside you. Reading again is learning, not cheating. Now. Let us go to Key West.

First, the word for the day itself: La boda — the wedding. Boda means wedding. La boda. Say it with me: La boda. Again, like a man who has a date with it: La boda. It is a warm, round word — BOH-dah — and it names the whole event: the ceremony, the celebration, the day everybody dresses for and cries at and remembers forever. Not the marriage that comes after — Spanish keeps those in separate drawers — la boda is the day. The party and the promise, folded into one word. When people in Key West ask you that week what brings you to town, your answer can be one proud phrase: La boda — the wedding. Say it once more: La boda.

Where does la boda happen? For you, in the place you two chose: La playa — the beach. Playa means beach. La playa. Say it: La playa. Key West gives you playa in every direction — sand, warm water, that light that makes everybody look like the best version of themselves. A wedding on la playa means the ocean is a guest, the wind is a guest, and shoes are optional in a way that makes everybody relax. And the sentence that puts your day in its place is simple, built from pieces you own: La boda es en la playa — the wedding is on the beach — es, is; en, in, on, at — en is the little word Spanish uses for all three, and context sorts it out. La boda es en la playa. Say it with me: La boda es en la playa. Again: La boda es en la playa. That sentence is a postcard, Bill, and you just wrote it in Spanish.

Now the objects of the day, because a wedding is carried by small things with enormous weight. First, the smallest and the heaviest: El anillo — the ring. Anillo means ring. El anillo. It sounds like ah-NEE-yoh, and hear the double l doing its old trick, the y sound, the same one living inside llamo from lesson one. Say it with me: El anillo. Again, slower, the way you would say it looking at it in its little box the night before: El anillo. A circle with no end — every culture on earth picked the same shape for the same promise, and Spanish names it anillo. You will hold one in your hand on la playa, and now you can name what you are holding, in the language of the day, while you hold it.

Second object, the one everybody will talk about: El vestido — the dress. Vestido means dress. El vestido. Say it: El vestido. In your case, el vestido is Jillian's — the wedding dress, the one you will not see until the day, because some traditions are smarter than curiosity. Spanish vestido comes from the same family as the English word vest — clothing words, both of them — cousins again, shaking hands under the table of the language. When she walks toward you on that beach, Bill, there will be a moment where the whole day narrows to one picture, and the picture has el vestido in it, and the wind off the water moving it a little. You do not need a long sentence for that moment. You may not have any sentence at all, in any language, and that is also correct. But the word is yours now for all the days around the day — the fittings, the talk, the careful carrying of it to Key West: el vestido.

Now the verb of the day, the action the whole event exists for: Casarse — to get married, to marry. Casarse means to get married. It is built on casa — house, home — and that is not an accident and it is not small: casarse, getting married, carries the house inside it, because in the deep logic of Spanish, marrying is making a home, founding a house, two people becoming one casa. I have taught this verb for years and that root still stops me. English marry is a fine word, but casarse tells you what the day is for. Say it with me: Casarse. Again: Casarse. And the way a man says it about himself, in the present, as a fact approaching on the calendar — me caso — I am getting married — me, I; caso, marry, from the same house-root. Me caso. Say it, groom: Me caso. Once more, standing a little straighter: Me caso.

Put the verb in its day and its place and you have the sentence that answers half the questions Key West will ask you: Me caso en la playa — I am getting married on the beach. And with the date riding on it, using lesson six: Me caso mañana — I am getting married tomorrow — mañana, tomorrow — the sentence you will get to say exactly once in your life, the day before, probably to a bartender or a stranger on a dock, and it will feel like electricity. Say both now: Me caso en la playa. Me caso mañana. Beautiful. And who is the man getting married marrying? You own that word from lesson one and it has been waiting six lessons for its biggest day: Mi prometida — my fiancée — the promised one. Mi prometida se llama Jillian — my fiancée's name is Jillian. On the day itself, at the start of it, she is still tu prometida — your fiancée — and then the day does its work, and a word changes. Hold that thought; the new word is coming, and it is one of today's treasures.

The ceremony has a heart, and the heart is spoken: Los votos — the vows. Votos means vows. Los votos. Say it: Los votos. A voto is a vow, a solemn promise — the same family as the English word vote, believe it or not, because a vote is also a kind of declared promise, a man stating where he stands. Los votos are where you stand, stated out loud, in front of witnesses, forever. At a wedding, everything else is decoration around los votos: la playa is the room, el vestido is the picture, el anillo is the symbol — los votos are the act itself. Words that change a life are the rarest things in any language, and you are about to own yours in two languages.

And at the center of the ceremony stands the smallest exchange in the whole day — two words from you that the entire event leans on: Sí, acepto — yes, I accept. Sí means yes — and notice sí carries an accent mark, the little leaning line, because Spanish has a twin word, si without the accent, which means if; the accent is how the written language tells yes from if, and your voice tells them apart by weight: sí, yes, said like a door opening. Acepto means I accept. Sí, acepto. Say it with me, at ceremony volume, which is not loud — it is clear: Sí, acepto. Again: Sí, acepto. When the question is asked on that beach — do you take this woman — the whole wedding, the whole year of planning, the whole life before it, narrows to those two words. A man does not need a speech at that moment. He needs two words he has practiced until they cannot shake. Sí, acepto. One more time, like the real one: Sí, acepto.

Now the phrase that turns two words into a lifetime: Para siempre — forever. Para means for — you own para from lesson five, para mí, para ella — for me, for her. Siempre means always. Para siempre: for always — forever. Say it with me, slowly, because this phrase should never be said fast: Para siempre. Again: Para siempre. Para siempre is the time signature of a wedding. Other promises have dates on them; this one refuses a date. When you say para siempre on la playa, you are telling the ocean and everybody on that sand: this does not expire. Hold the phrase gently. It is the heaviest light thing you will learn today.

And now, Bill, we arrive at the deepest water in this entire course, and I am going to teach it to you carefully and honestly, the way I promised you in lesson one that I would. You already own te quiero — I love you — the everyday one, the one that lives in the house, the one for the door in the morning and the coffee after a hard day. Today you meet its brother: Te amo — I love you. Te amo is the deep one. Amo comes from amar — to love, in the full, solemn, whole-life sense of the word. Te amo is not for the door. Te amo is not for Tuesdays. Te amo is the I love you of vows, of hospital rooms, of the biggest moments of a life — the one a man says when the sentence has to carry everything he has. Say it with me, once, at the volume it deserves, which is quiet and total: Te amo. Again: Te amo.

Hear the difference honestly, because a man should know the weight of his own words. Te quiero is love as daily bread — warm, constant, the love that shows up every morning and does the dishes. Te amo is love as oath — the same love, at its deepest register, spoken when the moment is as big as the feeling. Neither is false. Neither cancels the other. A marriage needs both: te quiero ten thousand times across the ordinary days, and te amo at the summits — and the first summit is la boda. This is why I seeded te quiero in lesson one and saved te amo for lesson seven: the everyday word had to become yours first, so that the deep one would land with its full weight when it arrived. It has arrived. Te amo, Bill. That sentence is the crown of this course, and it is yours as of today.

Let me make the difference physical, because your heart will need to choose between these two sentences for the rest of your life, and the choosing should be practiced, not guessed. I will give you a moment, and you say which sentence belongs in it — out loud, both words, so your mouth learns the choosing too. Moment one: she is leaving for the hospital in the morning, keys in her hand, and you are at the door. That is te quiero — I love you — the house one, the door one. Moment two: she has had the hardest day of her year, she is asleep before her head settles, and you are standing in the doorway looking at the woman you chose. Still te quiero, whispered — the everyday love covers the hard days too; it is not a lesser love, it is the daily form of the same love. Moment three: la playa, March the twenty-fifth, she has just walked toward you in el vestido, and it is your turn to speak los votos. That, Bill, is te amo. The summit. The oath. Moment four: fifty years from now, if God gives you both the years, an ordinary morning that is not ordinary at all because you can count what it cost and what it gave — a man may say te amo over coffee then, and no one who knows the story will think he used the big word carelessly. The rule under all of it is simple: te quiero is the river, flowing every day. Te amo is the source it flows from, and a man visits the source on the days that matter most. You own both now. Spend the river daily. Guard the source for the summits.

So now we build your vow — los votos — a short one, a real one, built only from words you own, that you can say standing on la playa with the wind doing whatever it wants, without notes, without fear. Here it is, in pieces first, the way we build everything in this room. Piece one, her name and the crown: Jillian, te amo — Jillian, I love you — the deep one, saved for exactly this. Say it: Jillian, te amo. Piece two, the place and the day: Hoy, en la playa — today, on the beach — hoy, today, from lesson six; en la playa, on the beach. Say it: Hoy, en la playa. Piece three, the gift: Te doy mi corazón — I give you my heart — doy means I give; mi corazón, my heart, from lesson one, the literal heart. Te doy mi corazón. Say it: Te doy mi corazón. Piece four, the time signature: Para siempre — forever. Say it: Para siempre.

Now the whole vow, joined, the way it will sound on the day: Jillian, te amo. Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre. Jillian, I love you. Today, on the beach, I give you my heart forever. Say it with me, slowly, every word standing up straight: Jillian, te amo. Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre. Again, at the speed of a man who is not reading — who is saying: Jillian, te amo. Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre. One more time, quieter, because the real one will be quiet — vows are said to one person, and everybody else just gets to witness: Jillian, te amo. Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre. Bill. That is a wedding vow. In Spanish. Yours. You can say that. You just did, three times, in my classroom, and March is still months away for you to live inside it.

And because a ceremony is a conversation, let us play the day itself, both sides, the way we played the restaurant — I will be the officiant and the world, and you will speak the groom's lines out loud, every one. The scene: la playa, late afternoon light, the guests in their chairs in the sand, el anillo waiting, and Jillian walking toward you in el vestido. Breathe. The officiant turns to you and asks, in Spanish, if you take this woman — and your whole part, the hinge of the day, is two words. Say them now, in the scene: Sí, acepto. Yes, I accept. The officiant nods. The day turns on its hinge. And then los votos — your turn to speak to her, only to her, with everybody listening. Say your vow, groom, the whole thing, standing in the sand in your head: Jillian, te amo. Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre. … There it is. El anillo goes on her hand — the ring, the circle with no end. The officiant says the final words. And the day does the thing it came to do.

Because when the ceremony ends, a word changes, and I told you to hold that thought — here it is, the last new word of the lesson, and you must use it correctly, because using it early is a mistake and using it after is a joy: Mi esposa — my wife. Esposa means wife. Mi esposa. Say it: Mi esposa. Before the ceremony she is mi prometida — my fiancée — the promised one. After the ceremony — after sí, acepto, after los votos, after el anillo — she is mi esposa, my wife. Spanish even keeps a small honest poetry in esposa: the word is family to esposas in its other life, and the old root carries the idea of being bound, joined — two lives fastened together, which is not a prison, Bill, it is a knot two people tie on purpose and call it the best thing they ever did. The first time you introduce her after the ceremony — at the reception, to a stranger, to the world — the sentence is: Mi esposa se llama Jillian — my wife's name is Jillian. Say it with me, and hear how the old sentence grew up: Mi esposa se llama Jillian. Again: Mi esposa se llama Jillian. That sentence is waiting for you on the other side of March the twenty-fifth, and it will be waiting for the rest of your life, every time you say it, para siempre.

Let us walk the whole day once more, in order, as a story, with you saying the Spanish as we pass it — the day in two languages, which is what your wedding day is actually going to be. Morning: hoy — today — the word from lesson six carrying the biggest day it will ever carry. You are early — temprano — early — because grooms who are temprano are grooms who can breathe. You see el vestido only when it is time. La playa is ready. The guests arrive. She walks toward you. The officiant speaks. Los votos are said — hers, and then yours: Jillian, te amo. Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre. The question comes, and your two words hold the whole day up: Sí, acepto. El anillo, the ring, on her hand, and yours on yours. And then the word turns: mi esposa — my wife. The sun goes down over the water in Key West, and somebody hands you a glass, and you are a married man whose wedding happened in two languages, and the Spanish parts of it were not decoration. They were the parts you prepared like they mattered, because they did.

One more scene, the evening after, because the day does not end at the ceremony and neither does your Spanish. The reception is on or near la playa — the beach — the light goes gold and then blue, and there is food, because a wedding that does not feed people is just a meeting. And here your whole course starts shaking hands with itself: the food arrives and it is good, and you say, to whoever cooked it and to the table: Está delicioso — it is delicious — lesson five's sentence, doing reception duty. You order a glass para ella — for her — lesson five's signpost, now pointing at your wife's glass, and the word wife is doing quiet work in that sentence already. Somebody asks you how it feels, and you do not need a speech. You have para siempre — forever — and you have the newest fact in your life to put next to it. The dancing happens. The ocean does its long, patient applause. And at the end of the night, when the day finally sets her down, lesson one closes the whole course's circle: Buenas noches, mi amor — good night, my love — buenas noches, good night; mi amor, my love — the first line you ever learned for her, now said by a husband to his wife, in the town where he married her. Same words as your kitchen in Michigan. New weight entirely. That is what fluency actually is, Bill — not more words. The same true words, at the true moments, without fear.

A quiet word from your profesora before your solo, because this lesson is different and we both know it. Some men learn a language to travel. Some learn it for work. You are learning it to stand in front of the people you love and say the truest sentences of your life in a language that says them warmer. When you practice your vow between now and March, practice it whole, and practice it out loud, and do not be embarrassed if your voice does something strange on te amo the first few times. That is not weakness. That is the sentence being real. By March, it will be steady. I have watched you work for seven lessons, Bill. It will be steady.

Now your solo — the guided try-it, and today it is the ceremony itself, one clean run, with me only prompting. You are on la playa. The officiant asks the question. Your answer, groom: Sí, acepto. Good. Clear, unshaken. Now los votos — she is in front of you, this is the part that is only hers. Piece one: Jillian, te amo. Piece two, three, four, joined: Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre. Whole vow now, one breath after another, no stopping: Jillian, te amo. Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre. … Perfecto — perfect. Now the reception, an hour later, sunset, and a kind stranger asks about the beautiful woman laughing by the water. Introduce her, with the new word, the after word: Mi esposa se llama Jillian. Say it once more, because you are going to say it ten thousand times and every time starts here: Mi esposa se llama Jillian. Scene complete. You just got married in Spanish in my classroom, Bill, and I did not even cry. Much.

Hooks, quickly, so the day-words stay. Boda — I remember it as the day's bouquet: boda, bouquet, the wedding and the flowers in one sound. Anillo — the ring — has that little y sound in the middle, the same y hiding in llamo, the name word; the ring and the name travel together, which at a wedding they literally do. Vestido — dress — is cousin to vest, clothing to clothing. Casarse carries casa — house — because marrying is founding a home; that one needs no hook, it is the hook. Esposa is the after word, prometida is the before word, and the ceremony is the door between them — sí, acepto is the key turning in that door. And para siempre: para, for, the giving word from your restaurant lesson — for her, for me — grown up into for always. Everything you ordered para ella in lesson five was rehearsal for para siempre in lesson seven. The course knew where it was going even when you did not.

Let us gather the lesson in order, one last time. La boda — the wedding. La playa — the beach. La boda es en la playa — the wedding is on the beach. El anillo — the ring. El vestido — the dress. Casarse — to get married, with the house inside it. Me caso — I am getting married. Los votos — the vows. Sí, acepto — yes, I accept, the hinge of the day. Para siempre — forever. Te amo — I love you, the deep one, the oath, saved for the summits — and te quiero — I love you — its everyday brother, still yours, still for the door and the dishes and the ten thousand ordinary mornings. Mi esposa — my wife, the after word. And your vow, whole, the sentence at the center of the lesson and the day: Jillian, te amo. Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre.

That is lesson seven, Bill, and of everything I will ever teach you, this is the lesson I most want you to keep. Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions — about la boda and la playa, el anillo and los votos, the difference between te quiero and te amo, and the vow itself. Nothing I did not teach you today. Answer out loud or type, whichever door you like; the lesson text stays open beside the questions, and reading it again is learning, not cheating — read the vow again as many times as you want; that is not reviewing, that is rehearsing. Your speaking practice is here too, phrase by phrase, until the green check lands. And your real assignment is the vow: once a day, out loud, whole — Jillian, te amo. Hoy, en la playa, te doy mi corazón para siempre — until it feels less like a lesson and more like a fact. Lesson eight will bring your Spanish back to earth gently — your house, your town, your everyday world — but today we stay on the beach a moment longer. Gracias — thank you — for letting your profesora teach you your wedding. Nos vemos en la playa — see you at the beach — nos vemos means see you, the way friends say it when the date is real. March the twenty-fifth, Bill. I will be the one crying in the back, in two languages.

lessons.title: Lesson 8 — Moving house: rooms, streets, and asking for what you need
paragraphs: Hola, Bill — hello, Bill. Soy Carmen — I am Carmen, your profesora, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Sit down, mi estudiante — my student — and take a breath, because today we do something very hopeful together. Today we learn how to talk about a house. Not a house in a textbook. Your house. The next house. The house you and Jillian are looking for, room by room, street by street, until one day you open a door and the two of you just know. By the end of our thirty minutes you will be able to name the rooms of a house, walk through a new place and ask where everything is, say whether a place is big or small or new, and — this is the part that changes everything — say clearly what you need and what you are looking for. As always in this room, we speak first. I say it, you say it back to me out loud, the way you mean it, and only then do we move on. When I say say it with me, I want to hear you, wherever you are. We are building a home in a new language, one word at a time, together.

Here is the map of the lesson, plainly, because I never hide the map from you. First, the house itself: la casa — the house. Then we walk through it the way your feet would go at a real viewing: la puerta — the door, la sala — the living room, la cocina — the kitchen, el baño — the bathroom, el cuarto — the bedroom, la habitación — the room, and la ventana — the window. Then we step outside to la calle — the street, because a house is also the street it stands on. Then the question that unlocks every viewing: ¿dónde está? — where is it? — and its two faithful answers: aquí — here, and allí — there. Then the describing words: grande — big, pequeño — small, and nuevo — new. And finally the two engines: necesito — I need, and busco — I am looking for, so you can stand in any house and say what you need like a man who knows his own mind. That is the whole lesson: a house, a walk, a question, and two engines. Hold onto that shape, and let us begin with the word the whole lesson stands on.

La casa — the house. Say it with me, out loud: La casa. Again, slower: la… casa. La casa. Casa is one of the warmest words in Spanish. It does not only mean a building with a roof. It means home — the place where your people are, where the food is, where the day ends. So when you learn la casa today, you are not learning a real estate word. You are learning the word for the life you and Jillian are building. Say it once more, like you mean that: La casa. Good. Now, houses come in sizes, and you need honest words for them, because house-hunting is no place for pretending. Grande — big, large. Say it with me: Grande. Una casa grande — a big house. Una — a, one, in the form it takes beside a word like casa. Una casa grande. And the opposite: Pequeño — small. Say it: Pequeño. Hear the letter ñ in the middle, the enye, with its little wave on top — it sounds like the ny in canyon, soft and quick: peh-KEH-nyoh. Pequeño. Una casa pequeña — a small house. Notice how the describing word dressed to match its partner, the way you learned in lesson one with buenos días — good morning — and buenas tardes — good afternoon. Casa takes the ending that ends in a, so pequeño becomes pequeña beside it, while grande is a generous word that wears the same coat for everybody. You do not need a grammar book for that tonight. You only need your ear. Say the pair with me, big and small: Una casa grande. Una casa pequeña. Una casa grande. Una casa pequeña. Beautiful. Your ear is doing grammar again, and we have barely opened the front door.

The third describing word is the one that matters most to a man who is moving: Nuevo — new. Say it with me: Nuevo. Una casa nueva — a new house. There is the matching coat again: nuevo beside a word like el cuarto, nueva beside casa. Una casa nueva. Now listen carefully, because there is a kindness hidden inside this word. Nuevo does not only mean newly built, fresh from the builder. It also means new to you. A house that is a hundred years old can be una casa nueva — a new house — for the family that just found it. You are not only looking for a new building, Bill. You are looking for a new beginning that happens to have walls. So if X, then Y — hold onto that: if the house is new to you and Jillian, then una casa nueva is an honest thing to call it, whatever year is carved over the door. Say the whole little family with me now: La casa. Una casa grande. Una casa pequeña. Una casa nueva. Good. You can already walk up to any house in the Spanish-speaking world and say what kind of house it is. Now let us do what you actually do at a viewing. Let us go inside.

Every viewing starts at the same place: La puerta — the door. Say it with me: La puerta. Again: La puerta. The door is the first promise a house makes you. A good door says you are welcome here, and also you are safe here, both at once. When you and Jillian stand in front of a house you might love, the first Spanish word out of your mouth can be this one: la puerta. Point at it, say it, smile at her. She will know you have been practicing, and she will love that you practiced on a door, because it means you were picturing the two of you arriving. Now we open it in our imagination and step into the first room of almost every house on earth: La sala — the living room. Say it with me: La sala. La sala is where life happens. It is where people sit and talk, where the family gathers, where you will one day fall asleep on a couch with the television still talking and Jillian will cover you with a blanket and pretend she did not. In many houses the sala is the biggest room: La sala es grande — the living room is big. Es — is. Es is the little bridge word that lets you describe anything. La sala es grande. And the other side: La sala es pequeña — the living room is small. Say both with me: La sala es grande. La sala es pequeña. Good. Hold onto es. La casa es nueva — the house is new. La sala es grande. One bridge, every description you will ever make, and we will cross it all lesson long.

From the sala, every house hunter on earth walks to the same place next, because the kitchen tells the truth about a house: La cocina — the kitchen. Say it with me, and say it with respect: La cocina. Again: La cocina. In Spanish, la cocina is not a utility room. It is the heart with appliances. It is where the coffee happens in the morning and where a man learns, over years, exactly how his wife takes her tea. When you walk into a viewing, walk into la cocina and ask yourself the only question that matters: can I see her here, in the morning light, half awake, laughing at something I said? If the answer is yes, the house is still in the running. If the answer is no, no sala in the world will save it. Say the room in full sentences now: La cocina es grande — the kitchen is big. La cocina es pequeña — the kitchen is small. Say them with me: La cocina es grande. La cocina es pequeña. And keep one question warm in your ear for a few more minutes: ¿dónde está la cocina? — where is the kitchen? When I teach it to you properly, you will already own every word in it except the asking itself. That is how this lesson is built, layer on layer, like a house.

Down the hall now — picture the hallway of this hopeful house we are inventing together — and here is the small room every guest asks about and every buyer checks twice: El baño — the bathroom. Say it with me: El baño. Hear the enye again, the same soft ny as in pequeño: BAH-nyoh. El baño. Baño comes from the word for a bath, and that is exactly what the room is for: washing, water, getting ready to face the world or to leave it behind for the night. Notice the little word in front changed its coat: la cocina, la sala, la puerta — and now el baño. El — the, in the form it takes beside a word like baño. Spanish nouns travel in two families, the la family and the el family, and you do not choose the family; the word brings its own. Baño is an el word. Cuarto, coming next, is an el word. Cocina, sala, puerta and casa are la words. Do not memorize a rule tonight. Just say each room with its own little word attached, the way I give it to you, and your ear will sort the families by itself. Say the set with me: La cocina. El baño. La cocina. El baño. Good. And in sentences: El baño es pequeño — the bathroom is small. There is pequeño in its first coat, beside an el word. El baño es grande — the bathroom is big. Say both: El baño es pequeño. El baño es grande. You are describing a house now, Bill, room by room, out loud, in Spanish. Feel how real that is.

Now the room where the day begins and ends, the room I saved for the middle of our walk because it deserves a slow moment: El cuarto — the bedroom, the room. Say it with me: El cuarto. Again: El cuarto. Cuarto has two jobs in Spanish, and I will teach you both honestly. Its first job is the one you need today: a room, and very often, in a house, the bedroom — the room where you sleep. It can also mean a fourth, a quarter — in an old house the rooms were counted off, and the sleeping room kept the counting word. For today, hold the house meaning tight. And Spanish gives you a second, longer word for the same place, and you should own them both, because agents and listings use them side by side: La habitación — the room, the bedroom. Say it with me, slowly first, it is a long, beautiful word: la ha-bi-ta-ción. La habitación. Again, whole: La habitación. Habitación comes from living, inhabiting — it is the room you inhabit, the room where your life actually sleeps. So here is your pair, and either one is correct in any house in any Spanish-speaking town: el cuarto, la habitación. Say the pair with me: El cuarto. La habitación. El cuarto. La habitación. In sentences: El cuarto es grande — the bedroom is big. La habitación es pequeña — the bedroom is small. Say both: El cuarto es grande. La habitación es pequeña. And picture it as you say it — not a showroom bed with forty pillows. Your bed. Her side and your side, already decided without a word, the way couples decide it. A word tied to a picture like that does not get forgotten. Your memory keeps what your heart files.

Speaking of her side of the bed, it has morning light coming through the last stop on our walk: La ventana — the window. Say it with me: La ventana. Again: La ventana. A ventana is where the street says good morning, where you check the weather with your own eyes, where Jillian will stand one day with coffee, looking out at a yard that is hers. Ventanas take your whole toolkit: La ventana es grande — the window is big. La ventana es pequeña — the window is small. Say them: La ventana es grande. La ventana es pequeña. Now let me give you a small, true scene to carry these rooms in, because a phrase is only yours when it survives a new room — you know that is my law. Picture the viewing. La agente — the agent, a woman showing you the house — opens la puerta and waves you in. You step into la sala, and it is bigger than the photos promised, and you say it out loud: La sala es grande. The agent smiles, because buyers who can talk are buyers who are serious. Jillian drifts, the way she will, straight to la cocina, and you follow her and say the honest sentence: La cocina es pequeña, pero bonita — the kitchen is small, but pretty. Pero — but. Bonita — pretty, beautiful, in the form beside a la word. Pero is the most honest word in house-hunting, Bill: every house has a pero, and the art is finding the house whose pero you can live with. Say it with me: La cocina es pequeña, pero bonita. Down the hall: El baño es nuevo — the bathroom is new. Nuevo in its first coat beside an el word; nueva beside la casa — you own both coats now. Then el cuarto es grande — the bedroom is big — and la ventana es grande — the window is big — and the morning light does the rest of the selling, the way morning light always does. There it is. You have walked a whole house, named every room and described every room, in Spanish, in sentences, out loud. That is not studying. That is viewing a house like a man who lives in the language.

Now we step outside, because a house is not only its rooms, and you know this in your bones from every place you have ever lived: La calle — the street. Say it with me: La calle. Again, and hear the double l doing its soft y work, the sound you tamed in lesson one inside llamo: la calle sounds like KAH-yeh. La calle. The street is where the house meets the world. When you hunt for a house with Jillian, you are hunting for a calle too: Una calle tranquila — a quiet street. Tranquila — quiet, calm, peaceful. Una calle tranquila. Say it: Una calle tranquila. And a house stands on its street with the little word en — in, on, at: La casa está en la calle — the house is on the street. Stop there with me, because a new giant just walked in and I want you to meet him properly. Está — is, is located, is right now. You already own es from our descriptions: la casa es grande — the house is big — that is what the house is like, its nature. Está is its brother, and está answers a different question: where is it, and how is it right now? Es tells you what a thing is. Está tells you where a thing is. La casa es grande, its nature. La casa está en la calle, its place. So if X, then Y — hold onto that with both hands: if you are describing what something is like, reach for es; if you are saying where something is, reach for está. That one distinction, learned today in a doorway, will carry you through years of Spanish. Say the pair with me, nature and place: La casa es grande. La casa está en la calle. La casa es grande. La casa está en la calle. Perfect. You just learned one of the great truths of this language standing on an imaginary sidewalk, in a sentence about a house you want.

And now, with está in your hand, I can finally give you the question I promised you in la cocina, the question that unlocks every viewing and every new town for the rest of your life: ¿Dónde está? — where is it? Say it with me, and notice the music: ¿Dónde está? Dónde — where. Está — is, is located. ¿Dónde está? Look at the marks around it, because Spanish dresses its questions properly: an upside-down question mark at the start, so your eye knows a question is coming before it arrives, and the ordinary one at the end. And hear the accent on dónde — that little leaning line tells your voice where to lean, the way I taught you with días — days — and corazón — heart: DOHN-deh, lean on the first beat. Say it again, leaning right: ¿Dónde está? Now put a room on the end of it and it becomes the most useful sentence in house-hunting: ¿Dónde está la cocina? — where is the kitchen? Say it with me: ¿Dónde está la cocina? ¿Dónde está el baño? — where is the bathroom? — the question every human asks in every new house, and now you ask it in Spanish. ¿Dónde está el cuarto? — where is the bedroom? ¿Dónde está la puerta? — where is the door? — the question you ask, politely, with a smile, when the visit is over and the house was not the one. Say the whole set with me, like a man walking a viewing with purpose: ¿Dónde está la cocina? ¿Dónde está el baño? ¿Dónde está el cuarto? ¿Dónde está la puerta? Ay, Bill, listen to yourself. Four questions, every room in the house, and not one of them in English. And the answers come back in the two smallest, hardest-working words in this lesson: Aquí — here. Say it: Aquí. Lean where the accent leans, on the end: ah-KEE. Aquí. And Allí — there. Say it: Allí. Also leaning on the end: ah-YEE, with that double l singing its soft y again. Allí. Aquí, allí. Here, there. The agent answers you: La cocina está aquí — the kitchen is here. El baño está allí — the bathroom is there. Say the answers with me, full sentences, pointing with your voice: La cocina está aquí. El baño está allí. La puerta está aquí. La ventana está allí. Good. Question and answer, a complete little machine: you ask ¿dónde está?, the world answers aquí or allí, and you are never lost in a house again. Never lost — in a new house, in a new town, in a new language. That is what we are really building here.

Now the two engines, the part of the lesson that turns a tourist into a buyer. First: Necesito — I need. Say it with me, strong, like a man stating a fact and not begging a favor: Necesito. Again: Necesito. Four clean beats, and the weight lands in the middle: neh-ceh-SEE-toh. Necesito is a complete engine because Spanish hides the I inside the verb itself — necesito already contains yo — I — inside it, so you never need a separate word for I with it. Necesito, full stop, is a whole sentence: I need. Put a house part behind it and it pulls real weight: Necesito una cocina grande — I need a big kitchen. Say it with me: Necesito una cocina grande. Necesito un cuarto grande — I need a big bedroom. Un — a, one, in the form beside an el word, the brother of una. Necesito un cuarto grande. Say it: Necesito un cuarto grande. Necesito una casa nueva — I need a new house. Say it: Necesito una casa nueva. Hear what you are doing: necesito plus a thing plus a description, and you can state any need a house can hold. Necesito una ventana grande — I need a big window — for her morning light. Necesito una calle tranquila — I need a quiet street — for your sleep and your peace. Say those two with me, the tender needs, the real ones: Necesito una ventana grande. Necesito una calle tranquila. A man who can say what he needs, plainly, without apology and without anger, is a man people help gladly. In English you are already that man. Today you became him in Spanish too.

And the second engine, necesito's brother, the hunter's word: Busco — I am looking for, I look for. Say it with me: Busco. Again: Busco. Two beats, strong as a bootstep: BOOS-koh. Busco comes from buscar — to look for, to search — and like necesito, it carries its I inside it: busco is a whole sentence all by itself. What is the difference between my two engines? Listen carefully, because people hear the difference. Necesito states a need — it is firm, it is about what must be true. Busco starts a search — it is open, it is about what you are hunting, and it invites the other person to hunt with you. An agent hears busco and reaches for her keys. A neighbor hears busco and starts thinking of the houses on his street. Lead with busco when you are opening a conversation; lead with necesito when you are drawing a line that matters. Now put it to work: Busco una casa — I am looking for a house. Say it with me, like you are saying it to a real agent on a real morning: Busco una casa. Busco una casa grande — I am looking for a big house. Say both: Busco una casa. Busco una casa grande. Busco una casa nueva — I am looking for a new house. Say it: Busco una casa nueva. And the full dream, the whole sentence, the one I want you to be able to say to any agent, any neighbor, any new friend, without notes and without fear: Busco una casa grande en una calle tranquila — I am looking for a big house on a quiet street. Take it in pieces first: Busco una casa grande… en una calle tranquila. Now whole, at the speed of a man who knows what he wants: Busco una casa grande en una calle tranquila. Again: Busco una casa grande en una calle tranquila. Bill, that sentence, said clearly in a stranger's office, starts houses appearing. Say it one more time and picture her standing beside you when you say it, because in the real version, she is: Busco una casa grande en una calle tranquila.

Time to do it, not just hear it — you know my rule: the doing is taught here, inside the lesson, with me beside you. This is your guided try-it, and we will run a whole viewing together, start to finish. I will be la agente, and you will be you. I open la puerta and wave you in, and first thing, polite as you were raised, you greet the room the way I taught you in lesson one: buenas tardes — good afternoon. Then you look around la sala and you tell me what you see, in a full sentence: La sala es grande. I nod — agents always nod — and you ask your first question, the unlocker: ¿Dónde está la cocina? And I point: La cocina está aquí. You walk in, you look at her face more than the counters — you are learning, Bill — and you say the honest sentence: La cocina es pequeña, pero bonita. Down the hall you go, and you ask again, all by yourself this time: ¿Dónde está el baño? Allí, I say — el baño está allí. You check it: El baño es nuevo. Good news, stated plainly. Then el cuarto, the room that matters most, and you stand in its doorway a moment longer than the others, and you say: El cuarto es grande. And la ventana es grande, and the morning light does the rest of the selling. Then, out on la calle, in the sun, I ask you the question agents ask, and you do not shrug and you do not wave vaguely at the sky. You use your engines. You say what you are hunting: Busco una casa grande en una calle tranquila. And you say the need that is not negotiable, the one you and Jillian agreed on in the car: Necesito una cocina grande. Now run that last part again in your own voice, both engines, out loud, right now: Busco una casa grande en una calle tranquila. Necesito una cocina grande. There it is. That was a viewing — a whole viewing, in Spanish, with you doing the talking. If you can do it in this room with me narrating, you can do it on a Saturday with her hand in yours, and Saturday is coming. And one day, after enough calles and enough puertas and enough ¿dónde está?, the answer will be aquí. Here. This one. Ours. The Spanish for that day is already in your mouth, and we put it there today, word by word, room by room.

So let us gather what you own now, in order, one last time, the whole walk in one breath. La casa — the house, the home, the whole dream in two syllables. The descriptions that ride on it: grande — big, pequeño — small, nuevo — new, and es — is — the little bridge: la casa es grande, la casa es nueva. The walk itself: la puerta — the door, la sala — the living room, la cocina — the kitchen, el baño — the bathroom, el cuarto — the bedroom, la habitación — the room, la ventana — the window, and outside, la calle — the street. The locator brothers: es for what a thing is like, está for where a thing is. The great question: ¿dónde está? — where is it? — with its two faithful answers, aquí — here — and allí — there. And the two engines that make you a buyer and not a bystander: necesito — I need — and busco — I am looking for — standing tall in their full sentences: Busco una casa grande en una calle tranquila. Necesito una cocina grande. And hang them on a hook you already own: necesito lives inside necessary — when you say necesito, you are saying this is necessary to me. That is lesson eight, Bill, and you did not just learn it — you walked it, room by room, out loud. Ay, do not argue with your profesora. I heard every word.

Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions: more than a few, all of them about what I taught you in this lesson and nothing else — nobody will ask you one single thing I did not teach. Most of them give you choices to pick from, and you can also answer out loud or type your answer, whichever door you like — and today you know the Spanish for door, so choose a good one. The lesson text stays open beside the questions, and if you want to read any part of it again before you answer, do it with my blessing. Going back to read is learning, not cheating; in this room it has always been learning. Your speaking practice lives in this lesson too: hear me say each phrase, then say it back until it lands. And your real assignment, the one that is not on any screen: the next time you and Jillian talk about houses — and that talk is coming, mi estudiante, sooner than you think — say one line of it in Spanish. Busco una casa grande en una calle tranquila. Say it to her in the car. Watch her face. That face is why we do this. Next lesson, we learn to ask anything — who, what, where, when, how much — every question word in Spanish, as one system, so no door of curiosity stays closed to you. Until then, la puerta of this room is always open to you. Ve — go — and go look at a house with your prometida — your fiancée. She is going to love hunting in two languages.

lessons.title: Lesson 9 — Questions: asking anything — quién, qué, dónde, cuánto
paragraphs: Hola, Bill — hello, Bill. Soy Carmen — I am Carmen, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Sit down, mi estudiante — my student — and bring your curiosity with you, because today is the lesson that opens every door the other lessons built. Until now, you have mostly answered the world: you greet it, you name yourself to it, you describe houses to it. Today you learn to interrogate it, gently, the way a friend does. Today we learn the question words of Spanish — all of them, as one system, a single ring of keys: Quién — who. Qué — what. Dónde — where. Cuándo — when. Cuánto — how much, how many. Cómo — how. And, lightly, por qué — why. Seven keys, Bill. A man carrying these seven words can ask anything, of anyone, anywhere Spanish is spoken — directions, prices, names, reasons, the whole world becomes answerable. And because this is lesson nine, this lesson also carries our Spanish-for-Jillian strand, the sweet thread of this course: today you learn to ask her about her day — and mean it — and to listen like a man who understands that listening, done right, is a love language all by itself. Your wedding is coming — el veinticinco de marzo — the twenty-fifth of March — in Key West, and by that day I want you asking her questions in Spanish at the kitchen table like you were born to it. Speak first, as always: I say it, you say it back out loud, and only then do we move on.
