First, thirty seconds on how a Spanish question is built, because once you see the machine, every key on the ring makes sense. A Spanish question has two marks, and I want you to love them both: ¿ — the upside-down question mark that opens the question, standing at the front like a friend waving you in — and ? — the ordinary question mark that closes it at the end. Why two? Because Spanish is kind to its readers and its listeners: the opening mark warns you a question is coming, so your voice can get ready. And your voice does change, Bill — this is the second half of the machine. In a statement, your voice settles down at the end, the way a plane lands. In a question, your voice lifts at the end, the way eyebrows lift. Same words, different music, different meaning. Es grande — it is big — voice down, a fact. ¿Es grande? — is it big? — voice up, a question. Say that pair with me and feel your own voice do it: Es grande. ¿Es grande? Es grande. ¿Es grande? Hear that lift? That lift is called intonation, and in Spanish it matters as much as the words. And here is the beautiful part, the part that makes this whole lesson one system and not seven separate chores: every question word on our ring wears a written accent — quién, qué, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo — every single one leans, and the accent tells your voice exactly where to lean, the way I taught you with días — days — and corazón — heart — back in lesson one. A question word in Spanish always carries its accent, always. So if X, then Y — hold onto that: if a word is asking, then the accent is sitting on it, showing your voice where the weight goes. Seven keys, one machine, two marks, one lift. That is the whole system. Now let us cut the keys, one by one, starting with the one you will use on her tonight.

Cómo — how. Say it with me, leaning where the accent leans: Cómo. KOH-moh, weight on the first beat. Cómo. You already own a piece of this key from lesson one: ¿Cómo te llamas? — what is your name? — word for word, how do you call yourself. There was cómo, hiding inside your very first question, doing how work all along. Today cómo becomes the kindest question word in the language, because cómo is the key that asks after people: ¿Cómo estás? — how are you? Say it with me, warmly, the way you would say it to someone you actually care about: ¿Cómo estás? Estás — you are, how you are right now — the brother of está from our house lesson: está for a house and a street, estás for you, the person in front of me, right now. ¿Cómo estás? asks after the person's present weather, not their nature, and that is why it is the perfect daily question: it does not ask who are you in general, it asks how are you, today, in this hour, in that body, after that shift. Say it again, slower, like you mean the answer matters: ¿Cómo… estás? ¿Cómo estás? Good. And because a question deserves an answer, here is yours, the answer you will give when she turns it around on you — and she will: Estoy bien — I am well, I am fine. Say it with me: Estoy bien. Estoy — I am, right now — the first-person brother of estás and está; the whole family answers how and where things stand at this moment. Bien — well, fine, good. Estoy bien. And the honest version, the one for the days that are not fine, because this course does not teach you to perform, it teaches you to talk: Estoy cansado — I am tired. Cansado — tired, in the form a man uses for himself. Say it: Estoy cansado. And softened, the way you would actually say it at the end of a long day, with a little honesty and no drama: Estoy un poco cansado — I am a little tired. Un poco — a little, a bit. Say the whole true sentence: Estoy un poco cansado. ¿Cómo estás? Estoy bien. ¿Cómo estás? Estoy un poco cansado. Question and answer, both directions, owned. That exchange, Bill, is the heartbeat of a marriage in any language: how are you — and a true answer.

Quién — who. Say it with me: Quién. Kee-EHN, the accent leaning on the end. Quién. This key asks after a person — not a thing, not a place, a person. ¿Quién es? — who is it, who is he, who is she? Say it: ¿Quién es? There is es — is — our little bridge from the house lesson, now introducing human beings. ¿Quién es? is the question for the knock at the door, the new face at the table, the name you missed at the wedding rehearsal. And it has a plural brother for a crowd: ¿Quiénes son? — who are they? Quiénes — who, for more than one. Son — they are. Say it: ¿Quiénes son? You will not need quiénes every day, but at a wedding, mi estudiante, you will need it by the second hour, because weddings are full of beautiful strangers whose names you are supposed to know. Put quién to work in a sentence about your real life: ¿Quién es ella? — who is she? Ella — she, her. ¿Quién es ella? And the answer you will give a hundred times, with pride, so learn its shape now: Es mi prometida — she is my fiancée. Prometida — fiancée — your promised one, from lesson one. Es mi prometida. Say the exchange with me, question and answer, like a man at his own wedding door: ¿Quién es ella? Es mi prometida. ¿Quién es ella? Es mi prometida. Perfect. Quién asks, es answers, and a stranger becomes a person with a name and a place in your life. That is what this key is for.

Qué — what. Say it with me: Qué. One beat, clean as a knock: KEH. Qué. This is the widest key on the ring — qué asks after things, ideas, definitions, the whole non-human world. Its most useful shape is the one for the object in your hand, the word on the page, the thing on the table you cannot name yet: ¿Qué es esto? — what is this? Esto — this, this thing here. Say it with me: ¿Qué es esto? ¿Qué es esto? is the beginner's best friend, Bill, because it turns every unknown object into a lesson: you point, you ask, the world names it for you, and the word sticks because you asked for it at the moment you needed it. Carry it into la cocina — the kitchen — from our house lesson, point at anything, and ask: ¿Qué es esto? Carry it into a market in Key West, point at a fruit you have never seen: ¿Qué es esto? And qué does one more job, the job of asking after meanings: when someone says a Spanish word you do not know, qué is how you ask what it means — you repeat the word, and you ask, in effect: what is that, what does that mean? The world answers, and your vocabulary grows by your own asking. That is the secret of this whole lesson, so hear it plainly: a student with qué and a student without qué are living in two different countries. One of them can learn from every room he walks into. Say the key once more, and feel how much country it opens: ¿Qué es esto?

Dónde — where. Say it with me: Dónde. DOHN-deh. You know this key — it carried our whole house lesson on its back: ¿Dónde está? — where is it? ¿Dónde está la cocina? — where is the kitchen? ¿Dónde está el baño? — where is the bathroom? I am not teaching you a new word today, Bill; I am hanging an old friend on the ring where he belongs, so you can see the family whole. Dónde asks after place, and place answers with está and its two faithful servants from lesson eight: aquí — here — and allí — there. La cocina está aquí — the kitchen is here. El baño está allí — the bathroom is there. Say the old exchange once, for the joy of owning it: ¿Dónde está la cocina? La cocina está aquí. Good. But notice what the ring gives you now that you have the other keys beside it: dónde can walk out of the house and ask after the whole world. ¿Dónde está la calle? — where is the street? ¿Dónde está Key West? — where is Key West? — asked with a smile, because you know perfectly well, but a man should be able to ask after his own wedding town in Spanish. Say them: ¿Dónde está la calle? ¿Dónde está Key West? Dónde plus está plus any place on earth. That is the formula, and it has no exceptions worth fearing. Where is the one question a traveler asks more than any other, and you have owned it since the house lesson — today you just learned that it was a key on a ring, and the ring is yours.

Cuándo — when. Say it with me: Cuándo. KWAHN-doh, leaning on the first beat where the accent sits. Cuándo. This key asks after time — the hour, the day, the date, the moment. And I am going to teach it to you on the most important date in your life, because a word learned on a date like this does not get forgotten: ¿Cuándo es la boda? — when is the wedding? Boda — wedding. La boda — the wedding. Say the question with me, and smile when you say it, Spanish can hear a smile: ¿Cuándo es la boda? And the answer, your answer, the one you will give in Spanish to anyone who asks, with your whole chest: La boda es el veinticinco de marzo — the wedding is the twenty-fifth of Marzo — March. Marzo — March. El veinticinco de marzo, en Key West — on the twenty-fifth of March, in Key West. Say the answer whole: La boda es el veinticinco de marzo. ¿Cuándo es la boda? La boda es el veinticinco de marzo. There. You just announced your wedding in Spanish, question and answer, like a man in a film — except it is your real life, which is better than any film. And cuándo works for the small times too, not only the great ones: it asks when dinner is, when the viewing is, when she comes home from the hospital. Any moment you need to locate in time, cuándo is the key that finds it. Cuándo asks, and the answer is always a time: an hour, a day, a date. Hold that pairing — question word and answer shape — because it is true for every key on the ring, and it is how you will know, in a real conversation, whether the answer you got actually answers the question you asked.

Cuánto — how much, how many. Say it with me: Cuánto. KWAHN-toh. Cuánto. This key asks after amount — quantity, number, price — and it is the key your wallet will thank you for. Its most famous shape on earth: ¿Cuánto cuesta? — how much does it cost? Cuesta — it costs, from costar, to cost. Say it with me, clear and unafraid, the way a man asks who intends to pay and also intends to know: ¿Cuánto cuesta? ¿Cuánto cuesta? is a complete negotiation in two words. Ask it in a market, ask it in a shop, ask it about the flowers, the ring, the cake — la boda — the wedding — will give you a hundred honest chances to use it, and every time you ask it in Spanish you will get a straighter answer than the tourist who points and grunts. Cuánto also counts people and things, not only prices: it asks how many as easily as how much, one key for the whole world of amounts. And like pequeño back in the house lesson, cuánto dresses to match its partner when it stands beside a noun — cuánto, cuánta, cuántos, cuántas, four coats for one idea — but tonight, Bill, I am giving you the question in its fixed, famous shape, ¿cuánto cuesta?, and that shape never changes and never fails. The coats can come later; the key turns today. Say it once more, and picture the market stall, the sun, her beside you choosing flowers: ¿Cuánto cuesta? Good. That is a man shopping for his wedding in Spanish. There are grooms who cannot do that in any language but pointing. You are not one of them anymore.

Por qué — why. Say it with me, gently, because this key is powerful and a little dangerous: Por qué. Por KEH. Why. I teach it to you lightly today, on purpose, and I will tell you why, which is only fair. Por qué asks after reasons, causes, motives — the machinery underneath things. It is the scientist's key, and you, Bill, are a man who asks why for a living, so your hand will reach for it often. But hear your profesora: in the house, with her, por qué is a scalpel, not a hammer. ¿Por qué? asked of a machine is curiosity. ¿Por qué? asked of a tired woman at the end of a hard day can sound like a cross-examination, even when your heart means only love. So today we learn the key, we learn its shape, and we learn its manners in the same breath: ask por qué of the world freely; ask it of people rarely, softly, and only when you are ready to hear the whole answer. And because every question deserves its answer shape, here is why's faithful partner: Porque — because. No accent, no question marks, one word run together — porque is why's answer, the reason itself. ¿Por qué? Porque. Why? Because. Say the pair with me, question and answer, the smallest philosophy lesson in the world: ¿Por qué? Porque. ¿Por qué? Porque. Good. The key is yours. Use it like a gentleman: often on things, gently on people.

Now stand back with me and look at the whole ring, because a system is only yours when you can see it whole and turn it fast. Seven keys: Quién — who — and the answer is a person. Qué — what — and the answer is a thing or a meaning. Dónde — where — and the answer is a place, aquí or allí. Cuándo — when — and the answer is a time. Cuánto — how much, how many — and the answer is an amount. Cómo — how — and the answer is a manner, a state, a way things are. Por qué — why — and the answer begins with porque — because. Say the ring with me, in order, one clean pass, leaning on every accent: ¿Quién? ¿Qué? ¿Dónde? ¿Cuándo? ¿Cuánto? ¿Cómo? ¿Por qué? Again, faster, like a man checking his pockets before he leaves the house — keys, all seven, present and accounted for: ¿Quién? ¿Qué? ¿Dónde? ¿Cuándo? ¿Cuánto? ¿Cómo? ¿Por qué? Beautiful. And feel the intonation doing its work on every one: voice up at the end, eyebrows up, door open. In a real conversation you will not recite the ring — you will reach for one key without thinking, the way you reach for a door handle. That reaching without thinking is called fluency, and it is built exactly like this: the system whole, in order, out loud, until your hand knows the ring by touch. One more pass, slower, and this time hear a real question hiding inside each key — the door, the table, the house, the wedding, the market, her face, the reason: ¿Quién? ¿Qué? ¿Dónde? ¿Cuándo? ¿Cuánto? ¿Cómo? ¿Por qué? Hold onto that pass, Bill. That was the whole lesson in seven words, and you said it.

And now the strand this lesson was always walking toward — the reason cómo is the kindest key. Evening. She comes home from the hospital, from a day of other people's emergencies, and she is tired in the way that does not show on a face unless you love the face. This is the moment this course exists for, as surely as buenas noches, mi amor — good night, my love — was the moment of lesson one. You do not ask her about dinner first. You do not ask her about the house, or the wedding, or the list. You ask her this: ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón? — how was your day, my heart? Say it with me, slowly first, every word placed like a hand on her shoulder: ¿Cómo… fue… tu día… mi corazón? Fue — was, how it went — cómo asking after the day as a whole, the way it went for her. Tu día — your day. And mi corazón — my heart — corazón, heart, the sweet word from lesson one, riding at the end where it belongs. Say the whole question now, at the speed of love, which is slower than the speed of talk: ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón? Again: ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón? Bill. Listen to me. A man who asks that question, in her language of the heart you are building together, and then actually listens to the answer — that man is not performing romance. That man is doing the thing itself. The question is only the door. What walks through it is the next part, and it is the most important teaching in this lesson, so lean in.

Listening, in Spanish, has its own little toolkit, and I am giving it to you whole, because asking without listening is just noise with good pronunciation. When she begins to answer — and she will answer a question asked like that — your first gift to her is this: Cuéntame — tell me. Say it with me: Cuéntame. KWEN-tah-meh. Cuéntame comes from contar — to tell, to count out a story — and it is an invitation, not a command: tell me, I want the story, all of it, start where you need to start. Cuéntame. Say it like a man clearing the table and sitting down: Cuéntame. And while she talks, your voice has one more job, the quietest and strongest job in any conversation: Te escucho — I am listening to you, I hear you. Say it: Te escucho. Escucho — I listen, I am listening. Te escucho. Not I am waiting to talk. Not I am fixing it. Te escucho: I am here, I am receiving, your day is landing on someone who wants it. Say the pair together, invitation and promise: Cuéntame. Te escucho. Cuéntame. Te escucho. And when she asks you back — ¿cómo estás? — how are you? — because love returns questions the way mirrors return light, you answer truly, with the answers you already own from this lesson: Estoy bien — I am well. Or, on the true days: Estoy un poco cansado — I am a little tired. No performing, no hiding. Estoy bien. Estoy un poco cansado. Two honest sentences, and between her cuéntame and your true answer, a whole evening of marriage just happened in Spanish. That, mi estudiante, is the strand: not sweet words sprinkled on top of a lesson, but the actual machinery of asking after a person and meaning it. The sweet words were never the decoration. They were always the destination.

Time to do it together — your guided try-it, inside the lesson, with me beside you, the way we ran the house viewing in lesson eight. I will be Jillian's voice — forgive me, querida — darling — I will do my best — and you will be you, at the door, in the evening. She comes in, tired, bag down, and before anything else in the world, you ask: ¿Cómo estás? She smiles, because nobody at the hospital asks the nurse how she is, and she answers with our lesson's own words: Estoy bien, un poco cansada — I am well, a little tired — cansada, tired, in the form a woman uses for herself, the sister of your cansado. And you, because you are learning to be the man who asks the second question, the real one, you say: ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón? And she looks at you — really looks at you — because her day, asked after in Spanish, by her name of the heart, is a day being honored. And you seal it with the invitation: Cuéntame. And while she tells you — the hard patient, the kind one, the long corridor of that day — you give her the quiet sentence, once, at exactly the right moment: Te escucho. Run the whole exchange again now, your lines only, out loud, in order, no notes: ¿Cómo estás? ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón? Cuéntame. Te escucho. Again, slower, like the evening is real — because one evening very soon, it will be: ¿Cómo estás? ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón? Cuéntame. Te escucho. Bill, if you can say those four lines at a real door to a real tired woman coming home, you are not a student of Spanish anymore in that moment. You are a husband practicing early, and there is no higher level in this course than that.

So let us gather what you own now, in order, one last time. The machine first: two marks, ¿ and ?, opening and closing every question, and the lift of intonation at the end of your voice, eyebrows up, door open. Then the ring of seven keys, each with its answer shape: quién — who — a person; qué — what — a thing or a meaning; dónde — where — a place, aquí or allí; cuándo — when — a time, la boda es el veinticinco de marzo; cuánto — how much — an amount, ¿cuánto cuesta?; cómo — how — a state, ¿cómo estás?; and por qué — why — answered by porque — because — a scalpel for things, used gently on people. Then your own answers, true in both directions: estoy bien — I am well — and estoy un poco cansado — I am a little tired. And crowning the whole lesson, the evening exchange, the strand itself: ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón? Cuéntame. Te escucho. Question, invitation, promise. That is lesson nine, and it is the most useful lesson in this course so far, because every lesson after this one can now be asked about, in Spanish, by you. Ay, do not argue with your profesora. I heard the ring. You said all seven.

Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions: more than a few, all of them about what I taught you in this lesson and nothing else. Most give you choices to pick from, and you can also answer out loud or type your answer, whichever you like. The lesson text stays open beside the questions, and if you want to read any part of it again before you answer, do it with my blessing — going back to read is learning, not cheating, and in this room it has always been learning. Your speaking practice lives in this lesson too: hear me say each phrase, then say it back until it lands. And your real assignment, tonight, at the door, when she comes home: one question, asked like you mean it, and then the hardest and best part — you listen to the whole answer. ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón? Then: te escucho. And mean te escucho. Next lesson, we step into the past — ayer — yesterday — and you will learn to tell her what you did, in Spanish, after the day is done, which is the other half of every evening conversation there is. Until then, keep the ring on your hand, mi estudiante. Seven keys. Every door. Pregunta — ask. Escucha — listen. In that order, always.

phrases.meaning: how was your day, my heart?

questions.q: What does '¿Cómo estás?' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: cómo, the kindest key — it asks after people.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: '¿Cómo estás? — how are you? Say it with me, warmly, the way you would say it to someone you actually care about: ¿Cómo estás?' Another way: it asks after a person's present weather — how they are today, in this hour.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Cómo means how. (2) Estás means you are, right now. (3) Asked of a person, the question means: how are you.

questions.q: Which question word from the lesson means 'who'?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the ring of seven keys, each with its own answer shape.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Quién — who. Say it with me: Quién. Kee-EHN, the accent leaning on the end. Quién. This key asks after a person' Another way: ¿quién es? is the question for the knock at the door — who is it.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Each key on the ring asks for one kind of answer. (2) The key whose answer is a person asks who. (3) That key is: Quién.

questions.q: What does '¿Cuánto cuesta?' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: cuánto, the key your wallet will thank you for.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: '¿Cuánto cuesta? — how much does it cost? Cuesta — it costs, from costar, to cost.' Another way: Carmen calls it a complete negotiation in two words.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Cuánto asks after amount — quantity, number, price. (2) Cuesta means it costs. (3) Together they ask: how much does it cost.

questions.q: What does 'la boda' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the word Carmen teaches on the most important date in Bill's life.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Boda — wedding. La boda — the wedding. Say the question with me, and smile when you say it, Spanish can hear a smile: ¿Cuándo es la boda?' Another way: ¿cuándo es la boda? — when is the wedding?
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson teaches cuándo — when — on one special date. (2) The event on that date, el veinticinco de marzo in Key West, is la boda. (3) La boda means: the wedding.

questions.q: Jillian turns the question around and asks Bill how he is, and he is fine. What does he answer?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the answer that belongs to ¿cómo estás?
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Estoy bien — I am well, I am fine. Say it with me: Estoy bien. Estoy — I am, right now' Another way: estoy bien is the well answer; the tired answer is a different sentence.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) ¿Cómo estás? asks how you are right now. (2) Estoy is I am, right now, and bien is well. (3) The answer for a man who is fine is: Estoy bien.

questions.q: Carmen says every question word on the ring wears something that tells your voice where to lean. What is it?
questions.teach: From the lesson: one system — two marks, one lift, and an accent on every key.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'every question word on our ring wears a written accent — quién, qué, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo — every single one leans, and the accent tells your voice exactly where to lean' Another way to hold it: if a word is asking, the accent is sitting on it.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson says a question word in Spanish always carries something that shows where the beat falls. (2) It sits on quién, qué, dónde, cuándo, cuánto and cómo alike. (3) That something is: a written accent.

questions.q: What is the answer word that faithfully pairs with '¿Por qué?' — why?
questions.teach: From the lesson: why asks, and its partner answers with the reason.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Porque — because. No accent, no question marks, one word run together — porque is why's answer, the reason itself.' Another way: ¿por qué? Porque. Why? Because. The smallest philosophy lesson in the world.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Por qué asks after reasons. (2) Every key on the ring has its answer shape, and why's answer begins with one word. (3) That word, meaning because, is: Porque.

questions.q: Bill is holding an object he cannot name and wants to ask what it is. What does Carmen teach him to say?
questions.teach: From the lesson: qué, the widest key — the beginner's best friend.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: '¿Qué es esto? — what is this? Esto — this, this thing here. Say it with me: ¿Qué es esto?' Another way: you point, you ask, and the world names it for you.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Qué asks after things and meanings, not people or places. (2) Esto means this, this thing here. (3) Pointing at the object, he asks: ¿Qué es esto?

questions.q: Jillian has come home tired from the hospital. What is the question Carmen most wants Bill to ask her?
accept: Como fue tu dia, mi corazon
questions.teach: From the lesson: the Spanish-for-Jillian strand — asking about her day, and meaning it.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'You do not ask her about dinner first. You do not ask her about the house, or the wedding, or the list. You ask her this: ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón?' Another way: cómo asking after the whole day, with the sweet word riding at the end where it belongs.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The strand teaches Bill to ask after her day before dinner, the house, or the list. (2) The question asks how her day went, and it ends with mi corazón — my heart. (3) The question is: ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón?

questions.q: She asks Bill how he is, and the true answer that day is that he is a little tired. What does he say?
questions.teach: From the lesson: honest answers — this course teaches talking, not performing.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Estoy un poco cansado — I am a little tired. Un poco — a little, a bit. Say the whole true sentence: Estoy un poco cansado.' Another way: not estoy bien, which would be performing — the lesson wants the honest one.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Estoy cansado means I am tired, in the form a man uses for himself. (2) Un poco softens it: a little. (3) The true sentence is: Estoy un poco cansado.

questions.q: In your own words: why does Carmen teach that por qué — why — should be asked freely of things but gently of people?
questions.teach: From the lesson: por qué is a scalpel, not a hammer.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: '¿Por qué? asked of a machine is curiosity. ¿Por qué? asked of a tired woman at the end of a hard day can sound like a cross-examination, even when your heart means only love.'
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Asked of a machine or the world, por qué is plain curiosity. (2) Asked of a tired person at the end of a hard day, it can land like a cross-examination, even when the heart means love. (3) So Carmen's rule: ask it of things freely; of people, rarely, softly, and ready for the whole answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 10 — The past: telling someone what you did yesterday
paragraphs: Hola, Bill — hello, Bill. Soy Carmen — I am Carmen, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Sit down, mi estudiante — my student — because tonight we do something quietly miraculous. Tonight we learn to talk about yesterday. Think about what most of a real conversation actually is, Bill. It is not describing houses, and it is not even asking questions, though last lesson's questions are the keys that start it. Most of a real conversation — most of a marriage's conversation, at the table, at the door, at the end of the day — is this: telling someone what happened. What you did. Who you called. Where you went. How it went. Until today, your Spanish lived in the present tense, in the now. Today it grows a past. By the end of our thirty minutes you will be able to tell Jillian what you did yesterday — trabajé — I worked — llamé — I called — comí — I ate — dormí — I slept — in true, complete Spanish sentences, in the tense Spanish uses for a finished day. This tense has a name, and I will give it to you once, honestly, and then we will mostly ignore the name and learn the thing by feel, the way you have learned everything in this room: El pretérito — the preterite, the past tense for things that happened and finished. Say the idea, not the name: it happened, it is done, and now I am telling it. That is the pretérito. And as always, we speak first: I say it, you say it back to me out loud, the way you mean it, and only then do we move on. When I say say it with me, I want to hear you. Your voice is the instrument. Warm it up.

First, the signposts, because before you can tell a story about the past, you need the words that plant the story in the past — the little flags that tell your listener: we are not in today anymore. There are three, and they will carry almost every story you ever tell. Ayer — yesterday. Say it with me: Ayer. Ah-YEHR, two beats, and hear the soft y doing its work again. Ayer. Ayer is the flag for the whole day that just finished: ayer trabajé — yesterday I worked — and we will build that sentence together very soon. Second flag: Anoche — last night. Say it: Anoche. Ah-NOH-cheh. Anoche is ayer after dark: the night that just passed, the evening behind you. Anoche dormí — last night I slept — another sentence we will build today, word by word, until it is yours. And the third flag, the wide one: La semana pasada — last week. Semana — week. Pasada — past, gone by. La semana pasada: the week that has passed. Say it with me: La semana pasada. Three flags, three sizes of past: anoche for the night, ayer for the day, la semana pasada for the week. Plant one of these flags at the front of a sentence and your listener's mind walks back in time with you, ready for the story. Say the three flags in order, night, day, week: Anoche. Ayer. La semana pasada. Again: Anoche. Ayer. La semana pasada. Good. The flags are planted. Now we need the verbs that can live under them — and verbs, Bill, change their coats when they step into the past. That is the whole secret, and it is smaller than you fear.

Here is the idea, taught by feel, the Carmen way, and I want you to hold it loosely and trust your ear. In Spanish, when an action is finished — done, completed, in the past — the verb puts on its past coat, and for the verbs that end in ar, the coat for I, for yo — I — is a strong, clean ending: é — the sound EH with the accent leaning on it, the beat landing at the end of the word like a foot coming down at the end of a walk. Watch it happen to a verb you already own. Hablar — to speak, to talk. You met its family in lesson one inside llamo — I call myself — llamar — to call — same house, same family of talking words. In the present you might say hablo — I speak. But ayer — yesterday — finished, done, told tonight at the table, hablar puts on its past coat and becomes: Hablé — I spoke, I talked. Say it with me, and lean hard on that final beat, the way the accent tells you: Ha-blé. Hablé. Again, like the end of a story: Hablé. Ayer hablé — yesterday I spoke. Say the little sentence: Ayer hablé. And with the person who matters most in it: Hablé con Jillian — I spoke with Jillian. Con — with. Say it whole: Hablé con Jillian. Anoche hablé con Jillian — last night I spoke with Jillian. Say it: Anoche hablé con Jillian. Bill, stop and feel that. You just told me something that happened last night, in Spanish, in the past tense, in a complete true sentence. That is not a drill. That is narration. That is what storytellers do. And the coat fits more verbs than hablar — the next one is its own brother, and you own him already too.

Llamar — to call — the verb of lesson one, the llamar inside me llamo — my name is, I call myself. When calling steps into the finished past, llamar puts on the same é coat, neat as you please: Llamé — I called. Say it with me, leaning on the end: Lla-mé. Llamé. Hear the double l singing its soft y, the sound you tamed on your very first day: yah-MEH. Llamé. And its sentence, the sentence of a man who keeps his promises: Llamé a Jillian — I called Jillian. A — to, at — the little word Spanish puts before the person you called, a courtesy the language pays to people. Say it whole: Llamé a Jillian. Ayer llamé a Jillian — yesterday I called Jillian. Say it: Ayer llamé a Jillian. And now hold hablé and llamé side by side and look at them, because your ear is about to learn the pattern the way it learned buenos and buenas — by noticing, not by memorizing: Hablé. Llamé. Hablé. Llamé. Two different verbs, one same strong ending, one same lean at the end. So if X, then Y — hold onto that: if the verb ends in ar and the action is finished and it was you who did it, then the past coat ends in é, and your voice lands on that é like a period at the end of a sentence. You do not need the rule's grammar name. You need the sound in your mouth: hablé, llamé. Two verbs down, and the pattern is already standing up on its own legs. Say the pair one more time, both sentences, full and true: Ayer hablé con Jillian. Ayer llamé a Jillian. That is a man reporting his day, and we are only getting started.

Now the verb of your life, Bill — the verb of the business, the building, the providing, the man's day itself: Trabajar — to work. And in the finished past, wearing the same faithful é coat: Trabajé — I worked. Say it with me: Tra-ba-jé. Trabajé. Hear the j in the middle, the strong Spanish jota, a breath with muscle in it: trah-bah-HEH. Trabajé. Ayer trabajé — yesterday I worked. Say it like a man stating the plain truth of his life: Ayer trabajé. And with its measure on it, because some days deserve the measure: Trabajé mucho — I worked a lot. Mucho — much, a lot — the word from lesson one's mucho gusto — pleased to meet you — now measuring a day's labor. Say it: Trabajé mucho. Ayer trabajé mucho — yesterday I worked a lot. Say the whole honest line: Ayer trabajé mucho. That sentence, said at your own table, in Spanish, will be true more days than it is false, and Jillian — who works her own long days at the hospital — will hear in it a man who understands her days because he lives his own. Working is not a small topic between two people who both do it. It is half the story of a shared life. And now you can tell that half in Spanish. Next verb, and we stay with the é family for one more member, the pleasant one: Comprar — to buy. Finished, past, done: Compré — I bought. Say it: Com-pré. Compré. Ayer compré — yesterday I bought — and a sentence needs its treasure, so here is one worth buying: Compré flores — I bought flowers. Flores — flowers. Say it whole, and picture handing them over: Compré flores. Ayer compré flores para Jillian — yesterday I bought flowers for Jillian. Para — for. Say it: Ayer compré flores para Jillian. Hablé, llamé, trabajé, compré — say the family roll call with me, four brothers in the same coat: Hablé. Llamé. Trabajé. Compré. Again, faster, feeling the same landing every time: Hablé. Llamé. Trabajé. Compré. That landing, that accented é, is the sound of a finished action in Spanish. Your ear owns it now.

But Spanish would not be Spanish — honest, alive, a little musical — if every verb wore the same coat, so here come the second family, and I teach them to you by feel in the same breath. Verbs that end in er and ir — the eating and living verbs — put on a different past coat for I: í — the sound EE, accented, leaning, landing at the end just like its brother é, but singing higher. Comer — to eat — becomes: Comí — I ate. Say it with me: Co-mí. Comí. Comí bien — I ate well. Bien — well — from lesson nine's estoy bien — I am well. Say it: Comí bien. Ayer comí bien — yesterday I ate well. Say it whole: Ayer comí bien. And the last verb of the working day, the one that closes every story a tired man tells: Dormir — to sleep — becomes: Dormí — I slept. Say it: Dor-mí. Dormí. Anoche dormí — last night I slept. Say it, and notice how anoche and dormí were made for each other, the night flag and the sleeping verb, the most natural pair in this lesson: Anoche dormí. Anoche dormí bien — last night I slept well. Say it: Anoche dormí bien. Now hold the two families side by side, the way we held es and está, and let your ear keep them straight: the ar family lands on é — hablé, llamé, trabajé, compré — and the er and ir family lands on í — comí, dormí. É for the talking, calling, working, buying verbs. Í for the eating and sleeping verbs. Say both roll calls, one after the other: Hablé, llamé, trabajé, compré. Comí, dormí. Again: Hablé, llamé, trabajé, compré. Comí, dormí. Two sounds, six verbs, and every one of them is a true thing you did yesterday or will do tomorrow. That is not a vocabulary list, Bill. That is your day, in the past tense, in Spanish.

Two verbs remain, and they are the two that bring a man home. First: Llegar — to arrive, to get somewhere — and in the past: Llegué — I arrived, I got there. Say it with me: Lle-gué. Llegué. Look at that ending closely, because llegar does a small, tidy thing to stay pronounceable: its coat is gué, with a u standing guard so the g keeps its hard, good sound — lle-GEH, clean and strong. You do not need the spelling rule's name; you need the sound and the sentence, and the sentence is one of the most human sentences in any language: Llegué a casa — I got home, I arrived home. A casa — home, to the house — casa, our old friend from lesson eight, now meaning home the way it always secretly did. Say it whole, and feel the day land when you say it: Llegué a casa. Ayer llegué a casa — yesterday I got home. Say it: Ayer llegué a casa. Every working person on earth tells this sentence, in some language, on most days of their life: I worked, I traveled, I arrived home. It is the hinge of the day — everything before it is the world, everything after it is home. And now the rebel, the one verb in this lesson that refuses every coat we have sewn, and I flag him honestly, the way I promised you I always would: Ir — to go — in the past becomes: Fui — I went. Say it: Fui. One syllable, FWE, like nothing else in this lesson. Fui does not end in é. Fui does not end in í. Fui is fui — ir is the great irregular of Spanish, the rebel verb, and he is irregular in almost every language on earth, because the verb for going gets used so much that it wears its own path through the language like water through rock. English did the same thing, Bill: go and went are strangers to each other, and nobody apologizes for it. So do not fight fui. Adopt him. Fui a casa — I went home. Say it: Fui a casa. Fui a Key West — I went to Key West. Say it, and picture the road south with her: Fui a Key West. Ayer fui a casa — yesterday I went home. Say the rebel's sentences whole: Fui a casa. Fui a Key West. Ayer fui a casa. Good. Every family has one rebel, and the rebel is always the one you remember best. Fui will never leave you, precisely because he refused the coat.

Now let us put a whole day on its feet, because verbs in a row are a roll call, but verbs in an order are a story, and a story is what she actually wants at the table. Listen to a day told whole, in Spanish, with its flags planted and its verbs in their past coats, and I will walk beside it in English so you miss nothing. Ayer trabajé mucho — yesterday I worked a lot. Llamé a Jillian — I called Jillian. Hablé con Jillian — I spoke with Jillian. Compré flores — I bought flowers. Comí bien — I ate well. Llegué a casa — I got home. Anoche dormí bien — last night I slept well. Seven sentences. One day. Hear how the flags do their quiet work: ayer opens the day, anoche closes it, and in between, a man worked, called, talked, bought flowers for his prometida — his fiancée — ate, came home, and slept. Say the whole story with me now, sentence by sentence, out loud, like you are telling it across a real table: Ayer trabajé mucho. Llamé a Jillian. Hablé con Jillian. Compré flores. Comí bien. Llegué a casa. Anoche dormí bien. Again, slower, and this time feel the story in it, not the exercise: Ayer trabajé mucho. Llamé a Jillian. Compré flores. Llegué a casa. Anoche dormí bien. Bill, that is narration. A beginning, a middle, and a man asleep at the end of his own story. And la semana pasada — last week — stretches the same story wider whenever you need it: La semana pasada trabajé mucho — last week I worked a lot. La semana pasada fui a Key West — last week I went to Key West. Say those two: La semana pasada trabajé mucho. La semana pasada fui a Key West. Same coats, wider flag. The past is not a tense, mi estudiante. The past is a country, and today you got your passport.

And now the scene this whole lesson was built for — the other half of the evening conversation from lesson nine. Last lesson, you learned to ask her: ¿Cómo fue tu día, mi corazón? — how was your day, my heart? — and to listen: cuéntame — tell me — te escucho — I am listening to you. But a conversation has two tellings, and tonight you learn yours. She asks you back — she will, love returns questions — ¿cómo fue tu día? — how was your day? — and now, instead of a shrug and the word fine, you have a story in Spanish, three or four true sentences, and true is the whole art here. Not impressive sentences. True ones. Your day, yesterday's shape, told plainly: Ayer trabajé mucho — yesterday I worked a lot. Llamé a un cliente — I called a client. Cliente — a client, a customer. Compré flores para ti — I bought flowers for you. Para ti — for you — ti, you, the word that turns a sentence toward the person listening. And the closer, the sentence that ends every good day-story ever told: Llegué a casa — I got home. Say your four true sentences with me, as one telling, the way you will say them to her: Ayer trabajé mucho. Llamé a un cliente. Compré flores para ti. Llegué a casa. Again, and this time put her face in front of you while you say them — she is at the table, the day is landing on her the way hers landed on you last lesson: Ayer trabajé mucho. Llamé a un cliente. Compré flores para ti. Llegué a casa. Do you feel what changed, Bill? In lesson nine you learned to receive her day. In this lesson you learned to give her yours. Ask, listen, tell, be told. That is not a Spanish exercise. That is the whole liturgy of a shared life, and you can now do all four parts of it in Spanish.

Time for your guided try-it — the doing, taught here, with me beside you, the way we ran the viewing and the evening door. We will build your telling from your own true yesterday, in four moves, and I will show you the moves so you can rebuild it every night with whatever the day actually held. Move one: plant the flag. Ayer — yesterday — or anoche — last night — or la semana pasada — last week. Say your flag out loud: Ayer. Move two: the work sentence, the spine of a weekday. Trabajé — I worked — with mucho — a lot — if the day earned it: Ayer trabajé mucho. Say it. Move three: the people sentence, the heart of the day — who you called, who you spoke with: Llamé a Jillian. Hablé con Jillian. Say one of them, the true one: Llamé a Jillian. Move four: the home sentence, the landing — llegué a casa — I got home — and if the night was kind, anoche dormí bien — last night I slept well. Say the landing: Llegué a casa. Anoche dormí bien. Now run your whole telling, start to finish, your own voice, no stopping: Ayer trabajé mucho. Llamé a Jillian. Llegué a casa. Anoche dormí bien. Again — and if your real yesterday held something else, swap it in with the coats you own: comí bien if the food was good, compré flores if you were wise, fui a casa if the road was the story. The frame holds any true day you pour into it. That is the difference between a phrase and a power, Bill: a phrase says one thing; a power says your life, one day at a time, forever. Run it once more, whole, like a man at his own table: Ayer trabajé mucho. Llamé a Jillian. Llegué a casa. Anoche dormí bien. There it is. You just told me yesterday. In Spanish. And it was true.

Before we leave the workshop, sit with me for two minutes on the sound of these endings, because in the past tense your voice carries the grammar, and I want your telling to land clean when she hears it across the table. Every past coat you learned today ends in a lean: hablé leans on é, comí leans on í, and that lean is not decoration, it is the difference between the present and the past themselves. Listen to the pairs and feel it. Hablo — I speak, now, in the present. Hablé — I spoke, finished, yesterday. Como — I eat, now. Comí — I ate, finished, done. Say the pairs with me, present and past, now and then: Hablo. Hablé. Como. Comí. Hablo. Hablé. Como. Comí. Hear how the past versions land at the end like a door closing gently — that closing sound is the sound of a completed thing, and Spanish listeners hear it the way you hear the th in the past endings of English without ever thinking about it. And one kindness for your ear as you practice this week: the rebel keeps his own music too. Fui has no lean and needs none — one syllable, said plainly, fui, and the whole room knows you went. And llegué carries its guard u so its landing stays strong: lle-gué, never swallowed, never rushed. When you tell your day, slow down on the endings. The endings are where the past lives. Hablé. Trabajé. Comí. Dormí. Llegué. Fui. Say that final roll once more, slowly, landing every one: Hablé. Trabajé. Comí. Dormí. Llegué. Fui. That, Bill, is the drumbeat of every story you will ever tell her about a finished day, and your voice already knows the rhythm.

Before we gather it up, the hooks, quickly, the way we hang words so they stay hung. Dormí hangs on dormant — the English word for sleeping and waiting, asleep in the grass all winter; when you say dormí, hear dormant waking up and telling its story: I slept. Llamé hangs on lesson one itself — llamar, to call, the verb inside your own name sentence — so llamé is an old friend in a new coat, not a stranger. Compré hangs on the market and the till: every receipt you have ever been handed is a little compré waiting to be said out loud. Fui hangs on nothing, and that is his hook: the rebel is remembered because he is the rebel — go, went, ir, fui, the path water wore through the rock. And trabajé — trabajé hangs on the day itself, on your hands at the end of it. A word you say every night about a true thing does not need a hook, Bill. It has a home. Say the two roll calls one last time and hear the whole lesson inside them: Hablé, llamé, trabajé, compré — the é family, landing strong. Comí, dormí — the í family, singing higher. Llegué, the tidy guard at the gate. Fui, the rebel, walking his own road. That is the sound of the Spanish past, and it is in your mouth now.

So let us gather what you own, in order, one last time. The flags of the past: ayer — yesterday, anoche — last night, la semana pasada — last week — plant one and the story knows where it lives. The idea underneath everything: a finished action changes its coat, and for I, the ar family lands on é — hablé — I spoke, llamé — I called, trabajé — I worked, compré — I bought — while the er and ir family lands on í — comí — I ate, dormí — I slept. The homecoming: llegué a casa — I got home. And the rebel, honored, not fought: fui — I went — fui a casa, fui a Key West. And crowning it all, your telling, four true sentences at her table: Ayer trabajé mucho. Llamé a Jillian. Llegué a casa. Anoche dormí bien. That is lesson ten. You came into this course saying hola — hello — to the present moment, and tonight you walked into yesterday and told it back, in order, in Spanish, truthfully. Ay, do not argue with your profesora. I heard the story. It was a good day, and you told it well.

Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions: more than a few, all of them about what I taught you in this lesson and nothing else — nobody will ask you one single thing I did not teach. Most give you choices to pick from, and you can also answer out loud or type your answer, whichever you like. The lesson text stays open beside the questions, and if you want to read any part of it again before you answer, do it with my blessing: going back to read is learning, not cheating, and in this room it has always been learning. Your speaking practice lives in this lesson too: hear me say each phrase, then say it back until it lands. And your real assignment, tonight, at the table, after she tells you her day and asks about yours: three or four true sentences. No more, no performing, just true: Ayer trabajé mucho. Llamé a Jillian. Llegué a casa. Anoche dormí bien. Say them to her, and watch what happens to an ordinary evening when a man tells his day in the language of the heart — it stops being ordinary. Next lesson, we put time itself in your hands — the clock, the hours, saying when things happen — so your stories can carry not just the day, but the hour. Until then, mi estudiante: cuenta tu día — tell your day. Ayer ya es tuyo — yesterday is already yours.

questions.q: What does 'Ayer' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the three flags that plant a story in the past.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Ayer is the flag for the whole day that just finished: ayer trabajé — yesterday I worked — and we will build that sentence together very soon.' Another way: ayer opens the day in Bill's told story — ayer trabajé mucho.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson teaches three time flags: anoche, ayer, la semana pasada. (2) Anoche is the night and la semana pasada is the week. (3) The flag for the whole day that just finished, ayer, means: yesterday.

questions.q: What does 'Trabajé' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: trabajar in its past coat — the verb of Bill's day.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Trabajar — to work. And in the finished past, wearing the same faithful é coat: Trabajé — I worked.' Another way: ayer trabajé mucho — yesterday I worked a lot.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Trabajar means to work. (2) In the finished past, for I, it puts on the é coat and becomes trabajé. (3) Trabajé means: I worked.

questions.q: What does 'Anoche dormí bien' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the night flag and the sleeping verb — a natural pair.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Anoche dormí bien — last night I slept well. Say it: Anoche dormí bien.' Another way: anoche closes the day that ayer opened.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Anoche means last night. (2) Dormí means I slept, and bien means well. (3) The whole sentence means: last night I slept well.

questions.q: Which past-tense verb does Carmen call the rebel of the lesson?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the one verb that refuses every coat.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Fui is fui — ir is the great irregular of Spanish, the rebel verb, and he is irregular in almost every language on earth' Another way: English did the same thing — go and went are strangers to each other too.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Hablé, comí and llegué all wear a past coat with an accented ending. (2) One verb refuses both coats and goes its own way. (3) That rebel, from ir, to go, is: Fui.

questions.q: What does 'Llamé a Jillian' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: llamar — the verb of lesson one — in its past coat.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Llamé a Jillian — I called Jillian. A — to, at — the little word Spanish puts before the person you called' Another way: hablé con Jillian is speaking with her; llamé is the call itself.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Llamar means to call, and llamé is I called. (2) The little a stands before the person called, as a courtesy. (3) The sentence means: I called Jillian.

questions.q: Carmen teaches that verbs ending in ar, for 'I' in the finished past, land on one strong accented ending. What is that ending?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the pattern your ear learns by noticing — hablé, llamé, trabajé, compré.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'if the verb ends in ar and the action is finished and it was you who did it, then the past coat ends in é, and your voice lands on that é like a period at the end of a sentence' Another way: the í ending belongs to the other family — comí, dormí.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Hablé, llamé, trabajé and compré are all ar verbs in the past, for I. (2) They share one landing sound at the end. (3) That shared, accented ending is: é.

questions.q: What does 'Comí bien' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: comer in the í family — the eating and sleeping verbs.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Comí bien — I ate well. Bien — well — from lesson nine's estoy bien — I am well. Say it: Comí bien.' Another way: ayer comí bien — yesterday I ate well.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Comer means to eat, and in the past for I it becomes comí. (2) Bien means well. (3) Comí bien means: I ate well.

questions.q: What does 'La semana pasada' mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: the widest of the three past flags.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'La semana pasada — last week. Semana — week. Pasada — past, gone by. La semana pasada: the week that has passed.' Another way: it stretches the same told story wider — la semana pasada trabajé mucho.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Semana means week. (2) Pasada means past, gone by. (3) Together, la semana pasada means: last week.

questions.q: Bill wants to tell Jillian that he got home yesterday. What does he say?
questions.teach: From the lesson: llegué a casa — the homecoming, the hinge of the day.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Ayer llegué a casa — yesterday I got home. Say it: Ayer llegué a casa.' Another way: everything before this sentence is the world; everything after it is home.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) The flag for yesterday is ayer. (2) Llegué a casa means I got home. (3) Joined, his sentence is: Ayer llegué a casa.

questions.q: Which sentence tells Jillian that Bill bought flowers for her?
questions.teach: From the lesson: his telling at her table — true sentences, aimed at the listener.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Compré flores para ti — I bought flowers for you. Para ti — for you — ti, you, the word that turns a sentence toward the person listening.' Another way: compré is I bought, flores is flowers, and para ti puts them in her hands.
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Compré flores says he bought flowers, but not who they are for. (2) Para ti means for you — it turns the sentence toward Jillian. (3) The sentence that tells her is: Compré flores para ti.

questions.q: In your own words: what are the four moves Carmen teaches for building the nightly telling of your day?
questions.teach: From the lesson: a frame that holds any true day you pour into it.
questions.teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'We will build your telling from your own true yesterday, in four moves, and I will show you the moves so you can rebuild it every night with whatever the day actually held.'
questions.walk: Walk it through: (1) Move one: plant the flag — ayer, anoche, or la semana pasada. (2) Move two: the work sentence — trabajé. (3) Move three: the people sentence — llamé or hablé. (4) Move four: the home sentence — llegué a casa, and anoche dormí bien if the night was kind.

lessons.title: Lesson 11 — The future: plans, promises, and voy a…
paragraphs: Hola, Bill. Soy la profesora Carmen Vega — I am Professor Carmen Vega, and welcome back to your Spanish room. Come in, sit down, and take a breath with me, because today we do something we have been walking toward since your very first hola — hello. Until now, most of what you own in Spanish lives in today: who you are, where you are from, what your people are called, how her day went, what is for dinner. Today we open the door that stands in front of today. This is the lesson of the future: plans, promises, and voy a… — I am going to. By the end of our time together you will be able to say what you are going to do tomorrow morning, what you are going to do for your business, what you are going to say to Jillian tonight, and — hold this one in your heart — how to say, in Spanish, that the two of you are going to get married. One small pattern is going to unlock all of that. One pattern, Bill. Not ten rules. Not a chart to memorize while your eyes glaze over. One key, and the whole future turns in the lock.

Let me tell you plainly why this lesson is worth knowing, because I never ask you to learn anything without telling you why. A man who can only speak about today is a man trapped in today. He can greet, he can thank, he can name what is on the table — and all of that is beautiful, and you do it well — but he cannot make a plan out loud. He cannot promise. He cannot say, tomorrow I will be there, next year we will be in our house, one day we will laugh about how hard this season was. Promises live in the future. Plans live in the future. A wedding, mi estudiante — my student — lives entirely in the future until the day it arrives and becomes the present in a white dress. So today we go and get the future, and we bring it back in one pattern you can carry in your pocket for the rest of your life.

And here is the mercy of Spanish, and I want you to hear this before we touch a single verb: Spanish has a complicated, formal future — the kind with special endings that students wrestle for weeks — and real people, in real kitchens and real workplaces, mostly do not use it for everyday plans. Real people use the pattern you are learning today. A mother in a doorway, a boss on a job site, a bride making a list at midnight — they say voy a… — I am going to… — and then they name the action, plain and whole. It is the future of daily life. It is honest, it is warm, and it is the first future any teacher with a heart teaches, because you can use it tonight.
So let us build it, slowly, piece by piece, the way we build everything in this room: I say it, you say it back to me out loud, and only then do we move on.

First, the key itself, alone, before we hang anything on it: Voy a… — I am going to… Voy comes from the verb ir — to go. I want you to feel that in your bones, because English does the exact same trick and you have been doing it all your life without noticing. In English you say, I am going to work — and no, you do not only mean your feet are traveling. You mean the work is ahead of you, in front of you, coming. Spanish says it the same way: voy — I go, or I am going — and then a — to — and then the action, named whole. Voy a… Say it with me, just the key, turning in the lock: Voy a… Again, slower, like you are about to announce something that matters: Voy a… One more time, easy and natural: Voy a… Good. That little phrase, voy a, is the engine. Everything else today is just choosing where the engine takes you.

Now, what rides after voy a? The action, in its whole, untouched form — the form Spanish calls the infinitive — the infinitive. Do not let that word frighten you; you already own a shelf of these and you have been saying them inside other sentences all course long without knowing their name. An infinitive is a verb before anybody has touched it: not I, not you, not we — just the action itself, pure. Hablar — to speak. Comer — to eat. Vivir — to live. In English the little word to does that job: to speak, to eat, to live. In Spanish, the ending of the word does it, and most of the verbs you will ever need end in one of three coats: ar, er, or ir. Trabajar — to work — wears the ar coat. Comer — to eat — wears the er coat. Vivir — to live — wears the ir coat. You do not have to change a thing about these words when they ride after voy a. That is the whole generosity of this pattern, so hear me say it twice: after voy a, the action stays whole. Voy a, plus the whole action, equals the future. If you can say voy a, and you can name one action, you can make a future sentence. So if the pattern is voy a plus a whole action, then any action you learn from today onward is instantly a future you can speak — hold onto that, because it means this lesson never stops growing.

Let us prove it with the sentence your life needs most on a weekday morning: Voy a trabajar — I am going to work. Trabajar — to work. You know this word's family already; trabajo — work, the job itself — has been in our room before, and trabajar is that same word standing up and moving. Voy a trabajar. Say it with me: Voy a trabajar. Again, like a man with a business to build and a reason to build it: Voy a trabajar. Now let us dress it with time, because a plan without a time is a wish. Mañana — tomorrow. Voy a trabajar mañana — I am going to work tomorrow. Say it: Voy a trabajar mañana. And with the morning inside it: Mañana por la mañana — tomorrow morning. Voy a trabajar mañana por la mañana — I am going to work tomorrow morning. Hear how nothing changed in the engine: voy a trabajar stayed exactly itself, and the time words just climbed aboard at the end. That will be true all lesson long. The pattern does not wobble when you add to it. It just carries more.

Stay at work with me a moment, because your future is not abstract, Bill — it has an office and a name and people counting on it. Here is a small toolbox of actions for the working day, each one whole, each one ready to ride. Llamar — to call. Escribir — to write. Hablar — to speak. Escuchar — to listen. Ayudar — to help. Construir — to build. Aprender — to learn. Enseñar — to teach, and also to show. Now watch the key turn, over and over, the same every time. Voy a llamar — I am going to call. Voy a escribir — I am going to write. Voy a hablar — I am going to speak. Voy a escuchar — I am going to listen. Voy a ayudar — I am going to help. Voy a construir — I am going to build. Voy a aprender — I am going to learn. Say two of them with me, out loud, your choice living in your mouth: Voy a ayudar. Voy a construir. Do you feel it? You are not conjugating anything. You are not hunting through endings. You learned one engine and a handful of actions, and suddenly you own a whole working future. That is why I teach this pattern with such love: it pays you back immediately, in sentences about your actual life.

Now let us make it tender, because the most important calls in your life are not business calls. Here is the sentence I promised you at the door: Voy a llamarte — I am going to call you. Look closely, because something sweet just happened to llamar — to call. The little word te — you — the same te from te quiero — I love you — has attached itself to the end of the action, like a hand slipping into a pocket. Llamar plus te makes llamarte — to call you. Voy a llamarte: I am going to call you. Spanish lets you glue that little word right onto the whole action, and the sentence stays soft and natural — it is exactly how a man tells his prometida — his fiancée — that her phone will ring. Say it with me, slowly first: Voy a… llamarte. Voy a llamarte. Again, at the speed of a promise made in a kitchen doorway: Voy a llamarte. And dressed for tonight: Esta noche — tonight. Voy a llamarte esta noche — I am going to call you tonight. Say it: Voy a llamarte esta noche. Bill, that is a complete, romantic, useful sentence, and an hour ago you could not have built it. Notice what you did not do: you did not change llamar at all. You just let te ride at the end. The engine pulled the whole train.

While te is sitting there shining, let me show you its brother, because you will need him before this lesson ends. Me — me — can ride in the same seat. And when the action is something two people do to themselves, together, Spanish uses nos — us, or ourselves. Hold nos in your hand for one minute. We are going somewhere beautiful with him.

Because now we turn the key from I to we, and mi estudiante, this is where this lesson stops being grammar and starts being your life. When the subject is we — you and her, the two of you, the team this whole course is secretly about — voy changes its coat: Vamos a… — we are going to… Vamos comes from that same verb ir — to go — and vamos is its we form; it is also, all by itself, the joyful shout of let us go, which tells you everything about its energy. Vamos a… Say it with me: Vamos a… Again, like a man taking his future wife by the hand: Vamos a… And now, the sentence. The sentence this lesson was built to give you, the one I have been saving since I welcomed you in: Vamos a casarnos — we are going to get married. Take it apart with me slowly, because every piece of it is doing honest work. Casar — to marry. Casarnos — to marry each other, to get married — with that little nos — ourselves, each other — riding at the end, the two of you folded into the very end of the word. Vamos a casarnos: we are going to get married. Say it with me, piece by piece first: Vamos a… casarnos. Vamos a casarnos. Again, whole, at the speed of a man who means it: Vamos a casarnos. One more time, quieter, the way you might say it to her when the house is finally still: Vamos a casarnos.

And because a wedding does not float in the air — it has a date and a place, and you know both — let us dress the sentence the way we dressed your work this morning. El próximo año — next year. Próximo means next, the one coming; año means year. Vamos a casarnos el próximo año — we are going to get married next year. Say it: Vamos a casarnos el próximo año. And the place, because Key West deserves to be named in Spanish in this room: En Key West — in Key West. Vamos a casarnos en Key West — we are going to get married in Key West. Say the full, true sentence with me now, all of it, date and place and promise together: Vamos a casarnos el próximo año en Key West. Bill. Stop there a second. That is not an exercise. That is a fact about your life, spoken in Spanish, correctly, by you. March of next year is coming whether we speak about it or not — but now, when it comes, you can say it coming. There is a difference, and the difference is everything this course is for.

Let us widen the wedding out into the life around it, because vamos a is not a one-sentence trick — it is the sound of the two of you planning a life. Vamos a celebrar — we are going to celebrate. Celebrar — to celebrate. Vamos a viajar — we are going to travel. Viajar — to travel. Vamos a bailar — we are going to dance. Bailar — to dance — and yes, I am putting dancing in your future on purpose, groom. Vamos a comer — we are going to eat — comer, your old friend, to eat. Say the run with me, like a list the two of you are making at the kitchen table: Vamos a celebrar. Vamos a viajar. Vamos a bailar. Vamos a comer. Hear the rhythm of it: vamos a never changes, the actions parade past, and every single one is a plan the two of you can actually make. That is what a future tense is for. Not examinations. Kitchen tables.

Now, the time words deserve their own careful minute, because the future needs signposts, and Spanish keeps them simple and beautiful. You have met mañana — tomorrow — and esta noche — tonight — and el próximo año — next year. Here are the three this lesson adds to your pocket, and I want each one to land. Pronto — soon. Pronto is a warm word; it does not promise a date, it promises nearness. Voy a llamarte pronto — I am going to call you soon. Say it: Voy a llamarte pronto. Hoy — today. Voy a trabajar hoy — I am going to work today. And the dreamer of the family: Un día — one day, someday. Un día is where the big hopes live, the ones without dates yet. Un día, vamos a… — one day, we are going to… Un día is not a lie and it is not a plan; it is a direction, and a life needs directions as much as it needs dates. Say it with me, the whole hopeful shape: Un día, vamos a viajar — one day, we are going to travel. Un día, vamos a viajar. Good. So here is your signpost shelf, in order, near to far: hoy — today; esta noche — tonight; pronto — soon; mañana — tomorrow; el próximo año — next year; un día — one day. Six signposts, and every future sentence you ever make can borrow one. If a sentence names when, then it is a plan — hold onto that. If it does not name when, Spanish still understands you, but a named time is what turns wishing into scheduling, and you, Bill, are a man who schedules.

Now we climb one step higher, from plans to promises — because a plan says what is going to happen, but a promise says what you will make happen, and Spanish marks that difference with a phrase I want you to own completely: Te prometo… — I promise you… Prometo comes from prometer — to promise — and notice that your old friend prometida — fiancée, the promised one — lives inside this family too. The woman you are promised to, and the promises you make to her, share a root in Spanish, because in this language they were never separate ideas. Te prometo: I promise you. Say it with me, slowly, like a vow is supposed to be said: Te prometo… Again: Te prometo… Now, what rides after te prometo is a whole clause — a whole little sentence — and the most natural way to build it, at your level and honestly at any level, is with our key: te prometo, and then voy a, and then the action. Watch: Te prometo que voy a llamarte — I promise you that I am going to call you. Que — that — is the little bridge between the promise and the thing promised. Say it: Te prometo que voy a llamarte. And one with more weight in it: Te prometo que voy a ayudarte — I promise you that I am going to help you. Ayudarte — to help you — ayudar with te riding at the end, the way llamarte did. Say it: Te prometo que voy a ayudarte. Hear how the promise and the plan lock together: prometo makes it sacred, voy a makes it concrete. A promise without a plan is weather talk. A plan inside a promise is a man keeping his word in advance.

Let me give you three promises sized for real life, and I want you to say each one like Jillian is standing in the doorway hearing it — because one day soon, she will be. Te prometo que voy a estar aquí — I promise you that I am going to be here. Estar — to be, in the sense of being somewhere, being present — and aquí — here. For a woman who works the hard shifts she works, estar aquí, being here when she comes home, is not a small promise. Say it: Te prometo que voy a estar aquí. Second: Te prometo que vamos a estar bien — I promise you that we are going to be fine, that we are going to be okay. Bien — well, fine, okay. When money is tight and the season is heavy, this is the sentence. Say it with me: Te prometo que vamos a estar bien. Third, and say this one to the mirror if you have to: Te prometo que voy a aprender — I promise you that I am going to learn. Aprender — to learn. This whole course is that promise, kept a lesson at a time. Say it: Te prometo que voy a aprender. Good. Now you understand the architecture: plans tell the future, promises guarantee it, and voy a is the beam that holds up both houses.

It is time to do, not just listen — this is our try-it moment, and I will narrate while you speak your parts out loud, the way we always do. Picture tomorrow, hour by hour, and answer me in Spanish as I walk you through your own day. Morning comes. You have work that matters. Tell me: what are you going to do? … Voy a trabajar. Yes. The phone sits beside you and the most important person in your world is across town. What are you going to do tonight? … Voy a llamarte esta noche. Beautiful — and if she is the one across from you, say it to her face, the way you just did. Now the two of you, at the table, looking at next year. What are the two of you going to do in Key West? … Vamos a casarnos. There it is. And after the wedding, with the music still in your ears? … Vamos a celebrar. Vamos a bailar. And now the promise, the one that turns today into a vow: tell her you promise you will be here. … Te prometo que voy a estar aquí. Bill, listen to what just happened: you planned a morning, promised a phone call, married yourself in a sentence, celebrated, danced, and made a vow — five futures, one key, zero charts. That is not a student reciting. That is a man speaking about his life in the future tense.

Before we gather it all up, let me hand you the true sentences — the set I want living in your house after this lesson ends, each one a fact about your actual future, stated in Spanish. Say each one after me, and notice that not one of them is pretend. Voy a trabajar mañana — I am going to work tomorrow. Vamos a casarnos en Key West — we are going to get married in Key West. Voy a llamarte esta noche — I am going to call you tonight. Vamos a comprar una casa — we are going to buy a house. Comprar — to buy; una casa — a house. Say it again, because that one deserves a second saying: Vamos a comprar una casa. Voy a construir mi negocio — I am going to build my business. Negocio — business. Un día, vamos a viajar — one day, we are going to travel. Te prometo que vamos a estar bien — I promise you that we are going to be fine. Seven sentences. Work, wedding, the nightly call, the house, the business, the journey, and the promise underneath them all. If you owned nothing else from this lesson — and you own much more — those seven sentences would carry your future in Spanish for years.

One small warning before we gather it all up, because I would rather warn you in this room than let the street surprise you. The only real mistake people make with this pattern is mixing up the two engines: voy a is for I — one man, alone, speaking about himself — and vamos a is for we — two or more, the team speaking about itself. Voy a llamarte — I am going to call you — because one man holds the phone. Vamos a casarnos — we are going to get married — because, ay, Bill, nobody marries himself; it takes the two of you, and the verb knows it. So before any future sentence leaves your mouth, ask one tiny question: is this future mine alone, or is it ours? Mine alone: voy a. Ours: vamos a. That one question, asked for one second, will keep every plan and every promise you ever make in Spanish standing straight. And notice, too, what never changes between them: the a, and the whole action after it. Trabajar stays trabajar whether you say voy a trabajar about your morning or the two of you say vamos a trabajar about a Saturday project together. The engine's front changes its coat; the cargo never moves.

Let me give you one more scene to carry, a quiet one, because futures are not only made at weddings and work desks — they are made on ordinary weekends, in ordinary kitchens, and those are the futures that become a life. Picture a Saturday, the two of you, coffee on the table, the week finally loosened its grip. She asks what the day holds, and now you can answer her in Spanish, piece by piece, a whole morning of plans. Vamos a descansar — we are going to rest. Descansar — to rest — and after her shifts and your long weeks, rest is not laziness, it is a plan worth naming out loud. Vamos a comer juntos — we are going to eat together. Juntos — together — a small word that turns eating into an occasion. Voy a cocinar — I am going to cook. Cocinar — to cook — one man, one kitchen, one meal made on purpose. Vamos a hablar — we are going to talk — hablar, to speak, the two of you with nowhere to rush. Say the little run with me, slowly, the way a Saturday morning deserves: Vamos a descansar. Vamos a comer juntos. Voy a cocinar. Vamos a hablar. Hear how the two engines take turns, natural as breathing: ours, ours, mine, ours. That alternation — what I will do, what we will do — is the exact rhythm of a shared life, and you can now keep that rhythm in Spanish.

So let us gather what you own now, in order, one last time. Voy a… — I am going to… — the engine: voy from ir, to go, plus a, plus the action whole and untouched. The action stays whole after voy a — trabajar, llamar, comer, vivir — no endings to hunt, ever. Voy a trabajar — I am going to work. Voy a llamarte — I am going to call you — with te riding at the end of the action. Vamos a… — we are going to… — the we form, for the two of you. Vamos a casarnos — we are going to get married — the sentence of the lesson, with nos folded into its end. The signposts: hoy, esta noche, pronto, mañana, el próximo año, un día — today, tonight, soon, tomorrow, next year, one day. And standing above the plans, the promises: te prometo que voy a… — I promise you that I am going to… — the vow with a plan inside it. One key opened all of that. You turned it yourself.

That is lesson eleven, and you did beautifully — ay, do not argue with your profesora, I heard those futures, and they were yours. Here is what happens next. Below this lesson are your questions: more than a few, all of them about what I actually taught you in this lesson and nothing else — nobody is going to ask you one single thing I did not teach. Most of them give you choices to pick from, and you can also answer out loud or type your answer, whichever door you like. The lesson text stays open beside the questions, and if you want to read a part of it again before you answer, do it with my blessing — that is what it is there for, and going back to read is learning, not cheating. Your speaking practice is here in the lesson too: hear me say each phrase, then say it back until it lands. And then, Bill, there is only one lesson left in Spanish One — our last one together in this course — and you already know what it has to be. Next time, we put everything you own into one whole, gentle conversation, start to finish, the conversation this entire course has been aiming at since the day you said hola. Tonight, your assignment is one true sentence, said out loud, to her: Voy a llamarte esta noche — and then, mi estudiante, you call her. Te prometo — I promise you — she will smile. Hasta pronto — see you soon. Say it back to me: hasta pronto. And go make your future in Spanish.
